title: No Stipulated Holdover Premium
bodyText: Delaware sets its own measure for a tenant who stays after the tenancy ends without your consent: a sum of up to double the monthly rent under the old lease, prorated daily, plus any further losses a court finds. Because the statute caps the daily sum, the library offers no clause stipulating a higher or fixed premium holdover rate for Delaware; a lease figure above double the rent would conflict with the statute, and a figure at or below it adds little to what a court can already award. Remember that a lease of a year or more becomes month to month if neither side gives the required notice (60 days from you, 45 days from the tenant), so a tenant who stays on in that case is not a holdover. A landlord who wants a fixed holdover figure within the statutory cap can add their own clause, and should take advice first.

title: Tenant Chores Need a Separate Agreement
bodyText: In Delaware, if you want a tenant to take on specified repairs or maintenance tasks, such as lawn care, landscaping, snow removal, filter changes or other chores, put them in a conspicuous writing separate from the lease, signed separately, and give the tenant adequate consideration for it apart from the lease (for example a rent reduction). The work must be for the primary benefit of the rental unit, cannot be work needed to bring the unit up to building or housing code, and you cannot make the agreement a condition of the lease. Delaware has no exception for single-family homes, so the library does not put lawn or snow chores in the lease itself; use the optional Tenant Maintenance Agreement, printed as its own document. The tenant's own statutory duties (keeping the part of the premises they occupy clean and safe, disposing of garbage, using facilities reasonably and not damaging the property) need no separate agreement.

title: Snow Removal
bodyText: Delaware's statutes don't assign snow and ice removal at a rental property to either party, but they do say how a tenant can take on a maintenance task: only by a conspicuous writing separate from the lease, with consideration apart from the lease. If you want the tenant to clear walks, driveways and steps, use the optional Tenant Maintenance Agreement as its own signed document; otherwise plan to do it yourself. Your duties to keep common areas clean and the premises safe stay with you, and some towns have their own sidewalk-clearing ordinances.

title: Payment Methods and Third-Party Rent Payments in Delaware
bodyText: Delaware does not regulate which payment methods you accept or bar fees for a particular method, but three rules apply. You may limit rent payments to the methods your lease accepts, yet you may not refuse a rent payment made by the tenant or by someone else on the tenant's behalf. After you file for nonpayment and before judgment, you may still insist on the lease's methods, and once a judgment for possession is entered you may require a certified check or money order; but in a nonpayment eviction neither limit applies to a payment from a charitable organization or government entity, and its electronic or written check counts as the tenant's own payment. You must keep an office or other permanent place in the county where the unit is located where rent can be paid; if you do not, the tenant gets 3 extra days past the due date. If you accept cash rent, give a receipt within 15 days and keep cash-receipt records for 3 years. Because the lease defines the accepted methods, list them in the lease; changing them mid-term by notice alone is risky where the change is a substantial modification.

title: No Delaware Algorithmic Rent-Setting Statute
bodyText: Delaware has no statute that bans or regulates using algorithmic or revenue-management software to set rents, and none on sharing rent or occupancy data with other landlords. Delaware's general antitrust law still makes every contract, combination or conspiracy in restraint of trade unlawful, and it is read in harmony with federal antitrust law, so agreeing with competitors, directly or through a shared pricing tool, to coordinate rents carries antitrust risk. No lease clause is needed.

title: Delaware Application Fee Cap and Screening Rules
bodyText: You may charge an applicant a fee to check credit worthiness, but it may not exceed the greater of 10 percent of the monthly rent or $50. Delaware also bars charging more than the specific cost of a credit or other investigation, so charge only your actual screening cost and never more than that cap. Give the applicant a receipt for the full amount paid and keep complete records of application fees for at least 2 years; keep each application's records for 6 months. If you demand more than the allowed fee, the applicant can recover double the fee charged. Apart from the application fee, you may take only a security deposit, a surety bond fee or premium, a pet deposit, or a deposit reserving the unit for a set time; any other up-front assurance money is prohibited. Delaware has no rule requiring you to refund an unused fee or to disclose screening criteria in advance, but your income and credit standards must be applied in a commercially reasonable way and without regard to source of income.

title: No Delaware Statute Authorizing Collection Fees
bodyText: Delaware's statutes do not authorize a landlord to add a collection-agency fee to a tenant's unpaid rent or damages, and they do not set a fee or a lease condition for one. Any lease term making the tenant pay attorneys' fees is unenforceable in Delaware, and a lease term that conflicts with the Landlord-Tenant Code and is not expressly authorized by it is unenforceable, so do not rely on a collection-fee clause. If you refer a debt to a collector, claim only the rent, late charges and damages the Code allows; a collection agency's own conduct is governed by federal debt-collection law.

title: No Delaware Rental Fee-Disclosure Statute
bodyText: Delaware has no rental fee-transparency statute: no all-in rent figure, no total-price advertising rule, and no required first-page fee list. General consumer law still applies to leases. Concealing or omitting a material fact about a rental with intent that the renter rely on it is an unlawful practice under the Consumer Fraud Act, and in a consumer lease of $50,000 or less it is a deceptive practice to knowingly or recklessly obscure terms with unintelligible wording. Separately, the only nonrefundable fee you may charge as a condition of occupancy is an optional fee for services actually provided, such as a pool or tennis-court fee. Best practice is to state the rent and every recurring or optional charge plainly in the lease. Delaware's automatic-renewal disclosure and reminder rules for consumer contracts do not apply to residential leases; lease renewals follow the Landlord-Tenant Code's notice rules. But if your lease itself renews automatically and its total price is $50,000 or less, the consumer-contract law still makes it a deceptive practice to knowingly or recklessly fail to give the tenant a cost-effective, timely and easy way to cancel.

title: Fees Only for Services Actually Provided
bodyText: Delaware bars every nonrefundable fee as a condition of occupancy except an optional fee for services actually rendered, such as a pool or tennis-court fee. So any amenity or service fee must be optional for the tenant and must pay for a service you actually provide; do not charge for a service you do not supply. If you bill utilities to the tenant, you may not charge more than your actual cost. Charging for services you promised but do not provide can also be an unlawful practice under Delaware's Consumer Fraud Act.

title: Which Charges Count as Rent in Delaware
bodyText: Delaware does not define rent broadly, and no statute lets a lease turn any fee into rent by labelling it. The Code itself makes these charges rent: late charges (as additional rent), utility charges you bill to the tenant, the cost of a requested meter test that shows the meter is accurate, and your bill for remedying a tenant's breach of a rule (due as additional rent on receipt). These can be included in a nonpayment demand and a rent action. Other fees, such as amenity or pet fees, are safest treated as separate charges that you collect by a breach notice or a damages claim rather than a rent demand. A lease may not make the tenant pay your attorneys' fees, even if it calls them rent. For federally subsidized units, federal rules control where they conflict.

title: No Delaware Rule on Passing Government Fees to Tenants
bodyText: Delaware has no statute on whether you may make a tenant reimburse you for a government fee on the property, such as a city rental license, registration or inspection fee. Because Delaware bars any nonrefundable fee as a condition of occupancy other than an optional fee for services actually provided, a lease clause requiring the tenant to repay your licensing fee is risky; recover the cost through the rent instead. A lease may allocate property taxes to the tenant, and a tenant who pays a property tax without such an agreement may set it off against rent. Check local ordinances for rental-license fees and any limits on passing them on.

title: Counting Delaware's Late-Charge Grace Period
bodyText: Delaware's late-charge rule has counting details that matter. A late charge is allowed only if the lease provides for one, may not exceed 5 percent of the monthly rent (there is no flat-dollar alternative), and may not be imposed within 5 days of the due date, or within 8 days if you keep no office or other permanent place in the county where rent can be paid. Under the Code's time rule, the due date itself is not counted, a period that ends on a Saturday, Sunday or legal holiday runs to the next business day, and for periods shorter than 7 days the intermediate Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays are skipped, so the 5-day window usually covers more than 5 calendar days. Late charges count as additional rent, so once the tenant pays all rent and late charges due before you file, you may not file for possession over that nonpayment. Delaware has no special late-fee grace rules for seniors, benefit recipients or federal workers, and no required advance notice of the fee.

title: Delaware Late Charge Cap
bodyText: Delaware caps a residential late charge at 5 percent of the monthly rent, and you may charge one only if the lease provides for it. You may not impose it within 5 days of the due date, or within 8 days if you keep no office or other permanent place in the county where rent can be paid. A late charge counts as additional rent. Any lease term setting a higher fee or an earlier charge is unenforceable in Delaware.

title: No Delaware Lease-Type Parity Rule
bodyText: Delaware does not require the same rent or terms for month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies and does not cap the difference between them, so you may price them differently, provided the difference is not based on a protected class. The Code itself sets some differences: a lease with no stated term is month-to-month; both types end on 60 days' written notice, but for month-to-month the 60 days start on the first day of the month after notice; the one-month security deposit cap applies to leases of 1 year or more, and to month-to-month or undefined tenancies once they have lasted a year (any excess must then be credited back); and a deposit increase of more than 10 percent of the rent is spread over the lease term, or over 4 months for a month-to-month tenancy.

title: No Delaware Rent Concession Statute
bodyText: Delaware has no statute on rent concessions such as a free month or move-in discount. If you give one, state it in the lease with its amount and the months it covers. Be careful with recapture terms: if a tenant abandons, Delaware limits your claim to the lesser of the remaining rent or your actual re-renting losses and requires you to mitigate, and if a tenant ends the lease early under one of the Code's statutory grounds, your re-renting claim against the deposit is capped at one month's rent. A clause making the full concession due on any default, or forfeiting it for late payment, may be unenforceable or may act as a late charge above the 5 percent cap.

title: No Statewide Rent Control in Delaware
bodyText: Delaware has no rent control or cap on rent increases for apartments and houses rented under the Landlord-Tenant Code, and no state statute was found that preempts local rent, rental-registration or inspection ordinances, so check your city or county code. Rent is whatever you and the tenant agree. Increases are still limited in other ways: an increase within 90 days after a tenant's good-faith code complaint, tenant organizing or exercise of a legal right is presumed retaliatory; an increase demanded of a tenant who is a victim of domestic abuse, sexual offenses or stalking and has sought help is barred, and within 90 days of an incident is presumed unlawful unless you show a statutory ground such as a tax or cost increase or comparable rents; you may not charge more rent for a protected fair-housing reason, including source of income; and a renewal at a higher rent needs at least 60 days' written notice. Tenants can petition a Justice of the Peace Court for a receivership when essential services or dangerous conditions go uncorrected, and the State Housing Authority can seek a custodianship over developments it finances. Manufactured home communities have separate rent-increase rules not covered here.

title: Collecting Rent When Repairs Are Outstanding
bodyText: Delaware does not forbid you outright from demanding or collecting rent while the unit has code violations, but unrepaired conditions sharply limit what you can collect. After written notice, a tenant may end the lease if you do not fix a condition that substantially deprives them of the bargain within 15 days, or immediately if the unit is uninhabitable or an imminent threat to health or safety; may repair and deduct up to the lesser of $400 or half a month's rent after 30 days (or 10 days without corrective steps); and, if heat, hot water, water or electricity fail for 48 hours after notice, may keep two-thirds of the daily rent or obtain substitute housing while rent abates. Rent also abates while you fail to deliver possession. Once Delaware's lead-safe certification chapter takes effect, you will need to file proof of lead compliance with any eviction complaint.

title: Mid-Term Rent Increases in Delaware
bodyText: Delaware has no statute written for rent escalation clauses. During a fixed term the rent is what the lease says, so an increase before the term ends is possible only if the lease itself states the new amounts and dates or an exact formula; otherwise you may change the rent only at renewal on at least 60 days' written notice. Any increase demanded within 90 days after a tenant's good-faith code complaint, tenant organizing or exercise of a legal right is presumed retaliatory, but you have a defence if the increase passes through a substantial tax or operating-cost increase you became liable for at least 4 months earlier, recovers a substantial capital improvement on a straight-line depreciation basis, or does not exceed the rent for similar units in the same complex. These defences do not depend on the lease having an escalation clause.

title: Delaware Rent Increase and Renewal Notice
bodyText: To raise the rent or change other terms at renewal, give the tenant at least 60 days' written notice before the lease expires, stating each changed term, the new rent or deposit and the date the change takes effect. Unless the tenant gives notice of termination at least 45 days before the last day of the term, the new terms are treated as accepted; a tenant who rejects them is treated as having given notice to end the lease. The rule covers fixed-term leases and, on its wording, month-to-month tenancies, so give 60 days before the end of a monthly period. You cannot raise rent during a fixed term unless the lease itself provides for it. These rules do not apply where HUD rules set the rent based on income. Delaware has no emergency price-gouging cap on rent.

title: Rent Installments in Delaware
bodyText: Delaware lets you and the tenant agree when and where rent is paid, so a lease may split the monthly rent into scheduled installments. Without an agreement, rent for a term of a month or less is due in full at the start, and for a longer term one month's rent is due at the start of each month. Keep late charges within the statutory limits: no more than 5 percent of the monthly rent in total, and none within 5 days of each installment's agreed due date.

title: Cash Rent Receipts in Delaware
bodyText: If you accept rent in cash, give the tenant a receipt within 15 days and keep a record of all cash rent receipts for 3 years. Also give a receipt for the full amount of any application fee. Delaware requires no receipt for rent paid by check or electronically, but giving one is good practice. A missing cash receipt is a Code violation the tenant can sue over; the statute does not make it an eviction defence.

title: No Delaware Rent Reporting Rule
bodyText: Delaware has no law requiring you to offer positive rent reporting to credit bureaus, and none barring or requiring tenant enrollment in a rent-reporting program. If you report rent payments, federal credit-reporting law governs accuracy and disputes.

title: Taxes on Rent in Delaware
bodyText: Delaware does not tax ordinary residential rent: there is no sales tax, and the state's commercial-lessor license and gross-receipts tax applies only to leases of commercial units, not dwellings. Short stays can be taxed. Hotels, motels and tourist homes collect an 8 percent occupancy tax, but not from a permanent resident who has occupied, or has the right to occupy, the room for at least 5 consecutive months. Short-term rentals of a residential dwelling to tourists or transient guests for 31 consecutive nights or less carry a 4.5 percent lodging tax on the rent, excluding security deposits and money from a month-to-month holdover, collected by the booking platform or broker, or by you if you arrange any of the rental yourself rather than exclusively through a third-party platform. Check local taxes separately.

title: Returned Checks and Payments in Delaware
bodyText: If a tenant's check bounces, Delaware's dishonored-check law lets you sue for the check amount plus court costs and $50 for the first bounced check in a year, or triple the check amount (up to $250) for a second or later one within a year, but only after a written demand at least 30 days before suing, and the tenant can avoid those damages by paying the check amount plus a $40 fee before you sue (or plus $40 and court costs after you sue). You may charge more than these limits only if the tenant agrees in writing, so put any returned-payment fee in the lease. You may limit payments to the methods the lease accepts, so a lease may provide that after a returned payment you can require a cashier's check, certified check or money order; after a judgment for possession you may require a certified check or money order. A returned-payment fee is not rent under the Code, so leave it out of a nonpayment notice.

title: No Delaware Fee-Listing Statute
bodyText: Delaware has no rule that every fee must be listed in the lease or that a fee missing from the lease cannot be charged, and no notice period for adding a fee. In practice, list every charge with its amount and purpose: a late charge is allowed only if the lease provides for it, separately billed utilities only if the lease says so, nonrefundable fees are barred except optional service fees for services actually provided, and a new rule that substantially changes the lease after move-in needs the tenant's written consent. New or higher charges at renewal need 60 days' written notice. You may not refuse a rent payment made by or on behalf of the tenant by a method the lease accepts, before or after you file (after a judgment you may require a certified check or money order, but you may not restrict the method of a redemption payment made by a charitable organization or government entity, whose electronic or written check counts as the tenant's payment); the statute does not say whether this reaches a partial payment.

title: Federal Worker Shutdown Protections in Delaware
bodyText: Delaware protects federal workers, including federal contractor employees, who live in Delaware and are furloughed or working without pay during a federal shutdown (a lapse in appropriations of more than 24 hours). From the start of the shutdown until 30 days after it ends, you may evict such a tenant for nonpayment only with a court order, and the court may stay the eviction for 30 days or longer if the shutdown materially affected the tenant's ability to meet the lease. The tenant may also ask a court to stay or suspend rent payments owed during the shutdown, for up to the covered period plus 90 days, with court-set installments. The Act does not itself bar late fees, but the Attorney General can seek penalties of up to $10,000 per violation.

title: Delaware Money Limits at a Glance
bodyText: Delaware's main money limits: security deposit no more than one month's rent for leases of a year or more, and for month-to-month or open-ended tenancies once they have lasted a year (no cap for furnished units); pet deposit no more than one month's rent, separate from the security deposit; a surety bond, alone or with a deposit, no more than one month's rent; application fee no more than the greater of 10 percent of monthly rent or $50; late charge no more than 5 percent of monthly rent and not within 5 days of the due date; no nonrefundable fees except optional fees for services actually provided; no lease clause for attorneys' fees. Tenants may repair and deduct up to the lesser of $400 or half a month's rent. A holdover tenant owes up to double the monthly rent, prorated daily, plus further losses. Penalties against landlords include double the deposit wrongfully withheld, 3 months' rent for knowingly enforcing a prohibited lease term, and the greater of 3 months' rent or treble damages for retaliation.

title: No Delaware Subsidy Rent-Proration Rule
bodyText: Delaware has no special rule for reducing rent on a subsidized unit when part of it becomes uninhabitable, or for splitting a reduction between the tenant's share and the subsidy. The general rules apply: after a fire or casualty, a tenant who lawfully stays may vacate the unusable part and the rent is reduced in proportion to the lost rental value; and when heat, water, hot water or electricity fail after notice, the tenant may keep two-thirds of the daily rent. For federally subsidized units, federal program rules control where they conflict with the Code, so follow the housing authority's rules on abatement of the subsidy portion.

title: Late Fees on Subsidized Rent in Delaware
bodyText: Delaware has no rule specifically barring a late fee when a housing subsidy's share of the rent arrives late. The general limits still apply: a late charge only if the lease provides for one, no more than 5 percent of the monthly rent, and not within 5 days of the due date. The safest practice is to charge any late fee only on the tenant's own share and only when the tenant's share is late. Federal program rules control federally subsidized units, and source of income is a protected class in Delaware. For leases signed from March 2027, if a state reentry fund stops paying because you did not follow its termination steps, the tenant is not liable for the fund's share.

title: Passing Property Taxes to a Delaware Tenant
bodyText: A Delaware tenant who pays a property tax on the rental may set it off against rent, unless the lease provides otherwise. So you may pass real estate taxes, or a share of a tax increase, to a tenant only through the lease. If you want a pass-through during a fixed term, state the tenant's exact share or formula and the base year in the lease; without such a clause, change the rent only at renewal on 60 days' written notice. Delaware does not require a refund of any later tax abatement, but crediting it back is fair practice. A rent increase that passes through a substantial tax increase you became liable for at least 4 months earlier is a defence to a retaliation claim.

title: Interest on Unpaid Rent and Damages in Delaware
bodyText: Delaware's Landlord-Tenant Code sets no interest rate on unpaid rent or damages and does not require interest terms in the lease. Under the general interest statute, where no contract rate is stated the legal rate is 5 percent over the Federal Reserve discount rate, and a judgment bears post-judgment interest at that rate or any lower contract rate. Do not add interest on late rent on top of your late fee: a charge for paying late may count toward the 5 percent late-charge cap and cannot be imposed within the 5-day grace period.

title: No Delaware Move-In Inspection Requirement
bodyText: Delaware does not require a move-in or move-out inspection, a written condition checklist, or any inspection notice. Doing one anyway is your best evidence, because you may keep deposit money only for damage beyond normal wear and tear, or that painting and ordinary cleaning cannot fix. Before renting a unit you must visually inspect it for signs of bed bugs. Within 20 days after the lease ends you must send an itemized list of damages with the estimated repair cost for each item; if you do not, the law treats you as agreeing no damages are owed. If the tenant accepts the refund sent with the list and does not object in writing within 10 days, the tenant is treated as agreeing to your damage figures.

title: No Pre-Set Deposit Charges in Delaware
bodyText: Delaware has no rule letting a lease pre-set cleaning, carpet or repair charges that you then take from the deposit. You may keep deposit money only for actual damage the tenant caused beyond normal wear and tear, or that painting and ordinary cleaning cannot correct, plus unpaid rent and certain re-renting costs, and you must itemize each damage item with its estimated repair cost within 20 days. A flat charge taken whatever the unit's condition works as a nonrefundable fee, which Delaware bars. If you use a price list, treat it only as your estimate of actual repair costs.

title: Unclaimed Deposit Refunds in Delaware
bodyText: A deposit refund you cannot deliver is unclaimed property under Delaware law, and you are its holder. If the tenant has not claimed it or shown interest in it, it is presumed abandoned 5 years after the tenant first had the right to it; you must then mail the tenant notice 60 to 120 days before your annual report (if the amount is $50 or more and you have a good address), report it online by March 1, and remit it to the State Escheator. A late report adds the lesser of 5 percent of the amount a month (up to 50 percent) or $100 a day (up to $5,000); a late payment adds 0.5 percent a month (up to 25 percent); and interest runs at 0.5 percent a month. Any lease clause saying an unclaimed deposit becomes yours is void. The Landlord-Tenant Code separately says that if the tenant left no forwarding address, the tenant must claim the unused deposit in writing within 1 year; that does not make the money yours, so keep it in the deposit account and handle it under the unclaimed property rules.

title: Deposit Increases Paid in Installments
bodyText: You may require the full security deposit before move-in; Delaware gives tenants no right to pay the initial deposit in installments, though you may agree to one. Deposit increases are different. You may raise the deposit along with the rent only if the lease says so, never above the deposit cap, and if the increase is more than 10 percent of the monthly rent the tenant pays it in installments: spread over the remaining lease term, or over 4 months for a month-to-month tenancy.

title: Prepaid Last Month's Rent in Delaware
bodyText: Delaware's Code mentions prepaid rent separately from deposits, so collecting last month's rent in advance is not barred. But the Code defines a security deposit as any deposit held for all or part of the lease term, so last month's rent you collect at signing and hold until the end could be treated as part of the deposit and counted against the one-month cap. Where the one-month cap applies (a lease of a year or more, or a month-to-month tenancy that has lasted a year, and not a furnished unit), keep the security deposit plus any prepaid last month's rent within one month's rent, and in any case consider holding the prepayment under the deposit rules (escrow account, return rules). A tenant has no right to skip the last month's rent and tell you to keep the deposit instead; unpaid last-month rent is ordinary nonpayment, and the deposit may then cover the arrearage.

title: No Move-Out Notice Condition on Deposit Refunds
bodyText: Delaware does not let you make the deposit refund depend on the tenant giving you advance notice of moving out. Whatever the lease says about notice, you must return the deposit, or the balance with an itemized list of damages, within 20 days after the lease ends. Two conditions are allowed. If the tenant gave no forwarding address in writing by the end of the lease and the lease states no address for the tenant, you are relieved of the notice and double-damage rules, though you still owe the unused deposit if the tenant claims it in writing within 1 year; where the lease states the tenant's address, send the refund there. And if your lease makes returning the keys a condition of the refund, it must spell out a clear key-surrender procedure and may not require the keys before the lease ends.

title: Deposit Timing After a Victim's Early Termination
bodyText: Delaware has no special deposit timetable when a tenant ends the lease early as a victim of domestic abuse, sexual offenses or stalking. Such a tenant may end the tenancy on 30 days' written notice, counted from the first day of the next month. The normal deposit rules then apply: return the deposit or an itemized list with any balance within 20 days after the tenancy ends, and any re-renting charge you take from the deposit for this early termination may not exceed one month's rent. If other tenants remain on the lease, the Code does not say when the departing tenant's share must be returned; where the lease requires key surrender, possession counts as returned only when all tenants on the lease have followed the key procedure.

title: No Expedited Deposit Procedure in Delaware
bodyText: Delaware has no expedited deposit procedure. You must return the deposit, or send the itemized damage list with any balance, within 20 days after the lease ends, and you may always do so sooner. Do not deduct an administrative or processing fee for handling the deposit; Delaware limits deposit use to damage, unpaid rent and certain re-renting costs, and bars nonrefundable fees. When a sole tenant dies, the 20 days run from when you get the unit back, or from the end of any required storage of belongings.

title: Surety Bonds in Place of a Deposit in Delaware
bodyText: Delaware allows only one alternative to a cash deposit: a surety bond the tenant chooses to buy from an insurer licensed in Delaware. You may not require a bond instead of a deposit, and you do not have to accept one. The bond, alone or combined with any cash deposit, may not exceed one month's rent. The surety must tell the tenant in writing that the premium is nonrefundable (unless you refuse the bond or no lease is signed), that the bond is not insurance for the tenant, and that the tenant may have to repay the surety for your claims. Before claiming on the bond you must let the tenant pay you directly or use any cash deposit first, and you must send an itemized damage list within 20 days after the lease ends. A buyer of the property must accept the bond. A monthly fee you charge in place of a deposit, outside this bond program, is a nonrefundable fee Delaware bars.

title: No Inspection-Notice Penalty in Delaware
bodyText: Delaware has no move-in or move-out inspection notice requirement, so there is no penalty for not offering an inspection. The penalties you face concern the deposit itself: if you do not send the itemized damage list within 20 days after the lease ends, you are treated as agreeing nothing is owed; if you do not return what is owed within 20 days, the tenant can recover double the amount wrongfully withheld; and if you do not keep the deposit in a qualifying Delaware bank account or do not disclose the account location within 20 days of a written request, you forfeit the deposit.

title: Furnished Units and the Delaware Deposit Cap
bodyText: In Delaware the one-month security deposit cap does not apply to a furnished rental unit, so you may ask a larger deposit for a furnished unit. The Code does not say how much furniture makes a unit furnished, so list every item you provide in the lease or an inventory the tenant signs. The pet deposit is still capped at one month's rent, and a surety bond in place of a deposit is still capped at one month's rent. Damage to your furniture beyond normal wear and tear can be deducted from the deposit like other damage, and all the usual deposit rules (escrow account, 20-day return and itemized list) still apply. Inspect furniture, mattresses and linens for signs of bed bugs before you rent.

title: Holding Deposits in Delaware
bodyText: Before a lease is signed, Delaware lets you take only an application fee, a security deposit, a surety bond fee or premium, a pet deposit, or a deposit that reserves the unit for the applicant for a set period. A holding deposit is therefore allowed only if it holds the unit until a stated date; any other up-front payment to assure the rental is prohibited assurance money. State in writing how long you will hold the unit and what happens to the money if the lease is signed (credit it to the deposit or first rent) or not signed. The Code does not say when a holding deposit must be refunded, so refunding it when you reject the applicant or do not offer the lease is the safe course; once the tenancy starts, keeping it as a nonrefundable charge would breach the ban on nonrefundable fees.

title: No Nonrefundable Deposits in Delaware
bodyText: Delaware does not allow a nonrefundable deposit or nonrefundable fee as a condition of renting, except an optional fee for services actually provided, such as a pool fee. So there is nothing to disclose as nonrefundable in a Delaware lease: every security deposit and pet deposit must be returned within 20 days after the lease ends, less only lawful deductions for damage, unpaid rent and certain re-renting costs. The one nonrefundable payment the law recognizes is a surety bond premium the tenant chooses to pay to a surety instead of a deposit, and the surety must disclose that in writing. The application fee is a separate, capped charge.

title: No Nonrefundable-Deposit Notice in Delaware
bodyText: Delaware has no separate nonrefundable-deposit notice because no part of a Delaware security or pet deposit can be made nonrefundable. When you collect a deposit, what you must do instead is tell the tenant where the deposit account is and give the tenant the Attorney General's Landlord-Tenant Code summary at the start of the tenancy.

title: Delaware Security Deposit Cap
bodyText: Delaware caps the security deposit at one month's rent for any lease of a year or more. For a month-to-month or open-ended tenancy, the cap applies once the tenancy has lasted a year, and you must then credit back any amount above one month's rent (counting any surety bond). On the statute's wording, fixed terms shorter than a year are not capped, and furnished units are not capped at all. A pet deposit is separate, may not exceed one month's rent for any lease length, and may not be charged for a trained support animal of a disabled resident. A surety bond plus any deposit may not exceed one month's rent. You may raise the deposit with the rent only if the lease says so, and an increase over 10 percent of the rent must be spread out. Federally assisted housing follows federal rules.

title: Holding Security Deposits in Delaware
bodyText: Put every security deposit and pet deposit in an escrow account designated as a security deposits account at a federally insured bank with a Delaware office that takes deposits, and never use that account for your business. Tell the tenant where the account is; if a tenant asks in writing and you do not disclose the location within 20 days, or if you hold the deposit anywhere else, you forfeit the deposit to the tenant and owe double if you do not return it within 20 days. The deposit belongs to the tenant ahead of your creditors, even in bankruptcy. There is no exemption for small landlords, no option to post a bond instead, and no Delaware rule on interest earned in the account. If a licensed broker manages the property, the broker's own escrow-account rules also apply.

title: No Deposit Interest Requirement in Delaware
bodyText: Delaware does not require you to pay interest on a tenant's security deposit or pet deposit, and its law does not say who keeps any interest the escrow account earns. The statute speaks only of holding the deposit principal for the tenant's benefit. If you state an interest policy in the lease, follow it.

title: Deposit Rights Cannot Be Waived in Delaware
bodyText: A Delaware lease cannot make a tenant give up any right under the Landlord-Tenant Code, including the security deposit rules on the cap, the escrow account, the 20-day return and itemized list, and the double-damages penalty. A waiver clause is unenforceable, and if you try to enforce a lease term you know is prohibited, the tenant can recover three months' rent plus court costs. The lease may vary deposit terms only where the Code allows, such as providing for a deposit increase when rent rises.

title: Deposits When a Delaware Rental Is Sold
bodyText: If you sell a rental, Delaware law says a buyer must accept a tenant's surety bond and may not demand an extra deposit during the current lease, or more than one month's rent in bond plus deposit at renewal. For cash deposits Delaware has no specific transfer rule. Because the deposit is held for the tenant's benefit ahead of your creditors and must be returned within 20 days after the lease ends, transfer each deposit (and its records) to the buyer at closing, tell the tenant in writing who now holds it and where the account is, and update the owner disclosure. A buyer who collects the rent is a landlord under the Code and must handle the deposits it receives under the Delaware rules.

title: Delaware Deposit Return Timing and Disputes
bodyText: Delaware's deposit-return clock runs 20 days from the date the lease expires or is terminated, not from move-out or a tenant demand, and a lease cannot change it. Within that time, return the full deposit or send an itemized list of damages with the estimated repair cost of each and the balance. Send it to the address in the lease or to the forwarding address the tenant gave in writing by the end of the lease. If the tenant cashes or accepts your payment and does not object in writing within 10 days of receiving it, the tenant is treated as agreeing to your damage figures. When a sole tenant dies, the 20 days run from when you get possession back (or from the end of required storage), and the refund goes to the estate's documented representative. Any refund you cannot deliver must be handled under the unclaimed property law, not kept.

title: Delaware Security Deposit Penalties
bodyText: Delaware's deposit penalties are strict. If you do not return the deposit, or the balance after itemized damages, within 20 days after the lease ends, the tenant can recover double the amount you wrongfully withheld. If you do not send the itemized damage list within 20 days, you are treated as acknowledging that no damages are owed. If you fail to deposit it in a federally insured institution with an office in Delaware that accepts deposits, or fail to disclose the account's location within 20 days of the tenant's written request, either failure forfeits the whole deposit to the tenant, and if you do not return it within 20 days after the forfeiture the tenant can recover double the full deposit. These rules also apply to pet deposits. If the tenant gave no written forwarding address and the lease states no address for the tenant, the double-damage penalty does not apply, but you still owe the unused deposit if the tenant claims it in writing within a year; where the lease states the tenant's address, send the refund there and assume the penalties still apply.

title: No Deposit-Standards Disclosure Rule in Delaware
bodyText: Delaware does not require you to post or give tenants the standards you use to set deposit amounts. You may charge different deposits based on legitimate screening factors such as credit or income, but apply them in a commercially reasonable way, never based on a protected class including source of income, and always within the deposit caps.

title: Utility Deposits Held by Delaware Landlords
bodyText: Delaware has no separate rule for a utility deposit you hold. Any extra deposit you take to cover utilities is treated as part of the security deposit: it counts toward the one-month cap where the cap applies, must sit in the escrow account, and must be returned or itemized within 20 days after the lease ends. If you bill the tenant for utilities, unpaid utility charges count as rent, so you may deduct them from the deposit as unpaid rent unless the lease says otherwise. Deposits the utility company itself holds are governed by the utility's rules, not by you.

title: Smoking and Marijuana Rules for Delaware Rentals
bodyText: You may ban smoking, including vaping, in a Delaware rental, and smoking is already illegal by statute in the lobbies, hallways and other common areas of apartment buildings, condominiums and other multi-unit residential buildings. Marijuana has a special rule: you may ban smoking or vaping it, but you may not ban a tenant's possession of marijuana or use by non-smoked means such as edibles, unless you live in the building and rent no more than 3 rooms to no more than 3 tenants, the housing is incidental to services such as student or medical housing, or allowing it would violate federal law or cost you a federal benefit (for example, some federally assisted housing). You may not refuse to rent to or penalize a registered medical marijuana patient or caregiver because of that status, unless renting to them would cause you to lose a monetary or licensing-related benefit under federal law or regulations. Put any smoking ban in the lease or rules at move-in; adding one mid-tenancy that substantially changes the lease requires the tenant's written consent.

title: Alterations, Locks and Disability Modifications
bodyText: A Delaware lease may require your written consent before alterations, but three state rules limit it. First, you must allow reasonable modifications a tenant with a disability needs, at the tenant's expense; where reasonable, you may condition consent on the tenant restoring the interior at move-out, less reasonable wear and tear. Delaware does not shift these costs to larger or assisted properties. Second, a tenant may install a new lock at the tenant's cost if the tenant tells you in writing and gives you a key, the lock fits the existing system, and the door is not damaged. Third, in a suit for waste a tenant has a defence for repairs or replacements made after reasonable notice that a prudent owner would make or that did not reduce the property's value, though a written lease term against alterations can still be enforced as a breach. If you want the tenant to do specific work, use a separate conspicuous written agreement with real consideration.

title: Occupancy Limits Under the Delaware Housing Code
bodyText: Delaware's State Housing Code limits occupancy by floor area, not persons per bedroom: each dwelling needs at least 150 square feet of habitable floor area for the first occupant and 100 more for each additional occupant (counting anyone over 1 year old), and each bedroom used by one person must have at least 64 square feet. Kitchens and non-habitable spaces may not be used for sleeping, and a code official can order an overcrowded unit's occupancy reduced. The State code applies statewide except where a city or county has its own equivalent housing code, so check local rules. Any occupancy limit you set in the lease must be reasonable and applied equally to everyone, and you may not limit occupancy in a way that discriminates against families with children or another protected group.

title: Residential Use Rule and Its Remedy in Delaware
bodyText: Even without a lease clause, Delaware requires a tenant to use the unit only as the tenant's home unless the lease allows otherwise, and a violation counts as breach of a rule. To enforce it, give written notice allowing at least 7 days to stop, or terminate immediately by notice to the tenant if the use causes or threatens irreparable harm to people or property, and then file for possession if needed. If a court finds, after a hearing at which the tenant appeared, that the tenant used the unit for a criminal nuisance purpose such as illegal drug activity, the lease becomes void at your option. A unit rented solely or primarily for commercial use falls outside the residential Landlord-Tenant Code.

title: Tenant Bed Bug Duties in Delaware
bodyText: Delaware puts specific bed bug duties on tenants: a tenant must not knowingly bring in furniture or belongings known or reasonably suspected to be infested, and must not unreasonably refuse entry for inspection, treatment or monitoring after you give the usual 48 hours' notice; a tenant who unreasonably refuses is liable for the resulting harm. If the tenant reports an infestation within 60 days after moving in, or within 30 days after one is found in an adjoining unit, you bear all investigation and treatment costs; later reports are still yours to remediate, but the tenant shares the reasonable cost of treating the tenant's unit (not in housing-authority properties). Your own duties are strict: acknowledge and inspect within 120 hours, if an infestation is confirmed, have a pest management professional treat it within 14 days of the tenant's report, check adjoining units within 5 days, notify affected tenants of the findings within 120 hours, and keep records for 2 years. Preparation steps you want tenants to take should be in your written rules.

title: No Delaware Cold-Weather Vacancy Notice Rule
bodyText: Delaware has no cold-weather rule requiring a tenant to tell you before leaving the unit empty in winter. You can get similar protection through the lease: Delaware lets a lease require written notice of any absence longer than 7 days, given by the first day of the absence, and a tenant who fails to give it must cover any harm the absence causes, such as frozen-pipe damage. During such an absence you may enter as reasonably needed for inspection, maintenance and safekeeping.

title: Common-Area Lighting in Delaware
bodyText: In Delaware, every common hall and stairway in a building other than a single-family home must be lit at all times, at least to the level of a 60-watt bulb, throughout the normally traveled stairs and passageways, and every public hall needs a light fixture. You must also keep common areas clean and sanitary. Delaware has no rule letting you charge a tenant for common-area lights wired to the tenant's own meter; the utility-charge rules allow billing only for a tenant's own separately metered use, at actual cost, so wire common-area lighting to a house meter. Local housing codes may add requirements.

title: Mechanics' Liens for Tenant Work in Delaware
bodyText: In Delaware, a contractor hired by your tenant cannot put a mechanics' lien on your property for repairs, alterations or additions unless you (or your authorized agent) gave prior written consent to the work. Your written approval of a tenant's alterations can therefore expose the property to liens. If you approve tenant work, consider conditioning approval on the tenant paying contractors directly and delivering lien waivers signed at or after payment; a lease clause saying your property will not be subject to liens has no basis in Delaware law, and contractors cannot be made to waive lien rights in advance.

title: No Delaware Family Child Care Rental Rule
bodyText: Delaware does not require you to let a tenant run a family child care home, and sets no lease conditions for one. Unless the lease says otherwise, a tenant must use the unit only as a home, so child care for other families is allowed only if you agree in the lease. If you allow it, you may require the tenant to be licensed and insured, but a clause releasing you from your own legal liability is unenforceable in Delaware. Smoking, including vaping, is barred by state law in a home while it is used for child care.

title: Home Businesses in Delaware Rentals
bodyText: Delaware gives tenants no statutory right to run a business from a rental home. Unless the lease says otherwise, a tenant must use the unit only as a home, and other use is a breach of rule you can enforce with a 7-day notice. Your lease may allow quiet home-office work while barring customer traffic, employees or signage. If a unit is rented mainly for business use, it is a commercial rental outside the residential Landlord-Tenant Code. Local zoning may separately limit home businesses.

title: Utility Liens on Rental Property in Delaware
bodyText: In Delaware, some unpaid utility charges become liens on your property even when the tenant ran up the bill. Unpaid Wilmington water rents become a lien on the owner's land after 30 days and last 5 years; county sewer charges are liens collectible with county taxes; and in New Castle County sewer service liens outrank the interests of owners and tenants alike. No state statute lets you avoid these liens through a lease clause or a filing with the utility, so check your city's or county's rules and consider requiring proof of payment of tenant-paid water and sewer bills. Remember that you may require a tenant to hold a utility account in the tenant's own name only if the unit is separately metered, or for flat, non-usage charges where the local government or utility allows it and the lease provides for it.

title: Statutory Prohibited Acts for Delaware Tenants
bodyText: Delaware law itself forbids a tenant to willfully or wantonly damage, deface or remove any part of the unit or its equipment (or let guests do so), to remove or tamper with a working smoke or carbon monoxide detector or its batteries, to knowingly bring in bed-bug-infested belongings, or to unreasonably interfere with other tenants' peaceful enjoyment. The State Housing Code also bars blocking exits with waste and storing more flammable materials than normal household use. Tampering with detectors can also bring a fine of $100 to $500. If a tenant is convicted of a class A misdemeanor or felony during the tenancy that caused or threatened irreparable harm to people or property, you may terminate immediately; most other breaches need a written notice with 7 days to cure.

title: Lease Void for Criminal Nuisance Use in Delaware
bodyText: Delaware has a statute that voids a lease when the property is used for a criminal purpose. If a court finds, after a hearing at which the tenant appeared, that the tenant used the unit for a criminal nuisance purpose, such as illegal drug activity, illegal firearms activity, prostitution, gang activity or a violent felony, the lease becomes void at your option and possession reverts to you. Owners who permit such a nuisance can themselves be sued, and a court can close the property and suspend rental licenses, so act promptly on known criminal activity. Separately, a tenant convicted during the tenancy of a class A misdemeanor or felony that caused or threatened irreparable harm may be terminated immediately.

title: No Delaware Rule on Tenant Insurance Claims
bodyText: Delaware has no statute on requiring a tenant to file a claim on the tenant's renters insurance. But a lease may not make the tenant cover your own legal liability or indemnify you for it, so you cannot use the tenant's policy to shift repairs or liability that the Code places on you; knowingly enforcing such a term can cost you three months' rent. You may require renters insurance for the tenant's own property and liability, and ask a tenant to report losses the tenant caused to the tenant's insurer.

title: Statutory Tenant Duties in Delaware
bodyText: Delaware law sets these tenant duties whatever the lease says: follow applicable codes; keep the part of the premises the tenant uses clean and safe; dispose of garbage, rubbish and flammable waste safely in covered containers; keep plumbing fixtures clean; use electrical, plumbing, heating and other facilities and appliances reasonably; not willfully damage or remove anything or let guests do so; not tamper with smoke or carbon monoxide detectors, and in a lease of a month or more keep their batteries working; obey reasonable rules; report defects to you in writing as soon as practicable and tell you in writing if served with a lawsuit against the property; allow reasonable access on notice; not disturb neighbors; and not bring in bed-bug-infested belongings. In a single-family rental the occupant handles routine pest extermination other than bed bugs. You enforce these with a written notice allowing 7 days to cure.

title: No Utility Shutoffs by Delaware Landlords
bodyText: Delaware gives no landlord a right to interrupt electricity, water or other utilities for nonpayment, even when you submeter and bill them. The law says outright that you may not discontinue or terminate utility service for nonpayment of rent, utility charges or any other breach; unpaid utility charges count as rent, so use the nonpayment notice and an eviction case instead. If you submeter, the lease must provide for the charges, meters must be approved by the Division of Weights and Measures, you may charge only your actual cost, you must bill at least monthly from actual readings (no more than two estimated bills in a row), and you must let the tenant inspect the bills and records.

title: Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Detectors in Delaware Rentals
bodyText: You must install smoke detectors in every Delaware rental, whatever its age, placed as the State Fire Prevention Regulations require (in older one- and two-family homes and townhouses, outside each sleeping area and on every story including the basement; in apartment buildings, interconnected hard-wired detectors with battery backup). You must also install carbon monoxide detectors in apartments, condominiums and other multi-unit rentals where a unit has a fuel-burning appliance, a fireplace or an attached garage, unless the unit is more than one story above or below the fuel source or garage, or is not connected to it by duct work or ventilation shafts. For leases of a month or more, the tenant must keep working batteries in the detectors inside the unit; you remain responsible for installing and otherwise maintaining them. Fines run $100 to $500 per offense for owners or tenants who fail to comply or who tamper with detectors. Failing to comply with the smoke detector law cannot be used as evidence of negligence in a fire injury lawsuit or insurance claim.

title: Excluding Appliances in Delaware Leases
bodyText: Delaware has no rule presuming that appliances left in a unit are yours to maintain, and no rule on excluding them in the lease. Your repair duty covers the electrical, plumbing and other facilities you supply, while equipment a tenant furnishes is the tenant's to install and keep in good working order. If a tenant brings a washer or a second refrigerator, say in the lease that it is the tenant's and that you do not maintain it. You cannot exclude code-required items: every unit must have heating that can keep rooms at 65°F, and stoves and refrigerators you install must be properly installed by you.

title: Substitute Housing Remedies in Delaware
bodyText: Delaware does not now require you to put a tenant up elsewhere during repairs (once the lead-certification chapter is implemented, you will have to provide alternative housing when a lead inspector finds a unit uninhabitable because of a lead-based paint hazard), but tenants can choose remedies that cost you money. If heat, water, hot water or electricity stays off after the tenant's notice, the tenant may move to equivalent substitute housing while rent abates, and you owe the tenant's extra cost up to half of the abated rent (unless performance was impossible). If you cannot deliver possession at the start of the lease because of code violations, the tenant may recover up to one month's rent in substitute housing costs. If you caused a serious condition willfully or negligently, a tenant who ends the lease may recover the amount by which the cost of equivalent substitute housing for the rest of the term exceeds the rent under your lease, or one month's rent plus the deposit if greater. Equivalent substitute housing means a unit of similar location, size, facilities and rent.

title: Condemned or placarded unit: no express rent bar, but you may not let it be occupied
bodyText: Delaware's statutes do not expressly bar you from collecting rent once a unit is condemned or ordered vacated. Other rules reach a similar result. Under the State Housing Code (which applies unless your city or county administers its own equivalent housing code), a code official may condemn a structure that is unsafe or unfit for human occupancy, placard it and order it vacated; a condemned structure may not be reoccupied without the code official's approval, and an owner who lets anyone occupy a placarded unit commits a misdemeanor (fine of $25 to $1,000, up to 30 days in jail, each day a separate offense). After a compliance order or violation notice you may not lease the property to someone else until the violations are corrected, unless you first give the new lessee a copy and file the lessee's signed, notarized acceptance of responsibility for the repairs with the code official; that alternative does not fit a residential tenancy, because the Landlord-Tenant Code keeps code compliance on you and bars a tenant agreement to do code-compliance work, so make the repairs before renting. Under the Landlord-Tenant Code you must keep the unit fit and code-compliant; if a condition makes the unit uninhabitable or poses an imminent threat to health or safety, the tenant may give notice and end the lease immediately, and after a fire or casualty that substantially impairs the unit the tenant may quit and owes rent only to the date of vacating (if they notify you in writing within a week). If the government files a code-violation notice and you then seek possession, raise rent or cut services within 90 days, retaliation is presumed. Where a court closes premises as a criminal nuisance, it may order an owner who knew of the nuisance to pay uninvolved tenants' relocation costs and lost rent. Cautious course: do not charge rent for any period a unit is placarded or may not lawfully be occupied, and refund prepaid rent for that period.

title: Habitability rules other states have that Delaware lacks (and some it has)
bodyText: Several habitability rules found in other states have no Delaware counterpart, while some common gaps are filled. (1) No statutory list of 'imminently dangerous conditions': tenant receivership covers lack of heat, running water, light, electricity or adequate sewage facilities you are bound to provide, plus 'any other conditions imminently dangerous', decided case by case. (2) Air conditioning is not an essential service under the Landlord-Tenant Code's withholding remedy (that remedy covers hot water, heat, water and electricity), but the State Housing Code requires heating, cooling or humidity facilities that are integral to the building to be maintained and operated continuously at their designed capacity. (3) No court-administered rent escrow for repairs: the tenant's routes are written notice and termination, repair-and-deduct (up to $400 or half a month's rent, whichever is less), keeping two-thirds of per-diem rent while an essential service is off, damages, and a receivership petition. (4) Delaware does set a heat standard: heating facilities able to keep habitable rooms, bathrooms and toilet rooms at 65°F (State Housing Code). (5) There is no separate habitability non-waiver chapter, but the lease cannot waive any right or remedy under the Landlord-Tenant Code at all. (6) The tenant must report defects to you in writing as soon as practicable (not needed where you already have actual notice); the essential-services remedy runs from 'actual or written notice'.

title: No Delaware rule lets the lease name who does tenant repair-and-deduct work
bodyText: Delaware's statutes do not let, or forbid, a lease naming the person or firm who must do repairs a tenant makes at your expense. The tenant's repair-and-deduct remedy requires only that the work be done 'in a professional manner': if you fail to remedy a repair problem within 30 days of the tenant's written notice, or fail within 10 days to start reasonable corrective measures (such as getting an estimate), the tenant may do or have the work done and deduct a reasonable sum, not more than $400 or half a month's rent, whichever is less, on submitting receipts. The tenant is liable for damage caused by the tenant or the tenant's repairer, cannot use the remedy for conditions the tenant's household caused, and cannot use it while delinquent in rent. Because a lease may not make a tenant waive any right or remedy under the Landlord-Tenant Code, a clause that requires the tenant to use only your contractor could be read as cutting down the remedy and would then be unenforceable. You may still ask that repair requests come to you and use your own contractors for work you do.

title: Disability accommodations and modifications (Delaware Fair Housing Act)
bodyText: Under the Delaware Fair Housing Act it is disability discrimination to refuse to make reasonable accommodations in your rules, policies, practices or services when they may be necessary to give a person with a disability an equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling, or to refuse to let a tenant with a disability make, at the tenant's expense, reasonable modifications of the premises that may be necessary for full enjoyment. For a rental you may, where reasonable, condition permission for a modification on the tenant agreeing to restore the interior to its prior condition, reasonable wear and tear excepted. Delaware does not require that restoration right to be written into the lease, and has no rule for an interest-bearing restoration deposit. You may not ask applicants whether they have a disability or about its nature or severity, though you may ask all applicants questions about their ability to meet tenancy requirements, qualification for disability-specific housing or priorities, and current illegal drug use. You need not rent to a person whose tenancy would be a direct threat to others' health or safety or would cause substantial physical damage to others' property. The accommodation and modification rules do not apply to rooms or units in a building of up to four families where you live in one of the units (the advertising ban still does). A person who is blind or partially blind with a guide dog is entitled to full and equal access to rental housing and may not be charged extra for the dog, but is liable for damage it causes; and you may not take a pet deposit for a certified and trained support animal of a disabled resident. Courts may consider higher federal, state or local standards when deciding the scope of the accommodation duty.

title: No Delaware statute on renting the same unit or room to two tenants
bodyText: Delaware's statutes do not address renting the same unit or room to two different tenants for the same period, and set no special rent-abatement remedy for it. The general possession rules cover the problem. You must supply the unit bargained for at the start of the term and put the tenant into full possession. If you don't, rent abates while the tenant can't move in; the tenant may give notice and end the lease and get back all money paid, including prepaid rent and pet and security deposits; and if the failure is your wrongful doing due to substantial building or housing code noncompliance, the tenant may recover up to one month's rent for substitute housing. If a holdover tenant is blocking the new tenant and you have not filed for possession, the new tenant may file a summary possession action against the holdover and claim those costs and substitute-housing expenses from the rent. Double-renting would also expose you to a claim for unlawful exclusion (treble damages or three times per-diem rent).

title: No Delaware background-screening mandate for apartment employees
bodyText: Delaware has no statute requiring you to run background checks on apartment employees, maintenance staff or managers who have keys to or enter tenants' units, and none forbidding it. Your staff's entries still count as yours: you are liable to the tenant for any theft, casualty or other harm proximately resulting from an entry by you, your employees or agents (or anyone you let in) when the tenant is absent and has not specifically consented, when the tenant is present and able to consent but did not, or in any case where the harm is due to your negligence, and a lease term exempting you from that liability is void. Careful hiring and key control reduce that exposure. Separately, anyone who leases or offers to lease, or negotiates rental agreements for, property owned by someone else generally needs a Delaware real estate license; an owner and the owner's regular employees managing the owner's own property are exempt. If you do screen job applicants, Delaware employment law (not landlord-tenant law) governs how.

title: How serious a defect must be for each Delaware tenant remedy
bodyText: Delaware's tenant remedies turn on how serious the problem is. Ending the lease in the first month of occupancy requires that you fail to substantially conform to the rental agreement or a material noncompliance with a code governing maintenance or operation of the premises. Ending the lease later requires a condition that deprives the tenant of a substantial part of the benefit or enjoyment of the bargain that you don't remedy within 15 days of written notice; if the condition makes the unit uninhabitable or poses an imminent threat to health, safety or welfare, the tenant may end the lease immediately on notice, without going to court. The essential-services remedies apply when you substantially fail to provide hot water, heat, water or electricity, or fail to remedy a condition that materially deprives the tenant of a substantial part of the bargain, for 48 hours after notice. Repair-and-deduct reaches any failure to repair, maintain, keep sanitary or perform as required by statute, code, ordinance or the lease, if after the tenant's written notice you do not remedy it within 30 days or do not start reasonable corrective measures (such as getting an estimate) within 10 days. The termination and repair-and-deduct remedies are not available for a condition the tenant, the tenant's family or guests caused through want of due care (the essential-services section has no such exclusion, but lets you avoid liability by showing impossibility of performance). Evidence that the unit complies with the applicable building and housing codes is prima facie evidence that you have met your duties. The State Housing Code's minimum standards are enforced against a deviation that poses an imminent threat to occupants' health, safety and general welfare, and the code is to be read to minimize displacement where deviations pose no imminent threat.

title: Shifting repair or maintenance duties to the tenant: only by a separate conspicuous writing
bodyText: Delaware lets you and the tenant agree that the tenant will perform specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling only by a conspicuous writing separate from the rental agreement, and only if all of these hold: the work is for the primary benefit of the rental unit; it is not work needed to bring a noncomplying unit into compliance with a building or housing code; the tenant gets adequate consideration apart from the lease, or a rent reduction; the agreement is made in good faith and not to evade your obligations. You may not make such an agreement a condition of any lease term. Your core duties (code compliance, a unit that does not endanger health or safety, clean common areas, repairs, and keeping supplied facilities in good working order) apply 'at all times during the tenancy' and cannot otherwise be waived: a lease may not make the tenant waive rights or remedies under the Landlord-Tenant Code or exculpate you from liability, and conflicting terms are unenforceable. Two duties depend on the lease itself: you must provide garbage receptacles and removal, and supply water, hot water, heat and electricity, only if the rental agreement so specifies (see the utilities and services rows). The rule is the same for month-to-month and fixed-term leases.

title: Habitability presumptions in Delaware: code compliance helps you; no presumption of breach
bodyText: Delaware's statutes create no presumption that you breached your repair or habitability duties because a unit violates a code or lacks a facility, and none presuming you had notice or took too long to repair; the tenant proves the condition and the notice the remedy requires. The one statutory habitability presumption runs in your favor: evidence that the unit complies with the applicable building and housing codes is prima facie evidence that you have complied with your Landlord-Tenant Code duties. Presumptions do run against you in two related settings: if you seek possession, raise rent or cut services within 90 days after a tenant's good-faith code complaint, a government code-violation notice, tenant-organizing activity or the tenant's pursuit of a legal remedy, your action is presumed retaliatory; and an adverse action within 90 days of an incident in which the tenant was a victim of domestic abuse, a sexual offense or stalking is presumed unlawful. Both presumptions are rebuttable on the grounds the statute lists.

title: No required lease statement that the unit is fit for habitation
bodyText: Delaware does not require your lease to state that you will deliver or keep the unit fit for habitation. The duties apply whether or not the lease mentions them: at all times during the tenancy you must comply with applicable state and local codes, provide a unit that does not endanger the health, welfare or safety of tenants and occupants and is fit for the purpose for which it is expressly rented, keep common areas you maintain clean and sanitary, make the repairs needed to keep the unit in as good a condition as it was (or ought to have been) at the start, and keep supplied electrical, plumbing and other facilities in good working order; and you must supply the unit bargained for at the beginning of the term. The required written-lease disclosures are different: owner and agent names and addresses, and, once Delaware's lead-safe certification program is implemented, a lead certification disclosure for units built before 1978.

title: No health-district rental rules or duty to hand out health regulations
bodyText: Delaware has no local health districts with their own rental-unit regulations, and no statute requiring you to give tenants copies of health or housing regulations on request or to refer them to a health agency. Rental housing standards come from the State Housing Code, enforced by your city or county (or, where a community has not undertaken enforcement, by the Director of the Delaware State Housing Authority as code official), and from local housing codes that meet or exceed it. The code official may inspect at reasonable times, issue correction orders and condemn unfit units. Some older town charters and statutes still mention local boards of health (for example, a neglected privy well declared a nuisance by two board members exposes the owner and the tenant in possession to a small fine if not cleaned within a week of notice). What you must hand tenants is set by the Landlord-Tenant Code instead: the Attorney General's summary of the Code at the start of the term and the right-to-representation materials (see those rows).

title: Heating: 65°F capable facilities; supplying the heat itself depends on the lease
bodyText: Two different duties apply. First, the facilities: under the State Housing Code every dwelling unit must have heating facilities capable of keeping all habitable rooms, bathrooms and toilet rooms at 65°F (measured 3 feet above the floor and 3 feet from an exterior wall), with heating equipment kept free of leaks and obstructions and safe, safety controls working, and integral climate-control systems operated continuously at designed capacity; and you must keep facilities you supply in good working order. Second, the fuel or energy: you must supply heat (and water, hot water and electricity) only if the rental agreement so specifies. Otherwise the tenant may pay for it, but you may not require the tenant to contract directly with a utility for service unless the unit is separately metered, and you may bill a tenant for metered fuel or electricity yourself only if the lease provides for it and the unit is separately metered. If heat is your obligation (by the lease or by code) and you substantially fail to provide it for 48 hours after the tenant's actual or written notice, the tenant may, on written notice, end the lease or keep two-thirds of per-diem rent while heat is off, or move to substitute housing with rent abated and you liable for up to half the abated rent in extra cost; you can avoid liability only by showing impossibility of performance. A lack of heat you are bound to provide that lasts 5 days after notice is also a ground for tenant receivership. Utilities have their own winter rules (no gas or electric shutoff for nonpayment on mornings 35°F or below, and 14 days' written notice during the November 1 to March 31 heating season).

title: Tenant remedies when you breach the lease or the Landlord-Tenant Code
bodyText: When you breach the lease or your statutory duties, a Delaware tenant has several routes, and the lease cannot take them away. Either party may sue in any court of competent civil jurisdiction for a violation of the lease or the Code, and material promises on each side are mutual and dependent. Specific remedies: (1) in the first month of occupancy, written notice and termination if you fail to substantially conform to the lease or materially fail a maintenance code (15 days' notice if a promised fix fails and the same problem recurs within 6 months); (2) a condition depriving the tenant of a substantial part of the bargain that you don't fix within 15 days of written notice lets the tenant end the lease (immediately on notice if the unit is uninhabitable or an imminent threat), with enhanced damages if you caused it wilfully or negligently; (3) repair and deduct after 30 days' written notice (up to $400 or half a month's rent, whichever is less); (4) for hot water, heat, water or electricity failures lasting 48 hours after notice, termination, keeping two-thirds of per-diem rent, or substitute housing; (5) rent abatement and termination if you don't deliver possession; (6) proportional rent reduction or termination after a fire or casualty; (7) for an unlawful lockout, recovery of possession or termination plus treble damages or three times per-diem rent; (8) liability for harm from unconsented or negligent entries, and termination for repeated unreasonable entry; (9) retaliation damages of 3 months' rent or treble damages; (10) a receivership petition for serious conditions. Delaware gives the tenant no lien on your property or on rent. Lease terms awarding attorneys' fees to either side are unenforceable, and the statutory damage awards exclude attorneys' fees.

title: Delaware repair and maintenance duties, timelines and code backdrop
bodyText: Alongside the shared maintenance clause, Delaware law sets these duties, which a lease cannot waive. At all times during the tenancy you must: comply with every applicable state or local code governing maintenance, construction, use or appearance of the unit and property; provide a unit that does not endanger the health, welfare or safety of tenants or occupants and is fit for the purpose for which it is expressly rented; keep common areas you maintain clean and sanitary; make all repairs and arrangements needed to keep the unit and appurtenances in as good a condition as they were, or ought by law or agreement to have been, at the start; and keep electrical, plumbing and other facilities you supply in good working order. Timelines run from the tenant's written notice: start reasonable corrective measures (such as getting an estimate) within 10 days and remedy within 30 days, or the tenant may repair and deduct up to $400 or half a month's rent, whichever is less; an essential-service failure (hot water, heat, water, electricity) triggers remedies after 48 hours; a condition depriving the tenant of a substantial part of the bargain allows termination after 15 days. If the unit fails a maintenance code or the lease in the first month, the tenant may end the lease on written notice. Delaware has no statutory list of 'imminently dangerous conditions' and does not treat air conditioning as an essential service, although the State Housing Code requires integral heating, cooling or humidity systems to be kept running at designed capacity. Outside the Landlord-Tenant Code, the State Housing Code (or your city or county's equivalent code) makes every owner who lets a dwelling keep it to minimum standards, enforced by correction orders, misdemeanor fines of $25 to $1,000 per day, condemnation, and liens for demolition or closing costs. Delaware has no separate blight statute giving private actions against inactive owners.

title: Which maintenance duties can move to the tenant in Delaware
bodyText: Delaware's minimum-standards law (the State Housing Code) does not let a lease shift any listed condition to the tenant; it allocates duties by its own terms. The owner must keep buildings and premises to the code, supply approved rubbish containers and covers for every dwelling unit and remove the rubbish, clean shared areas of buildings with 2 or more units, and exterminate before renting and in shared areas. The occupant must keep the part they occupy clean and sanitary, put rubbish and garbage into the containers, keep plumbing fixtures clean, keep a unit rat-proof (paying for extermination if they fail to), and, in a single-family dwelling, handle extermination inside and in exterior areas (except bed bug costs, which follow the bed bug rules).
