Under the Landlord-Tenant Code, any further shift of repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling to the tenant needs a conspicuous writing separate from the lease, for the primary benefit of the unit, not code-compliance work, with consideration apart from the lease or a rent reduction, in good faith, and never as a condition of the lease. Garbage receptacles and removal, and supply of water, hot water, heat and electricity, are your Landlord-Tenant Code duties only if the rental agreement so specifies, but the housing code's rubbish-container and removal duty applies regardless.

title: Specific facilities Delaware requires beyond the general repair duty
bodyText: Beyond the general repair duty and the duty to keep facilities you supply in good working order, Delaware's State Housing Code (or your city or county's equivalent code) names specific facilities: door locks in good repair and capable of tightly securing the door; weathertight windows and doors, openable windows held by hardware, and exit doors openable from inside; common halls and stairways (other than in 1-family dwellings) lit at all times with at least a 60-watt bulb; in each unit its own toilet and lavatory, a bathtub or shower, and a kitchen sink, with hot and cold running water, and water heating able to deliver at least 110°F; heating able to hold 65°F; cooking and refrigeration equipment properly installed by the owner (refrigerators able to keep below 45°F), which the occupant keeps clean; at least two outlets per habitable room and three in kitchens, and a light fixture in halls, bathrooms, laundry and furnace rooms; maintained fire alarms, suppression systems, extinguishers and exit signs, with a safe, unobstructed means of egress; approved rubbish containers; and minimum space (150 square feet for the first occupant and 100 for each additional, 64 square feet per single sleeping room, ceilings of 7 feet 4 inches). Fire-safety law separately requires owners to install smoke detectors (tenants on leases of a month or more keep the batteries working) and, in apartments and similar lodging establishments with fuel-burning appliances or attached garages, carbon monoxide detectors (see the alarm row). Delaware's statutes do not require window screens, mail receptacles or posted street numbers.

title: Promises to repair: no writing or date rule, but oral promises count
bodyText: Delaware has no rule that your promises to clean, repair or improve a unit be in writing, carry a completion date or be made before the lease is signed. Promises you make do bind you: the Landlord-Tenant Code treats every agreement, written or oral, that sets or modifies the terms of occupancy as part of the rental agreement, and it gives the tenant specific rights tied to your promises. If you fail to substantially conform to the lease or a maintenance code at move-in, the tenant may end the lease on written notice during the first month of occupancy, and keeps that right while remaining in reliance on your written or oral promise to correct the problem. If the tenant stays relying on your promise and substantially the same problem recurs within 6 months, the tenant may end the lease on at least 15 days' written notice specifying the breach and the date. Put any promised work, and its completion date, in the lease or a signed addendum so both sides know what was promised.

title: Quiet possession: no express covenant statute, but Delaware protects possession and peaceful enjoyment
bodyText: Delaware's Landlord-Tenant Code does not write out a general covenant of quiet possession or quiet enjoyment, though it refers to one (a landlord renting single rooms in their own home may end an unwritten tenancy 15 days after written notice of a breach of the covenant of quiet enjoyment or similar conduct), and the right-to-counsel law lists 'violation of quiet use and enjoyment' among the landlord-tenant claims it covers. The protections that do the work: you must put the tenant into full possession at the start of the term; you may not remove or exclude the tenant except under a valid court order (the tenant may recover possession or end the lease and recover treble damages or three times per-diem rent); you may not abuse your right of entry or use it to harass, and repeated unreasonable entry demands let the tenant end the lease; and all tenants and their guests must not unreasonably interfere with the peaceful enjoyment of other tenants, which you may enforce under the rules-breach procedure.

title: No statute separating rent receipt from habitability duties, but rent collectors are landlords
bodyText: Delaware has no statute saying a lease, assignment, deed, trust deed or security instrument cannot let someone collect the rent free of the duty to keep the unit fit. The Landlord-Tenant Code reaches the same people another way: 'landlord' includes the owner, lessor or sublessor, anyone authorized to manage the premises, and anyone who directly or indirectly receives rents (other than a bona fide purchaser) without an obligation to pass the whole of them on, as well as anyone you hold out as the party to accept performance and anyone the tenant normally deals with as landlord. Each of them carries the landlord's duties. A mortgagee in possession is an 'owner'. Owners and resident agents not dealing with the tenant remain responsible for the required owner disclosure, and a lease may not exculpate the landlord or make the tenant waive Code rights. Where a tenant receivership is ordered, the receiver collects the rents ahead of any assignment of rents to fix the conditions.

title: Rental inspections: code-official inspections, no statewide rental license
bodyText: Delaware has no statewide rental registration, licensing or periodic inspection program; some cities and counties run their own (flagged, not resolved). Under the State Housing Code, the code official (your city or county, or the Delaware State Housing Authority's Director where a community has not undertaken enforcement) may cause periodic inspections and may enter any structure or premises at any reasonable time to inspect, after showing credentials; if an owner or occupant refuses or obstructs entry, the official may seek a court order. The Director charges $25 for an initial inspection and $10 for each follow-up on the same complaint where the Director enforces the code, and may waive them for good cause. Every occupant must give you, your agent or employee access at reasonable times to inspect, maintain, repair or alter as needed to comply with the code; under the Landlord-Tenant Code the tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to entry for inspection or repairs on 48 hours' notice. No Delaware statute lets the lease itself authorize a housing inspector to enter without the tenant's separate consent, so leave inspector access to the official's own powers. Once Delaware's lead-safe certification program is implemented, pre-1978 units will need inspection and certification by a Department-approved lead inspector.

title: No small-landlord opt-out from tenant repair remedies
bodyText: Delaware has no notice or other procedure that lets a landlord with only a few units opt out of tenants' repair remedies. Repair-and-deduct, the essential-services remedies, termination for an unremedied condition, casualty rights and the receivership petition apply however few units you own, and a lease may not waive them. Delaware's small-landlord rules are different and need no notice: (1) a tenant cannot get free right-to-counsel representation in a case against a landlord who owns an interest in 3 or fewer rental units and is not represented by an attorney or authorized agent; (2) if you rent single rooms in your own primary residence (no more than 3 rooms rented and no more than 3 tenants), a written lease may be ended immediately on notice for a material violation of a regulation given at the start, and an unwritten one 15 or 30 days after written notice; (3) the fair housing accommodation and modification duties (but not the advertising ban) do not reach rooms or units in an owner-occupied building of up to 4 families.

title: Repair notice: written reports required, but actual notice also counts
bodyText: Delaware ties tenant duties and remedies to different kinds of notice. The tenant must report any defective condition the tenant has reason to believe you (or another tenant) must repair in writing, as soon as practicable, and is responsible for harm to you from failing to report in time; but that duty does not apply where you already have actual notice of the condition. The tenant remedies mostly need written notice: termination in the first month, termination after 15 days for a condition depriving the tenant of a substantial part of the bargain, and repair-and-deduct after 30 days (or 10 days to start corrective measures) all run from written notice. The essential-services remedy starts when a failure of hot water, heat, water or electricity continues for 48 hours after the tenant gives you actual or written notice, though the tenant then gives written notice to terminate or withhold. Under the Code a person has notice of a fact if they actually know it, received a Code notice, or have reason to know it from all the facts and circumstances. A lease may ask tenants to make repair requests in writing (and the shared clause does), but because a lease cannot waive Code remedies, it cannot cut off a remedy the statute starts from your actual knowledge, and a lease that lets tenants report verbally does not waive the written-notice steps the statute requires. Written notices must be served by the methods the Code allows (personal delivery, leaving with an adult, registered, certified or first-class mail with a certificate of mailing, or posting plus mail); the Attorney General's summary says email and texts are not valid.

title: Locks and rekeying in Delaware: secure door locks, tenant lock right, rekey after a writ
bodyText: Delaware has no statute requiring deadbolts, door viewers or peepholes, or window latches in rentals, and no general duty to rekey between tenants. Three rules apply. (1) Under the State Housing Code (or your local equivalent), door locks in dwelling units must be in good repair and capable of tightly securing the door, exterior doors, hinges and latches must be in good condition, windows must be held by hardware, and exit doors must open easily from inside. (2) A tenant may install a new lock at the tenant's own cost if the tenant notifies you in writing and gives you a key, the lock fits the existing system, and the installation does not damage the door. (3) When you regain possession through a summary possession case and plan to re-lease the unit, you must have the locks changed at the time of actual repossession; if you don't, you are liable to a new tenant injured by the dispossessed tenant's entry with an old key. Rekeying at every turnover is a sensible practice in any case.

title: No work-card or background-check rule for staff in 55+ housing
bodyText: Delaware has no work-card, licensing or background-check requirement for maintenance or management staff in housing for older persons, or in any other private rental housing. Delaware's senior-housing law is a fair housing exemption: you may make rental units available exclusively to senior citizens (62 or older), and the age and familial-status rules do not apply to qualifying 'housing for older persons' (state or federal elderly programs, housing solely for persons 62 or older, or housing intended and operated for at least one person 55 or older per unit, with at least 80 percent of units so occupied and published age policies). Your liability for harm from entries by your employees or agents applies in senior housing as anywhere else.

title: No express duty to supply a stove or refrigerator
bodyText: Delaware's statutes do not expressly require you to supply a stove, range, oven or refrigerator. The State Housing Code regulates them when they are there: in a dwelling unit that contains cooking and baking facilities, they must be properly installed by the owner and kept clean and in sanitary working condition by the occupant; a refrigerator in the unit must be able to keep an average temperature below 45°F and must likewise be installed by the owner and kept clean by the occupant; and all cooking equipment must be kept free of leaks and obstructions and free from fire, health and accident hazards. The same code says every space used or intended for food preparation must contain suitable space and equipment to store, prepare and serve food in a sanitary manner, and defines a dwelling unit as having permanent provisions for cooking, so supplying basic cooking equipment is the cautious course; check your local housing code, which may be more specific. Appliances you supply are 'facilities supplied by the landlord' that you must keep in good working order, and listing them in the lease avoids disputes.

title: Tenant receivership and code enforcement for substandard rentals
bodyText: Delaware has a tenants' receivership and code-enforcement tools, whatever the building's size. Receivership: any tenant or group of tenants may petition the Justice of the Peace Court if, for 5 days or more after notice to you, there has been a lack of heat, running water, light, electricity or adequate sewage facilities that the lease or a code requires you to provide, or any other condition imminently dangerous to the tenants' life, health or safety. The court notifies the Attorney General's Director of Consumer Protection of each petition. Defenses are that the condition no longer exists at trial, that petitioning tenants or their households or guests caused it wilfully or by gross negligence, or that a petitioner refused reasonable access. Before judgment you (or a mortgagee or lienor) may ask to fix the conditions yourself on posting security. Otherwise the Division of Consumer Protection becomes receiver: it may record a lien, collect and use the rents (ahead of any assignment of rents) to correct the conditions, bring the property into code compliance, pay operating costs and compensate tenants, and if future profits can't cover the work the court may end the leases and order the building vacated. Code enforcement: the State Housing Code official (or your local code agency) may issue correction orders, condemn and placard unfit structures, issue emergency vacate orders, order demolition, and recover closing or demolition costs as a lien collected like real estate taxes. For Delaware State Housing Authority-financed developments, the Authority may also petition the Court of Chancery for a custodianship on similar grounds or for financial mismanagement.

title: No Delaware rule on cable, satellite or internet access in rental buildings
bodyText: Delaware has no statute giving tenants a right to cable television, satellite, broadband or other telecommunications access in a rental building, requiring you to let a provider wire your building, barring exclusive provider arrangements, or barring different rent for cable subscribers. Delaware's cable law governs franchising by the Public Service Commission; a franchisee may acquire an easement across private land only where a public utility already has poles, wires, conduits or cables, through an eminent-domain taking with compensation, and the chapter preempts county cable regulation. Federal rules apply independently (for example, the FCC's over-the-air reception devices rule on tenant antennas and dishes in areas within the tenant's exclusive use). If you charge tenants for a service such as cable, it is not a 'utility service' under the Landlord-Tenant Code (water, sewer, electricity or fuel), so the separate-metering rules do not govern it, but a charge required as a condition of occupancy must not be a nonrefundable fee; offer it as an optional service fee for actual services rendered.

title: Delaware repair-and-deduct, withholding and the consequences of wrongful withholding
bodyText: If you fail to repair, maintain or keep the unit sanitary, or to perform as a statute, code, ordinance or the lease requires, and after the tenant's written notice you either fail to remedy within 30 days or fail within 10 days to start reasonable corrective measures (such as getting an estimate), the tenant may have the work done in a professional manner and deduct a reasonable sum, no more than $400 or half of one month's rent, whichever is less, by giving you receipts covering at least the amount deducted. The remedy is unavailable for conditions caused by want of due care by the tenant, the household or guests, and to a tenant otherwise delinquent in rent; the tenant is liable for damage the tenant or the tenant's repairer causes. For hot water, heat, water or electricity failures (or a condition materially depriving the tenant of a substantial part of the bargain) lasting 48 hours after notice, the tenant may, on written notice, keep two-thirds of per-diem rent for the period, or procure substitute housing with rent abated and you liable for extra cost up to half the abated rent; withholding does not bar the tenant's larger damages claim, and you can avoid liability by showing impossibility of performance. If you sue for possession and the court finds the tenant withheld or deducted wrongfully, you get possession or the amount wrongfully withheld (double if in bad faith), payable within 10 days, failing which the judgment becomes one for that amount plus possession without further notice. A tenant sued for waste over repairs made after advance notice has a complete defense if the work was what a prudent owner would do or did not reduce your reversion's value (and the tenant posts any security the court requires). Delaware has no court rent-escrow program while a unit is certified unfit and no rule barring eviction during such an escrow.

title: Services and utilities you provide: what the lease controls and how far you can limit liability
bodyText: In Delaware the lease decides whether you supply garbage receptacles and removal and whether you supply water, hot water, heat and electricity: you must provide them only if the rental agreement so specifies. Facilities you do supply (electrical, plumbing and others) must be kept in good working order, and the State Housing Code independently requires heating facilities able to hold 65°F, hot and cold running water to fixtures, and rubbish containers with removal. Once you are obliged to supply hot water, heat, water or electricity, a substantial failure lasting 48 hours after the tenant's notice triggers the tenant's remedies (termination, keeping two-thirds of per-diem rent, or substitute housing), and the only statutory escape is a showing of impossibility of performance. A lease may not exculpate or limit your liability arising under law, and knowingly enforcing such a term exposes you to an action for 3 months' rent. So a general lease sentence excusing you for interruptions 'beyond your reasonable control' should be read no wider than the statute's impossibility standard and should not be used to deny a tenant the statutory remedies. You may never discontinue or terminate utility service for nonpayment of rent, utility charges or other breach.

title: Utilities included in rent: lease controls, and bulk-purchased service must stay in the rent
bodyText: When you pay for utilities and include them in rent, the lease's list is what binds you: water, hot water, heat and electricity are your Landlord-Tenant Code duties only if the rental agreement so specifies, and once they are, a 48-hour failure after notice triggers the essential-services remedies. If you buy utility services in bulk, you may not charge tenants individually for them unless each unit is individually metered or the cost is included in each monthly rent payment as the lease provides; you may not later add a separate charge for a utility that is not separately metered (except metering systems already in use before July 17, 1996). Charges that are not based on consumption (for example a flat sewer or trash fee from a local government) may be passed through at actual cost, and apportioned among units in a multi-unit building, only if the rental agreement so provides. You may not cut off utility service for nonpayment of rent or other breach.

title: Utility allowances with tenant overage payments are not allowed unless the unit is separately metered
bodyText: Delaware has no statute on utility allowance plans as such (you pay a utility up to a set monthly amount and the tenant reimburses the excess), but the metering rules decide them. A landlord may not separately charge a tenant for any consumption-based utility service (water, sewer, electricity or fuel) unless it is separately metered (metering systems in use before July 17, 1996 excepted), and may charge for metered service only if the rental agreement so provides. If you buy service in bulk, the cost must either be individually metered or included in each monthly rent payment. So an overage charge on a master-metered utility is barred. Where the unit is separately metered and the lease provides for charges, you may bill only actual cost (no markup, including through a company you own in whole or part), at least monthly, with actual readings at the start and end of the lease and no more than 2 consecutive estimated bills; tenants may inspect the bills and records, which you must keep for 1 year. The Public Service Commission has no jurisdiction over landlords who submeter; the Attorney General's Consumer Protection Unit enforces these rules. Utility charges you make are rent for all Code purposes.

title: Splitting shared utility bills: only non-consumption charges, only if the lease provides
bodyText: Delaware lets you split a shared bill among tenants only for utility charges that are not calculated on consumption (for example, a flat local-government sewer or trash charge). For those, if the rental agreement so provides, you may pass on the actual cost (as charged to you or a company you own in whole or part), prorate or apportion it among units in a multi-unit or apartment building so long as the total charged to all units does not exceed your actual cost, and bill monthly or quarterly as the lease sets out; the tenant may inspect the bills. For consumption-based utilities (water, sewer, electricity or fuel), you may not separately charge a tenant unless the service is separately metered to the unit (metering systems already in use before July 17, 1996 excepted), and if you buy in bulk the cost must otherwise be built into each month's rent. So a ratio, square-footage or headcount split of a master-metered utility bill is barred in Delaware. Separately, you may not require a tenant to contract directly with a utility unless the unit is separately metered (for non-consumption charges, only if the local government or utility permits). These rules apply to every residential lease whatever its term.

title: Getting notice of a tenant's pending gas or electric shutoff: the tenant can name you as third party
bodyText: Delaware has no procedure for an owner, by a separate document, to authorize the utility to warn the owner of a tenant's pending disconnection. What exists instead is a customer-side program: every gas and electric utility (and every municipal electric company) must keep a voluntary third-party notification program under which the account holder may designate, in writing, a third party to also receive the shutoff notice; the third party must agree in writing and is not liable for the bill. So a tenant who holds the account may name you as the third party, but the program is voluntary for the customer, and Delaware law does not make the designation a lease term. Utilities must also give occupants 72 hours' notice, and in the heating and cooling seasons gas and electric utilities must give the account holder 14 days' written notice; where the billing address differs from the unit, that notice goes to both addresses, and for master-metered buildings deferral notices go to every occupant.

title: When the utility account is in your name: shutoff protections and tenant remedies
bodyText: Delaware has no statute letting tenants pay your overdue utility account and deduct it from rent, no liquidated damages for failing to identify tenants to the utility, and no rent receiver triggered by your unpaid utility bill alone. The protections that apply: (1) Utility shutoff rules protect the occupants even when the account is yours: a gas, electric or water utility must give the occupants at least 72 hours' notice before cutting service to a dwelling unit for nonpayment; during the heating season (November 1 to March 31) and cooling season (June 1 to September 30) gas and electric utilities need 14 days' written notice to the account holder, sent to both the billing address and the unit address if they differ; no gas or electric shutoff on days at or below 35°F at 8 a.m., and no electric shutoff on days with a forecast heat index of 95°F or more; none from December 21 to January 1; and for master-metered buildings deferral notices go to every occupant. (2) If the lease makes you responsible for water, hot water, heat or electricity and service fails for 48 hours after the tenant's notice, the tenant may terminate, keep two-thirds of per-diem rent, or move to substitute housing at your partial expense. (3) If a lack of heat, running water, light or electricity you must provide lasts 5 days after notice, tenants may petition for a receivership that collects the rents to fix it. (4) You may never cut off utility service yourself for nonpayment of rent, utility charges or other breach.

title: Utility shutoff rules: 72 hours, seasonal 14-day notice, weather and holiday bans
bodyText: Delaware's utility shutoff statute protects every dwelling unit, whoever holds the account. A gas, water, wastewater or electric seller may not cut service for nonpayment without at least 72 hours' notice to the occupants. During the heating season (November 1 to March 31) and the cooling season (June 1 to September 30), gas and electric utilities need at least 14 calendar days' written notice to the account holder (to the billing address and the unit if different), with documented phone, text or email attempts (two on separate days in the heating season, one after 5 p.m.; one in the cooling season); this is a longer notice period, not a moratorium. Absent a safety emergency, no shutoff outside 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. Monday to Thursday (unless payment and restoration are available at all times), and none from December 21 to January 1. No gas or electric shutoff on a day the 8 a.m. temperature at the county airport is 35°F or below, and no electric shutoff when the forecast heat index is 95°F or more. A physician's, physician associate's or advanced nurse practitioner's certificate that shutoff would harm an ill occupant blocks termination for 120 days (renewable with good-faith payments). Municipal electric companies follow parallel rules. As a landlord you may never shut off a tenant's utilities yourself for nonpayment or breach.

title: No cutoff of landlord-name utilities when a tenant fails to transfer them
bodyText: Delaware has no rule letting you shut off utilities still in your name because a tenant did not move the account into the tenant's name, and no opt-in lease procedure for it. A landlord may not discontinue or terminate utility service for nonpayment of rent, utility charges or other breach; excluding the tenant from use of the unit except under a court order exposes you to treble damages or three times per-diem rent; and if the lease (or a code) makes the utility your duty, a 48-hour failure triggers the essential-services remedies. What you may do: require in the lease that the tenant contract directly with the provider for utilities that are separately metered to the unit (you may not require it for a utility that is not separately metered), treat the failure to transfer as a breach under the 7-day notice-and-cure procedure, and, if the lease so provides and the unit is separately metered, bill the tenant for actual-cost usage in the meantime (those charges are rent). Keep paying, or ask the utility to switch the account, rather than letting service lapse.

title: Submetered utility billing rules (beside the main-pass optional clause)
bodyText: Delaware regulates landlord submetering in the Landlord-Tenant Code, not through the utility regulator, and sets no prescribed disclosure form, type-size rule or building-size thresholds. If you install meters to measure each unit's use: the metering system may be inspected by and must be approved by the Division of Weights and Measures; you may charge only if the rental agreement so provides and only for separately metered service (systems in use before July 17, 1996 excepted); you may charge no more than the actual cost billed to you (or to a company you own in whole or part); you must bill at least monthly, make reasonable efforts to get actual readings that reasonably coincide with your bulk bill, send no more than 2 consecutive estimated bills, and take actual readings at the start and end of the lease; tenants may inspect the bills and records during regular business hours at your office, and you must keep them 1 year; on a tenant's request you must have the meter tested, the tenant paying as additional rent if it is accurate and you paying and replacing it if not. Utility charges are rent for all Code purposes (so the late-charge and nonpayment rules apply), and unless the lease says otherwise they are enforced like rent as to the security deposit, but you may never shut off service for nonpayment. You are not a public utility and the Public Service Commission has no jurisdiction; the Attorney General's Consumer Protection Unit enforces the section and may enter to test meters.

title: Lock changes for abuse victims: no landlord duty, but any tenant may add a lock and courts can award exclusive possession
bodyText: Delaware has no statute requiring you to change locks at a domestic-violence, sexual-offense or stalking victim's request, or letting a victim change locks outside the ordinary rule. The ordinary rule covers most situations: any tenant may install a new lock at the tenant's own cost if the tenant notifies you in writing and gives you a key, the lock fits the existing system, and the installation does not damage the door. In a protection-from-abuse case the Family Court may grant the petitioner (or another resident) exclusive possession of the residence regardless of whose name is on the lease, and may order the abuser to return keys; such an order does not change the lease or title, but you should honor it, for example by not giving a key or entry to the restrained person. The state victims' compensation program can reimburse a crime victim's cost to change locks. Delaware also bars you from evicting, raising rent or cutting services where a tenant is a victim of domestic abuse, a sexual offense or stalking and sought help, and lets such a tenant end the lease on 30 days' notice (see the domestic-violence rows).

title: No key-control or staff background-check mandate
bodyText: Delaware does not require apartment owners, at any size of complex, to adopt a key-control policy, keep a key log, restrict master keys or background-check employees who can enter units. Related duties make key control prudent: you are liable for theft, casualty or other harm resulting from entries by you, your employees or agents, or anyone you let in, when the tenant has not consented or the harm is due to your negligence, and a lease cannot excuse that liability; you must give 48 hours' notice and enter only between 8 a.m. and 9 p.m. except for tenant-requested repairs and emergencies; a tenant who adds a lock must give you a key; and after recovering a unit through a writ of possession you must change the locks before re-leasing or be liable to a new tenant hurt by entry with an old key.

title: Entry in Delaware: consent not unreasonably withheld, notice exceptions, and remedies both ways
bodyText: Beside the main-pass entry clause, these Delaware rules govern. Entry rests on the tenant's consent: the tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent for you to enter to inspect, make necessary repairs, decorations, alterations or improvements, supply agreed services, or show the unit to prospective purchasers, mortgagees or tenants, so a lease 'right of access' should be read as that consent duty, not as a right to enter over a reasonable objection. You must give at least 48 hours' notice and enter only between 8 a.m. and 9 p.m.; no notice is needed for repairs the tenant requested, and in an emergency you may enter at any time. The 48 hours applies to showings too; only for prospective tenants or purchasers may the tenant waive it, and only in a signed addendum or other separate signed document (see the main-pass waiver row). Other entry rights: reading utility meters at reasonable times; entering as reasonably necessary for inspection, maintenance and safekeeping during an extended absence (more than 7 days); and access the State Housing Code gives you for code-required inspection and repairs. Bed bug inspections and treatment entries use the same 48-hour notice. If the tenant unreasonably refuses access, the tenant is liable for harm it proximately causes and a court may enjoin the tenant. If you abuse access or harass, you are liable for theft, casualty or other harm from entries made without the absent tenant's specific consent, without a present tenant's actual consent, or through negligence; repeated unreasonable entry demands or an unconsented unreasonable entry let the tenant end the lease or get an injunction; and a lease clause exempting you from this liability is void, except consent to a particular entry. Delaware has no landlord-initiated temporary-relocation procedure for nonemergency work outside the lead-hazard rules.

title: No no-notice entry for regularly scheduled services, even if the lease says so
bodyText: Delaware has no exception letting you enter without notice for regularly scheduled services such as pest control, filter changes or smoke-alarm checks, even if the lease conspicuously reserves the right. Supplying services 'as agreed to' is one of the purposes for which the tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent, but every non-emergency entry still needs at least 48 hours' notice and must be between 8 a.m. and 9 p.m. The only notice exceptions are repairs the tenant requested and emergencies, and the only notice waiver is for showings to prospective tenants or purchasers in a separate signed document. A lease term dispensing with the 48-hour notice for scheduled services would be a waiver of Code rights, which is unenforceable. Practical approach: give one written notice that lists each scheduled service visit date and time window at least 48 hours ahead.

title: No Delaware statute on smart locks or app-based entry
bodyText: Delaware has no statute aimed at smart locks, keypads, key fobs, biometric or app-based entry in residential rentals, and no rule requiring you to offer a physical key instead. The general rules apply whatever the technology: an electronic lock or remote unlock is still an entry that needs at least 48 hours' notice and must occur between 8 a.m. and 9 p.m. (except tenant-requested repairs and emergencies); you are liable for harm from unconsented or negligent entries by you or anyone you let in, so control access codes and credentials as you would master keys; a tenant may add a lock that fits the existing system if the tenant gives you a key; door locks must be in good repair and able to secure the door tightly; and after a writ of possession you must change the locks (for electronic systems, reset the credentials) before re-leasing.

title: A tenant's belongings left behind: Delaware's judgment-based 7-day rule, the 1-year court track, and no lease shortcut
bodyText: Delaware gives you a short disposal route only after a court judgment. If a tenant wrongfully quits and unequivocally shows by words or deeds an intent not to return, that abandonment entitles you to proceed for summary possession; once you have a judgment for possession and the writ is executed (or, for abandonment and non-abode cases, once there is no appeal), you may immediately remove and store the tenant's belongings at the tenant's expense for 7 days, and if the tenant does not claim them and reimburse your reasonable removal and storage costs, they are deemed abandoned and you may dispose of them without further notice or liability. If the tenant has appealed, storage runs until 7 days after the appeal is decided. Every writ must carry the statutory notice to the tenant. For a deceased sole tenant the 7-day storage is at the estate's expense. Outside those routes there is no statutory notice-and-dispose procedure: property is 'abandoned personal property' only after its owner has left it in another's custody and failed to claim it for 1 year, and title passes only by court order on a sworn petition with lien searches, mailed and posted notice and newspaper advertisement (with a sheriff's or constable's sale if there are lienholders). You have no lien on the tenant's belongings and may not hold them for rent, and a lease cannot exculpate you from liability for them, so lease legends that release you from responsibility for storage or disposition, or that let you keep sale proceeds for rent, are unenforceable in Delaware. Your separate duty to mitigate by re-renting applies after abandonment. Delaware has no 'seven days without electricity' abandonment presumption, no protection-from-abuse hold, no attorney-files rule and no separate plain-language disposition notice beyond the writ language.

title: Abandonment damages and the duty to mitigate
bodyText: If a tenant wrongfully quits the unit and unequivocally shows by words or deeds an intent not to return, the tenant is liable for the lesser of: (1) the entire rent for the rest of the term plus actual damages (beyond normal wear and tear) in preparing the unit for a new tenant; or (2) the rent accrued during the period reasonably necessary to re-rent at a fair rental, plus the difference between that fair rental and the lease rent, plus re-renting expenses, repair of tenant damage beyond normal wear and tear, and a reasonable commission if you paid one. In any event you have a duty to mitigate. After a writ of possession the lease is cancelled, but you may still claim rent due under the lease, you must exercise diligence to re-rent and you bear the burden of showing that diligence; you may sue for rent and possession at the same hearing, and recover the reasonable value of use and occupation up to your actual recovery of the premises. A filed case or a notice does not by itself end the tenant's rent liability, but the measure is limited by the lesser-of rule and your mitigation. A tenant who ends the lease under one of the statutory early-termination grounds owes at most one month's rent for your renovating and re-renting expenses out of the deposit. Delaware's 'extended absence' (more than 7 days) is not abandonment: it lets you enter for inspection, maintenance and safekeeping and, if the lease requires notice of the absence and the tenant didn't give it, makes the tenant indemnify you for resulting harm.

title: Attorney's fees: any lease fee clause is unenforceable in Delaware, for either side
bodyText: Delaware makes unenforceable any rental-agreement provision for the recovery of attorneys' fees by either party in any suit, action or proceeding arising from the tenancy, so there is no reciprocity question: a landlord-only, mutual or prevailing-party fee clause all fail. The Justice of the Peace Court's civil rules add that attorney's fees are never allowed in residential cases brought under the Landlord-Tenant Code. The Code's own tenant damage awards (for prohibited lease terms, unlawful ouster, retaliation) likewise include costs of suit but exclude attorneys' fees. You may still recover court costs: the summary possession judgment awards the successful party the costs of the proceeding, and JP Court costs go to the prevailing party unless the court directs otherwise. Fee awards remain possible only where a separate statute allows them outside the Landlord-Tenant Code, for example to a prevailing tenant in a fair housing civil action, or to a person damaged by a criminal nuisance. Including a fee clause is not one of the listed prohibited terms that carry the 3-months'-rent penalty for knowing enforcement, but it is void; leave it out of Delaware leases (the shared default clause's fee sentence should not be used in Delaware).

title: Fire and casualty: tenant rights, rent, deposits and your possession remedy
bodyText: Beside the main-pass optional casualty clause, Delaware's statute sets these rules. If fire or casualty damages the unit (or property or appurtenances needed to enjoy it) so that enjoyment is substantially impaired, and the tenant's household or guests were not at fault, the tenant may either (1) immediately quit and notify you in writing within 1 week after vacating, ending the lease as of the vacating date (if the tenant doesn't notify you, rent runs to the date you actually learn of the vacating or further occupancy becomes impossible); or (2) if continued occupancy is lawful, vacate the unusable part and pay rent reduced in proportion to the drop in fair rental value. If the lease ends, you must timely return the security deposit, pet deposit and prepaid rent, less what the Code lets you keep, with rent accounted as of the date of the fire or casualty. Rent is not otherwise abated by statute, and the tenant has no casualty termination right when the tenant's side caused it. If a tenant refuses to give up a unit rendered partly or wholly unusable by fire or casualty and you need possession to repair, that is a ground for summary possession. The Code gives you no automatic right to end the lease after a casualty; any landlord termination right must come from the lease and cannot cut down the tenant's statutory rights (a lease cannot waive Code remedies). Delaware has no separate rule letting you modify the repair covenant only in leases of a year or more, and no statutory belongings-retrieval rule after a casualty. The same rules apply to month-to-month and fixed-term leases.

title: Converting a rental building to a condominium or cooperative: 120 days and a 60-day purchase offer
bodyText: Under the Delaware Uniform Common Interest Ownership Act, a declarant (and any dealer) of a common interest community containing conversion buildings must give each residential tenant and subtenant in possession notice of the conversion, with the public offering statement, at least 120 days before they must vacate. The notice must generally describe the tenants' rights and be given as the Act requires. No tenant may be made to vacate on less than 120 days' notice except for nonpayment of rent, waste, or conduct disturbing other tenants' peaceful enjoyment, and the tenancy terms may not be changed during that period; failure to give the notice is a defense to an action for possession. For 60 days after the notice the tenant must be offered the unit, and for the next 180 days the unit may not be offered to others on more favorable price or terms (with exceptions for units restricted to nonresidential use or reconfigured). The conversion does not relieve either side of Landlord-Tenant Code obligations, does not let the declarant end a lease against its terms, and a conversion notice that names a vacate date can double as the statutory notice to vacate (so the Code's 60-day end-of-term notice rules still apply). The public offering statement must include an engineer's or architect's condition report and any uncured code violations. Delaware requires no special 'first clause' or capital-letters conversion statement in the lease, and the Act does not address local conversion moratoria (it says conversions must also comply with all other applicable laws).

title: Criminal activity: immediate termination, the criminal-nuisance law and your exposure
bodyText: Beside the main-pass optional criminal-activity clause, Delaware law gives you these tools and duties. If a tenant's breach causes or threatens irreparable harm to any person or property, or the tenant is convicted during the tenancy of a class A misdemeanor or felony that caused or threatened irreparable harm, you may, without a cure notice, immediately terminate on notice and file for summary possession (and remedy the breach and bill it as rent); such a conviction is also its own ground for summary possession, and cases where you show substantial or irreparable harm are excused from the eviction-diversion mediation and may get a forthwith (expedited) summons. Under the criminal-nuisance law, a property where drug dealing, illegal firearms activity, a violent felony, prostitution or gang activity has occurred is a 'criminal nuisance'; any owner, agent or lessee who permits it is liable, the Attorney General (or a private person on the State's behalf) may sue in Superior Court for closing orders, lease suspension, receivership and civil penalties of $25,000 or up to $1,000 a day, and your failure to start an eviction after certified-mail notice of a tenant's criminal-nuisance activity is prima facie evidence that you knowingly permitted it (both for penalties and for damages suits by injured neighbors). It is an affirmative defense if you prove you tried to abate the nuisance before receiving the State's written notice of intent to sue; sending a § 5513 breach or termination notice, filing for possession, or helping police prosecute are examples of such attempts. If a court finds, after a hearing at which the tenant appeared, that the tenant used the premises for a criminal-nuisance purpose, the lease becomes void at your option and possession reverts to you; the lease need not recite this. Knowingly failing to halt prostitution on premises you control within a reasonable time is a misdemeanor. Delaware has no statute requiring a crime-free lease addendum or making eviction for crime a mandatory landlord duty, and no separate permitting-drug-use crime for landlords.

title: Notice-and-cure tracks and the grounds for summary possession
bodyText: Delaware has separate tracks. Nonpayment: after the late-fee window, you may demand the past-due rent and give written notice that unless paid within the time stated (at least 7 days after the notice is given or sent) you may file to terminate; paying all rent due before you file bars a nonpayment action, and paying all rent due after filing ends that action (in a nonpayment possession case the tenant may also redeem, until the eviction order is actually executed, by paying the past-due amounts the court determines plus court-awarded costs and fees, unless 2 nonpayment possession judgments were entered against the tenant in the 18 months before the case was filed). Rules and covenants: for a breach of a rule or covenant material to the lease, give written notice that substantially specifies the rule, allows at least 7 days to remedy, states that it is given under the statute, and warns that if the violation continues you may terminate and file, and that a substantially similar breach within 1 year lets you rely on the same notice to file. Breaches that are also a material violation of a code or statute duty let you terminate and file; and a breach causing or threatening irreparable harm, or a qualifying criminal conviction, allows immediate termination on notice with no cure. Repairable breaches (cleaning, repair, replacing an item) you may fix and bill as rent. Grounds for summary possession, 'unless otherwise agreed in a written rental agreement': holdover after the lease ends; wrongful failure to pay rent; wrongful deduction from rent; breach of a lawful obligation relating to use of the premises; tenant-employee holdover (30 days after termination, or 15 days if for cause); holdover more than 5 days after a perfected foreclosure sale; wrongful ouster of the rightful tenant; refusal to yield a fire- or casualty-damaged unit you need to repair; a qualifying class A misdemeanor or felony conviction; and the death of a sole tenant. Rule-breach complaints must plead the rule, when and how it was given, the facts, the notice, the continued violation and the rule's purpose. Lease terms cannot shorten the statutory notices (a lease may not waive Code rights).

title: After a tenant default: no self-help, what a possession judgment can include, and repeat breaches
bodyText: Beside the main-pass default clause, these Delaware rules shape your remedies. You may not remove or exclude a tenant except under a valid court order; doing so lets the tenant recover possession or end the lease plus the greater of treble damages or three times per-diem rent, so a lease cannot give you a direct termination-and-reentry right outside the summary possession process. In a summary possession case the judgment awards costs to the successful party, and you may sue for rent and possession at the same hearing; the writ cancels the lease, and you may recover sums due when you filed plus the reasonable value of use and occupation until the writ and until you actually recover the premises, while exercising diligence to re-rent. Delaware does not treble a possession judgment (a fixed sum may be awarded only in forcible-entry or forcible-holding-out cases), and no attorneys' fees are recoverable (lease fee clauses are void). A judgment for rent arrears or unlawful destruction of property may be enforced by wage attachment as provided by law. For rule breaches, a § 5513 notice lets you file on a substantially similar breach within 1 year without a new cure period; Delaware has no rule limiting cures to twice a year. Payment of all rent due before you file bars a nonpayment case, the tenant may redeem until execution (with exceptions for tenants with 2 nonpayment judgments in 18 months), and you may not refuse rent paid by or for the tenant, though you may restrict the method (certified check or money order after judgment), except that a redemption payment by a charitable organization or government entity, including its electronic or written check, must be accepted as if the tenant paid it.

title: No special tenancy rule after a declared disaster; the casualty rule governs
bodyText: Delaware has no statute that ends a tenancy, suspends rent, sets debris-removal or hazard-mitigation duties, or limits rent increases because of a declared natural disaster or state of emergency. The fire-and-casualty rule applies to disaster damage the tenant did not cause: if enjoyment of the unit is substantially impaired, the tenant may quit immediately and give written notice within a week of vacating (ending the lease as of the vacating date), or, if continued occupancy is lawful, stay and pay rent reduced in proportion to the lost rental value; deposits and prepaid rent are then returned with rent accounted as of the date of the casualty. If the unit is unusable and you need possession to repair, refusal to yield is a summary-possession ground. Your ordinary habitability duties continue, and code officials may issue emergency vacate orders for unsafe structures. During a declared emergency, the State Housing Code official's emergency-order power and local emergency rules may also apply.

title: No statute on drug-free or crime-free lease addenda; certified recovery houses are outside the Code
bodyText: Delaware has no statute requiring, authorizing, setting the wording of, or barring a drug-free or crime-free lease addendum, so one is an ordinary lease term enforced through the Landlord-Tenant Code: a material rule or covenant needs a written notice and at least 7 days to cure, unless the breach causes or threatens irreparable harm or the tenant is convicted during the tenancy of a class A misdemeanor or felony that caused or threatened irreparable harm, in which case you may terminate immediately on notice. Any such rule must meet the Code's tests for rules (reasonable, clear, applied fairly to all tenants, given at the start or agreed in writing if a substantial change). Federally assisted housing has its own HUD lease terms. Certified recovery houses (substance-free homes certified under the state program) are excluded from the Landlord-Tenant Code; their admission agreements must state termination and relapse policies, be signed before residence, and on termination the house must make a reasonable effort to connect the resident with services.

title: Protection from eviction and retaliation for victims of domestic abuse, sexual offenses or stalking
bodyText: You may not file for summary possession, demand a rent increase, decrease services or otherwise cause a tenant to leave where the tenant is a victim of domestic abuse, a sexual offense or stalking and has obtained or sought help from any court, police, medical emergency, domestic violence or sexual offenses program or service. If the tenant proves you took such an action within 90 days of an incident in which the tenant was a victim, it is presumed unlawful. You can rebut the presumption by showing, for example, a termination notice given before the incident; a good-faith need of the unit for your own immediate residence, for substantial alteration or demolition, or to stop renting it for at least 6 months (or a sale with a purchaser's representation to that effect); a qualifying tax or cost increase or capital improvement (at least 4 months before the rent demand, prorated); that the rent does not exceed that of similar units in the complex; competent evidence that the abuse poses a viable and substantial risk of serious physical injury to a tenant living in another unit of the same building; or that you stopped the prohibited action after being told the tenant is a victim. A tenant who is otherwise delinquent in rent cannot use this protection. Victim status is verified by an official document (such as a court order) or a statement from a reliable third-party professional, which the victim must supply (see the qualifying-documents row). Delaware's fair housing law does not list victim status as a protected class, and Delaware has no separate eviction defense or repayment-plan clock for victims beyond this section.

title: Early termination for victims of domestic abuse, sexual offenses or stalking
bodyText: A tenant who is the victim of domestic abuse, sexual offenses or stalking, or who has obtained or is seeking relief from domestic violence or abuse from any court, police agency, or domestic violence program or service, may end the tenancy on 30 days' written notice, with the 30 days starting on the first day of the month after you actually receive the notice (so the tenancy ends 30 days counted from the first day of the following month, around the end of that month; after a February start it runs a day or two into the next month). When the tenant rightfully terminates, both sides' duties under the lease end and remaining obligations are settled as soon as practicable; your deposit claim for renovating and re-renting expenses caused by a termination under this section is capped at one month's rent, though you may still deduct rent owed through the termination date and damage beyond normal wear and tear. 'Domestic abuse' covers any act or threat that is a crime under Delaware law or meets any Delaware Code definition of domestic violence or abuse; the statute does not limit who the abuser must be (household member, co-tenant or stranger), and has no special perpetrator-only termination or landlord-as-abuser route. The statute speaks of 'the tenancy' being terminated and does not say whether co-tenants stay bound; treat that as unresolved and address it in any agreement with the remaining tenants. The right applies to month-to-month and fixed-term leases and cannot be waived by the lease.

title: What documents verify domestic abuse, sexual offense or stalking status
bodyText: Delaware lets victim status be verified by an official document, such as a court order, or by a reliable third-party professional: for domestic abuse, a law-enforcement agency or officer, a domestic violence or domestic abuse service provider, or a health care provider; for sexual offenses and stalking, a law-enforcement agency or officer, a sexual assault service provider, or a health care provider. It is the victim's responsibility to provide the reliable statement from the third party. The statute sets no form, no deadline for producing the document, no confidentiality rule for it, and no right for you to demand the perpetrator's name. Use the verification only to apply the victim protections and early-termination right, and keep it private.

title: Early termination in Delaware: the statutory 30-day rights, deposit cap and abandonment test
bodyText: Beside the main-pass early-termination clause, Delaware sets statutory early-termination rights that a lease cannot take away or burden. On 30 days' written notice (the 30 days starting the first day of the month after you actually receive it) a tenant may end the tenancy when: the tenant's current employer moves the job so the tenant must relocate more than 30 miles; serious illness of the tenant, or death or serious illness of an immediate family member living there, requires a permanent move; the tenant is accepted into senior housing, a group or cooperative living facility or retirement home, or into government- or nonprofit-subsidized housing; the tenant enters active military duty after signing; the tenant is a victim of domestic abuse, a sexual offense or stalking or is seeking relief from abuse; or, on the tenant's death, the surviving spouse or personal representative ends it. For these terminations your deposit claim for renovating and re-renting costs is capped at one month's rent, so a lease early-termination fee should not be charged on top of a statutory termination. A contractual early-termination option (the tenant chooses to leave on notice and pay an agreed amount) is not one of these rights; Delaware has no statute requiring it to be in a separate addendum or capping its amount, but it should not exceed what you could recover for a wrongful early departure, which is the lesser of the remaining rent plus turnover damage, or rent for the reasonable re-renting period plus any rent shortfall, re-renting expenses, damage repair and a reasonable commission, always subject to your duty to mitigate. A tenant who simply moves out without notice has not necessarily abandoned the unit: abandonment requires that the tenant wrongfully quit and unequivocally indicate by words or deeds an intent not to return; a mere absence of more than 7 days is an 'extended absence' that lets you enter for inspection, maintenance and safekeeping. Even after abandonment you regain possession through summary possession, not by declaring the lease ended.

title: No statute on the lease or rent after an eminent-domain taking; displaced tenants get relocation benefits
bodyText: Delaware has no statute saying what happens to a residential lease, or to the rent, when the government takes all or part of the property by eminent domain, and none letting the condemnation court cancel the lease and end the rent; the lease and court decisions govern, so the library's casualty and condemnation language is the place to address it. Two statutes protect your tenants when a public agency acquires the property. An agency must schedule its project so that, as far as practicable, no lawful occupant must move from a dwelling without at least 90 days' written notice, and if it lets an owner or tenant stay on a short-term rental basis it may charge no more than fair rental value for a short-term occupier. A tenant displaced from a dwelling occupied for at least 90 days before negotiations began is entitled to moving expenses and a replacement-housing payment of up to $5,250 to rent a comparable dwelling for up to 42 months (or apply toward a down payment). If the taking makes the unit unusable, the fire-and-casualty rule does not literally apply, but the tenant's habitability remedies may.

title: An LLC or corporation landlord may appear in JP Court through a certified non-lawyer agent
bodyText: If your rental is owned by a corporation, LLC, partnership or other artificial entity, it may prosecute or defend a civil action in the Justice of the Peace Court (where summary possession cases are heard) through an officer or employee who is not a lawyer, if that person has the entity's authorization, has filed a Certificate of Representation with the Chief Magistrate (with a $20 annual registration fee), and complies with Delaware Supreme Court Rule 57 (the JP Court's 'Form 50' agent). A statute likewise lets a corporation prosecute a JP civil action through a Rule 57-qualified officer or employee. Summary possession appeals are heard by a three-judge panel of the Justice of the Peace Court itself; cases in other courts generally need a Delaware lawyer. Representation matters for right-to-counsel eligibility: tenants of a landlord that owns 3 or fewer units and is not represented by an attorney or a Rule 57 agent are not eligible for free counsel, and the annual right-to-representation report tracks the experience of Form 50 agents.

title: No statutory termination right for environmental or public-health events
bodyText: Delaware gives neither you nor the tenant a statutory right to end a lease because a sudden environmental or public health event (contamination, a chemical spill, mold, wildfire smoke, flooding) or a government order makes occupancy impossible or unsafe. The general rules apply instead: fire-and-casualty rights where the damage is a casualty the tenant did not cause; the tenant's termination right for a condition depriving the tenant of a substantial part of the bargain, immediately on notice if the unit is uninhabitable or an imminent threat; essential-services remedies; and code officials' emergency vacate and condemnation orders. Once the lead-safe certification program is implemented, a unit found uninhabitable because of a lead-based paint hazard requires you to provide alternative housing during abatement, with at least 10 days' notice before the tenant must move. Because a landlord termination option for such events is not authorized by the Code and a lease cannot cut down the tenant's remedies, any such clause should be drafted narrowly and reviewed for Delaware.

title: No hardship stay in Delaware evictions; the stays that do exist
bodyText: Delaware has no statute or JP Court rule letting the court postpone an eviction because of the tenant's hardship, age, disability, children, the weather or the season. The delays that exist are specific. (1) Appeal window: the court may not issue the writ of possession during the 5-day period to request an appeal (the JP Court's civil rule says no writ for 10 days after judgment unless an appeal is filed); after it, the writ may issue on your request even if the tenant appealed, unless the tenant filed a bond or other assurance (or obtained in forma pauperis status) to stay it. If you execute before the appeal is decided and the tenant wins, you owe reasonable cover damages such as substitute housing or relocation costs, plus court costs and fees. (2) Good-faith rent dispute: if the nonpayment default arose from a good-faith dispute, the tenant may stay the judgment by paying all rent due and costs, or by an undertaking to pay within 10 days. (3) Redemption: in a nonpayment case the tenant may redeem until the eviction is actually executed by paying all past-due amounts the court determines, including rent due under the lease and court-awarded costs and fees; the court then stays and vacates the possession judgment (unless the tenant has had 2 nonpayment possession judgments in the prior 18 months). (4) Execution itself requires at least 24 hours' notice from the constable or sheriff and must occur between sunrise and sunset. (5) Before trial, nonpayment and breach cases go to the eviction-diversion mediation, which must be completed at least 48 hours before trial, though the tenant's failure to participate does not delay trial.

title: The Delaware summary possession process, step by step
bodyText: Delaware evictions are summary possession actions in the Justice of the Peace Court for the county (and territorial area) where the unit is. You may not use self-help. Before filing you give the required notice: for nonpayment, a written demand allowing at least 7 days after it is given or sent (served after the 5-day late-fee window); for a rule or covenant breach, a 7-day notice to cure; for the end of a term, 60 days' written notice. When you give a nonpayment or breach notice, and at signing and first renewal, you must also give the tenant the right-to-representation materials approved by the state's Right to Representation Coordinator. You file a complaint stating your interest, the tenant's interest, the unit, the facts (attaching the written notice) and the relief (rent may be included if the notice of complaint conspicuously says so); rule-breach complaints need extra detail. The court issues process and a hearing notice, served 5 to 30 days before the hearing, personally, by leaving it with a person of suitable age who resides or is employed in the unit, or, after reasonable effort, by posting plus certified or first-class mail with a certificate of mailing. Most cases are then scheduled for court-run mediation (eviction diversion) before trial, completed at least 48 hours before trial; trial may not start until you have engaged in mediation unless the tenant fails to engage within 15 days of service. The tenant may answer orally or in writing with any legal or equitable defense or counterclaim within the court's jurisdiction; either side may demand a jury (you when filing, the tenant within 10 days of service). Trial may be adjourned up to 10 days on a showing of need. Judgment awards costs to the winner (no attorneys' fees); a default judgment requires proof of actual notice (posting plus first-class mail counts) and may be vacated on motion within 10 days. Either side may appeal within 5 days to a three-judge panel (trial de novo after a bench trial), but an appeal stays the judgment only with a bond or other assurance (or in forma pauperis status). The writ issues only after the appeal time; the constable or sheriff gives at least 24 hours' notice and executes between sunrise and sunset. Delaware has no good-cause eviction rule after 12 months, no pay-into-court requirement while trial is adjourned, and no ban on court forms; the tenant may raise wrongful-withholding issues, and you may get double damages for bad-faith withholding.

title: Shielding of eviction records (25 Del. C. § 5720)
bodyText: Since January 2026 (6 months after the act's July 29, 2025 approval), a tenant who was the defendant in a summary possession case may ask the court to shield the record, with no filing fee, and the court must grant it if any of these applies: the judgment (on the merits, by default or stipulated) is 5 or more years old, any money award is paid, and the tenant has had no similar judgment within 5 years of the motion; the case was resolved by a stipulated agreement the tenant complied with; you withdrew the complaint; the court dismissed it; the tenant won; you and the tenant agree to shielding; or shielding is clearly in the interests of justice. A shielding order sets aside the judgment, the case is deemed never filed and the tenant may answer questions about it accordingly, and within 45 days the court removes it from public systems. Shielded records may be disclosed only to the Department of Justice (confidentially), to the tenant, or in redacted form when the court finds publication in the public interest. The statute does not give the landlord a formal right to object, but the eligibility findings are the court's to make, so you may be heard on whether a ground applies. Practical effects: you may not be able to find a shielded case in screening, and a stipulated settlement you sign can make the tenant eligible once the tenant complies, so consider that when negotiating.

title: No lease designation of a person to accept eviction papers
bodyText: Delaware does not provide for a lease naming someone to accept eviction papers or Code notices for the tenant. The statute fixes service. Code notices (such as the nonpayment demand or the 7-day breach notice) go to the tenant personally, by leaving a copy at the rental unit or usual abode with an adult residing there, by registered, certified or first-class mail with a certificate of mailing addressed to the leased premises, by posting combined with a return receipt or certificate of mailing, or by a court-appointed special process server. The summary possession complaint and hearing notice are served like a summons, or by leaving them with a person of suitable age and discretion who resides or is employed in the unit, or, after reasonable effort, by posting plus certified or first-class mail (with certificate of mailing) to the unit and any other address known to you as reasonably chosen to give actual notice. The JP Court's summons rule also allows delivery to an agent authorized by appointment to receive service, but no Delaware statute or rule recognizes a lease term as that appointment, so do not rely on one. The lease should, however, state your own address for notices (and your owners' and agents' names and addresses), since tenants serve you there.

title: No good-cause eviction rule in Delaware
bodyText: Delaware has no general good-cause or just-cause eviction rule for residential rentals, whatever the length of tenancy. Either you or the tenant may end a fixed-term lease at its expiration by at least 60 days' written notice before the end of the term, or a month-to-month tenancy on at least 60 days' written notice running from the first day of the month after actual notice; a lease of 1 year or more in which neither side gives timely notice becomes month-to-month on the same terms. A renewal on changed terms needs 60 days' written notice and is deemed accepted unless the tenant gives notice of termination at least 45 days before the term ends. Limits that do apply: you may not end or refuse to renew in retaliation for code complaints, tenant organizing or the tenant's pursuit of legal remedies (presumed within 90 days), or where the tenant is a victim of domestic abuse, a sexual offense or stalking who has obtained or sought help from a court, police, medical emergency, domestic violence or sexual offenses program or service (unless the tenant is otherwise behind on rent), or for a fair-housing-protected reason (including source of income); and for federally subsidized units, federal law and guidelines (which often require good cause) control where they conflict with the Code. The right-to-counsel law recognizes that some rental agreements may be ended only for good cause or material violation. Manufactured home communities have their own rules (out of scope).

title: Fast-track possession for dangerous conduct: immediate termination and the forthwith summons
bodyText: Delaware has no separate expedited eviction statute for drug or violent crime, but the ordinary process has fast lanes for dangerous conduct. If a tenant's breach causes or threatens irreparable harm to any person or property, or the tenant is convicted during the tenancy of a class A misdemeanor or felony that caused or threatened irreparable harm, you may terminate immediately on notice (no 7-day cure) and file for summary possession; the conviction is also its own ground. If you show the court by substantial evidence that the tenant has caused substantial or irreparable harm to your person or property, the JP Court must issue a forthwith summons to expedite the case, and such cases (and immediate-termination cases under § 5513(b)) are not sent to the eviction-diversion mediation. Separately, under the criminal-nuisance law the Superior Court may issue temporary closing orders barring a tenant defendant from residing at or contacting the premises, after notice and a hearing within 10 days (or ex parte orders against waste and evidence tampering), and a court finding at a hearing the tenant attended that the tenant used the premises for a criminal-nuisance purpose voids the lease at your option. Third parties (the Attorney General, or any person on the State's behalf) may bring criminal-nuisance actions, but those are abatement suits, not landlord-tenant evictions.

title: Tenants when the rental is foreclosed: notice, the purchaser's writ and the 5-day holdover ground
bodyText: Delaware has no state statute requiring you to disclose a pending foreclosure to tenants or making a lease survive a foreclosure sale, but it does set procedure. In a mortgage foreclosure (scire facias sur mortgage in Superior Court), tenants holding an estate for years or at will are not necessary parties, but must receive written notice as the Superior Court's rules prescribe. After the sheriff's sale, the purchaser may get a writ of possession against a person in possession whose rights arose after the mortgage (for an execution sale, after the order or judgment); a writ is not awarded against a defendant in possession bona fide as a tenant under another; and when the person in possession is a tenant, the court must stay execution until the usual expiration of the tenant's year according to local letting custom. Separately, a tenant who holds over for more than 5 days after the property has been duly sold on foreclosure and title perfected may be removed by summary possession in the JP Court. After any judicial or execution sale the purchaser is entitled to the rent from the day of sale, apportioned with the former landlord by time, and if the lease postdates the judgment or order and its rent is below a fair rent, the purchaser may demand a fair rent. Federal law (the Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act, 12 U.S.C. § 5220 note) independently requires a successor in interest after foreclosure on residential property to give bona fide tenants at least 90 days' notice and to honor bona fide leases to their end, with exceptions; it applies on top of these state rules. The Landlord-Tenant Code also counts a mortgagee in possession as an 'owner', so a lender that takes possession takes on landlord duties.

title: Undoing a nonpayment forfeiture: pay before filing, pay before judgment, or redeem until execution
bodyText: Delaware gives a tenant behind on rent three chances to stop a nonpayment eviction, in every residential tenancy. (1) Before you file: if the tenant, or anyone on the tenant's behalf, pays all rent due before you start a court action, you may not file for summary possession based on that nonpayment. (2) After filing, before judgment: if all rent due under the lease is paid after you file, you may not maintain the nonpayment action. (3) After judgment, until execution: under the right of redemption (effective September 1, 2026), the tenant may redeem by tendering all past-due amounts the court determines, including all rent due under the lease plus court-awarded costs and fees, at any time before the eviction order is actually executed; you must then immediately notify the court and the constable or sheriff and try to prevent execution, and the court stays and then vacates the possession judgment. Redemption is not available to a tenant with 2 nonpayment possession judgments in the 18 months before the case (a vacated judgment still counts). A check from a charity or government agency counts as the tenant's payment. Throughout, you may not refuse rent paid by or for the tenant; you may restrict the payment method to those the lease accepts before judgment, and require certified check or money order after judgment (except for charity or government payments), and after a posted writ you may ask the court to wait for checks to clear. A good-faith rent dispute also lets the tenant stay a judgment by paying rent due and costs, or by an undertaking to pay within 10 days. The former practice of preserving your case by a written reservation of rights when accepting rent was struck by the 2026 amendment.

title: Lease guaranties: a signed writing, no renewal or maximum-liability statute
bodyText: Delaware has no statute specific to lease guaranties: none limits a guarantor to the original term unless the lease states renewal terms, and none requires a separate guaranty to state a maximum liability or end date. Under the statute of frauds, a promise to answer for another's debt of $25 or more must be in a writing, or a memorandum, signed by the guarantor or someone the guarantor authorized in writing (smaller promises of $5 to $25 need a witness's oath or a signed note). Whether a guarantor stays bound through a renewal, a month-to-month extension (which a 1-year-or-longer lease becomes automatically if neither side gives notice) or a renewal on modified terms depends on the guaranty's wording and contract law, so state in the guaranty whether it covers renewals, extensions and modified terms, and for how long. The Code's money caps should be treated as reaching money taken from a guarantor too: the security deposit definition covers any deposit given to the landlord to be held for the rental term, capped at one month's rent for leases of 1 year or more (and for month-to-month tenancies after a year), and you may not take 'assurance money' or other payments beyond the listed application fee, deposits and surety-bond fees. A tenant may alternatively buy a surety bond in place of a deposit if you accept it. For right-to-counsel eligibility, a cosignor's household income is counted when the tenant is a full-time student.

title: Holdover in Delaware: one statutory measure, no older double-rent statute
bodyText: Beside the main-pass holdover clause, two points from the topic's questions. (1) Delaware has a single holdover damages rule, in the Landlord-Tenant Code: a tenant who stays after the lease expires or after you rightfully terminate, without your consent, owes a sum not to exceed double the monthly rent under the prior agreement, computed and prorated daily for each day of holdover, plus further losses a court determines. No older double-rental-value statute outside the Code survives for residential leases, so there is nothing to stack on top of that measure. (2) Holdover is distinct from the automatic month-to-month extension: if a lease of 1 year or more ends without either side's timely notice (60 days from you, 45 days from the tenant), the tenancy continues month-to-month on the same terms, and the tenant is not a holdover. A tenant who wrongfully stays is a 'holdover tenant' you may remove by summary possession; and if a holdover blocks a new tenant and you haven't sued, the new tenant may sue the holdover and charge the costs and substitute housing against rent owed to you.

title: Waiving judgment exemptions in a lease: only spouses jointly, limited value, wages protected
bodyText: Delaware has no general homestead exemption from collection of an ordinary judgment, and no statutory waiver wording for leases.
