Its execution exemptions cover listed personal property (family Bible, school books and library, family pictures, burial lot, wearing apparel, trade tools up to $75 in New Castle and Sussex or $50 in Kent, sewing machines, leased musical instruments) and, for a head of family, up to $500 of other personal property the debtor selects; 85 percent of wages is exempt from attachment, and only one wage attachment may be made at a time. The statute lets 'any husband and wife jointly' waive the personal-property exemptions in §§ 4902-4911, so a lease waiver signed by one tenant alone, or covering wages, is not effective; Delaware sets no lease form or type rules for such a waiver. Bankruptcy exemptions (up to $25,000 of personal property and non-residence equity, $200,000 of principal-residence equity, $25,000 each for a vehicle and trade tools) are separate and cannot be waived in a lease. Because the waivable exemptions are small and a waiver only helps collect a money judgment (you have no lien on, and may not distrain, the tenant's goods), the library offers no Delaware exemption-waiver clause.

title: Early termination for illness, moves to senior or care housing, and death
bodyText: Delaware lets a tenant end the tenancy on 30 days' written notice (the 30 days start the first day of the month after you actually receive it) when: the serious illness of the tenant, or the death or serious illness of a member of the tenant's immediate family living in the unit, requires a permanent change of residence; the tenant is accepted for admission to a senior citizens' housing facility (including subsidized public or private housing), a group or cooperative living facility, or a retirement home; or the tenant is accepted into a rental unit subsidized by a government or private nonprofit. On the tenant's death, the surviving spouse or the personal representative of the estate may end the tenancy the same way; for a deceased sole tenant, if an affiant or personal representative presents valid register-of-wills documentation, possession returns to you without a lawsuit once that person says access is no longer needed or 30 days after the death pass without written notice that it is; otherwise you must file for summary possession against the estate, serving the affiant or personal representative at the address they gave, or, if no documentation or good address was provided, serving the register of wills after first publishing notice of the action in a newspaper circulated in the county. The statute requires no medical certificate or minimum age and has no special rule for disabled tenants beyond fair housing accommodations. On a rightful termination both sides' duties end; your deposit claim for renovating and re-renting costs caused by these terminations is capped at one month's rent. The rights apply to fixed-term and month-to-month leases and cannot be waived.

title: No landlord lien or distress on a residential tenant's property
bodyText: Delaware abolished the landlord's right of distress for rent and makes unenforceable any landlord lien on the tenant's personal property and possessions (unless perfected before the Landlord-Tenant Code took effect). Distress survives only under commercial leases, as a court action in the Justice of the Peace Court. So a residential lease may not give you a contractual lien, a security interest in household goods, or a right to seize, hold or sell the tenant's belongings for rent; holding belongings until rent is paid would also be an unlawful exclusion risk, and a clause conditioning return of abandoned property on paying rent operates as a lien. Your remedies are a money judgment (with wage attachment as the law allows: 85 percent of wages exempt and one attachment at a time) and possession. One statutory priority remains: if another creditor's execution, attachment or sequestration seizes the tenant's goods on the premises, the goods are liable for up to 1 year's rent in arrears or growing due, paid to you from the sale before the other creditor, and the sheriff must give you 10 days' written notice of the sale. Execution exemptions can be waived only by husband and wife jointly.

title: Your remedies when the tenancy ends: possession, rent, or both, and money claims after
bodyText: In Delaware you may seek possession, rent, or both. After a proper nonpayment demand and the notice period, you may sue for rent alone (including accrued late charges as additional rent), or file for summary possession and include the rent due if the notice of complaint conspicuously says so; you may sue for both rent and possession at the same hearing. The writ of possession cancels the lease, but you may still recover sums payable when you filed, the reasonable value of use and occupation up to the writ and your actual recovery of the premises, and rent due under the lease, subject to your duty of diligence in re-renting (which you must prove). If the tenant abandoned, damages follow the lesser-of measure (rest-of-term rent plus turnover damage, or re-renting-period rent plus shortfall, re-renting expenses, repairs and commission). A holdover owes up to double the prior monthly rent per day plus further losses. For damage, the security deposit may be applied first with the itemized-list rules; beyond that you may sue for waste or breach of contract. A claim not filed in the summary possession case may be brought separately, and an action on a promise generally must be filed within 3 years. No attorneys' fees are recoverable; court costs go to the winner; and a judgment for rent arrears or property destruction may be collected by wage attachment.

title: Fixing the tenant's breach yourself and billing it as rent
bodyText: Delaware gives you a statutory self-cure right; no lease clause is needed, though stating it in the lease helps. If a tenant breaches a rule or covenant material to the lease and the breach can be remedied by you (for example by cleaning, repairing or replacing a damaged item), you may remedy it and bill the tenant for the actual and reasonable costs, and the bill is due and payable as additional rent immediately on receipt. Ordinarily you first give the written § 5513 notice allowing at least 7 days to remedy; if the breach causes or threatens irreparable harm to any person or property, you may remedy it without notice and bill the same way (and may also terminate immediately). Because the bill is additional rent, nonpayment can support the nonpayment remedies. Entry to do the work still requires 48 hours' notice between 8 a.m. and 9 p.m. unless it is an emergency, and you may not bill for normal wear and tear or for work that is your own repair duty.

title: No liquidated-damages statute for residential leases; statutory measures and caps govern
bodyText: Delaware's Landlord-Tenant Code and its other statutes do not address a residential lease term fixing in advance what a tenant owes for a breach, and no Delaware regulation in the searched corpus expressly permits keeping an agreed damages amount. The Code's own measures act as limits: abandonment damages are the lesser of the remaining rent plus turnover damage or the re-renting-period measure, with a duty to mitigate; holdover is capped at double the prior monthly rent prorated daily plus proven losses; late charges are capped at 5 percent of monthly rent and may not be imposed within 5 days of the due date; the security deposit may be kept only for actual damage beyond normal wear and tear, rent arrears and reasonable renovating and re-renting costs from premature termination (no more than one month's rent for statutory early terminations), with an itemized list; and you may not charge any nonrefundable fee as a condition of occupancy except optional service fees for actual services. A lease term that conflicts with the Code and is not expressly authorized is unenforceable, so an agreed damages figure that exceeds these measures (or forfeits the deposit as a penalty) is unlikely to be enforced. General contract law on penalties applies otherwise (no published case was searched).

title: No lockout for unpaid rent, even if the lease says so
bodyText: Delaware does not allow a lockout for unpaid rent, and a lease term giving you one is unenforceable. If you or your agent remove or exclude a tenant from the unit except under a valid court order, the tenant may recover possession or end the lease, and recover the greater of treble damages or three times the per-diem rent for the time excluded, plus costs. You also may not shut off utilities for nonpayment or other breach, may not use entry to harass, and may not hold the tenant's belongings for rent (there is no landlord lien). A clause allowing self-help would be a waiver of Code remedies, which a lease cannot contain, and knowingly trying to enforce a prohibited provision exposes you to an action for 3 months' rent. The only lawful route is the nonpayment notice and summary possession; after a writ of possession is executed, you must change the locks before re-leasing.

title: Minors in eviction cases: no filing bar, but guardian, service and default rules
bodyText: Delaware has no statute or JP Court rule barring you from naming a minor as a defendant in a summary possession case, and none dismissing a complaint that does. Practical rules make naming minors unhelpful: possession runs against the tenant (the person entitled under the rental agreement to occupy) and the writ removes all persons, so household minors who are not tenants need not be named. If a minor is a party, the JP Court rules require service on the minor's guardian (or, if none, on an adult with whom the minor lives), let a guardian or next friend defend, require the court to appoint a guardian ad litem for an unrepresented minor, and bar a default judgment against a minor not represented by a guardian or similar representative. A default judgment is likewise barred against a servicemember protected by the federal relief act. Delaware has no statute letting unaccompanied minors contract for housing; a minor's lease is subject to general contract law on minors' capacity (not searched).

title: The Delaware nonpayment demand: timing, contents, service and what cannot be waived
bodyText: Before suing for nonpayment you must give a written demand. Timing: you may send it only after the period between the rent due date and the date late fees may be imposed (late fees may not be imposed within 5 days of the due date, and the due date itself is extended 3 days if you keep no office or payment place in the county). Contents: demand the past-due rent and state in writing that unless it is paid within the time given, which must be at least 7 days after the notice is given or sent, you may file a court action to terminate the rental agreement. Delaware prescribes no verbatim form and no type size. Service: personally, by leaving it with an adult residing at the unit, by registered, certified or first-class mail with a certificate of mailing to the unit, by posting combined with a return receipt or certificate of mailing, or by a court-appointed special process server; email and text are not listed methods. With the notice you must also give the right-to-representation materials approved by the state's Right to Representation Coordinator. Payment of all rent due (by the tenant or anyone on the tenant's behalf) before you file bars a nonpayment case, and you may not refuse rent tendered by or for the tenant, though you may restrict payment methods to those in the lease; Delaware does not limit how often a tenant may cure by paying. A lease cannot waive or shorten the notice, and the lease itself cannot serve as the notice. For leases entered into on or after the March 2027 effective date, if state reentry funds pay part of the rent, you must also help the tenant with a discharge plan and notify the fund (and, where applicable, the Department of Correction and local police) before terminating. Note that the Attorney General's summary (Oct. 2024) still describes the former 5-day notice; the 7-day period applies to notices since September 1, 2026.

title: No Delaware rule allowing a fee for preparing or serving a default notice; treat it as barred
bodyText: No Delaware statute allows, caps or expressly bans a fee charged to the tenant for preparing or serving a nonpayment demand, breach notice or termination notice, but several rules point against one. Code notices may be served by you personally or by mail with a certificate of mailing, so service need not cost much. A fee triggered by late rent is in substance an additional late charge, and the late charge may not exceed 5 percent of the monthly rent or be imposed within 5 days of the due date. A lease term that conflicts with the Code and is not expressly authorized by it is unenforceable, attorneys' fees for notices or cases are never recoverable under a lease, and nonrefundable fees as a condition of occupancy are barred. In a court case, filing and service costs are recovered as court costs awarded to the successful party. The cautious course is not to charge a notice fee in Delaware. (Old fee schedules for officers in commercial distress proceedings do not apply to residential tenancies.)

title: A Delaware lease cannot waive or shorten the statutory notices
bodyText: A Delaware lease may not waive or shorten the notices the Landlord-Tenant Code requires before you end a tenancy: the 7-day nonpayment demand, the 7-day notice to cure a material rule or covenant breach, and the 60-day notice to end a fixed term at expiration or a month-to-month tenancy. A rental agreement may not provide that the tenant waives or forgoes rights or remedies under the Code, a conflicting term is unenforceable, and knowingly trying to enforce a prohibited term exposes you to an action for 3 months' rent. You may agree to give longer notice. The Code itself dispenses with notice only in listed cases: breaches causing or threatening irreparable harm, or qualifying criminal convictions (immediate termination on notice); written leases for single rooms in your own primary residence with no more than 3 rooms and 3 tenants (immediate termination on notice for a material violation of a regulation given at the start); and a substantially similar rule breach within 1 year of a prior § 5513 notice. The only notice the tenant may waive by agreement is the 48-hour entry notice for showings to prospective tenants or purchasers, and only in a signed addendum or other separate signed document.

title: Delaware's criminal-nuisance law: closing orders, receivers, lease suspension and penalties
bodyText: Delaware's nuisance-abatement statute reaches rental property where drug dealing, illegal firearms activity, a violent felony, prostitution, gang activity or another public nuisance has occurred. The Attorney General, or any other person on the State's behalf (for example a neighbor or community group, serving the State Solicitor within 5 days), may sue in Superior Court; the owner, landlord and the involved tenant are in personam defendants, and every tenant or resident who may be affected gets court-ordered notice and a chance to be heard. Remedies include temporary and permanent closing of the premises or part of it (up to 1 year, and only if no less onerous remedy will work), injunctions, seizure and sale of property used in the nuisance, court-ordered repairs with the cost as a lien, suspension or revocation of rental licenses and leases, suspension of government subsidies such as tenant-assistance payments to you, and a receiver who collects all rents and may bring possession actions. Civil penalties are $25,000 or up to $1,000 a day against anyone who knowingly permitted the nuisance; your failure to start an eviction after certified-mail notice of the tenant's criminal-nuisance activity is prima facie evidence that you knowingly permitted it, and neighbors damaged by the nuisance may sue for actual damages and their costs and attorney fees. You may be ordered to pay relocation assistance (moving costs, deposits, lost rent) to uninvolved tenants displaced by a closing if you knew or had reason to know of the nuisance. It is an affirmative defense if you prove you tried to abate the nuisance before the State's written notice of intent to sue; serving a § 5513 breach or termination notice, filing for possession or helping police prosecute are examples of such attempts. Delaware has no rule requiring the lease to summarize this statute.

title: No owner-move-in termination right; end the tenancy at the term or on 60 days for month-to-month
bodyText: Delaware has no statute giving you a right to end a lease mid-term so you or a relative can move in, no just-cause rule that makes owner move-in a special ground, and no rule that a lease must reserve such a right. To recover the unit you give at least 60 days' written notice before a fixed term expires, or 60 days' written notice for a month-to-month tenancy (running from the first of the month after actual notice). A good-faith need to occupy the unit immediately as your own residence matters in two places: it is a defense to a retaliation claim, and it rebuts the presumption that an action against a domestic-abuse victim is unlawful. Because the Code lists the landlord's termination routes and makes conflicting lease terms that it does not expressly authorize unenforceable, a lease clause letting you end a fixed term early to move in is untested in Delaware and the library offers no Delaware version; a shorter lease term or a month-to-month tenancy is the safer way to keep flexibility.

title: No end-of-term possession bond, and no confessed judgment in a Delaware lease
bodyText: Delaware has no statute letting a residential tenant give a bond to deliver possession at the end of the term enforced by a confessed judgment, and a rental agreement may not authorize anyone to confess judgment on a claim arising out of the lease; such a provision is void, and knowingly trying to enforce it exposes you to an action for 3 months' rent. The only bonds in Delaware summary possession practice are the tenant's appeal bond (to stay a judgment pending appeal) and the good-faith-dispute undertaking. If a tenant stays after the term, your remedies are holdover damages (up to double the prior monthly rent per day plus proven losses) and summary possession. A tenant may, with your acceptance, buy a surety bond in place of a security deposit, but that is a deposit substitute, not a possession bond.

title: Failure to deliver possession: rent abates and the tenant may end the lease at any time
bodyText: Delaware sets the remedy when you can't put the tenant into full possession at the start of the term, and a lease cannot narrow it. Rent abates for any period the tenant is unable to enter. On notice to you, the tenant may end the lease at any time the tenant is unable to enter, and you must return all money paid for the unit, including prepaid rent, the pet deposit and the security deposit; the statute sets no waiting period. If the inability to enter is caused wrongfully by you (or someone with your consent or license) because of substantial failure to conform to existing building and housing codes, the tenant may also recover reasonable substitute-housing expenses for up to one month, capped at one month's agreed rent, by suit or by deducting from rent on submitting receipts. If a holdover tenant is the cause and you haven't sued, the incoming tenant may bring the summary possession action against the holdover and charge its costs and substitute housing against the rent. Delaware has no statute requiring alternate housing during a later habitability failure beyond the essential-services substitute-housing remedy and, once implemented, lead-hazard alternative housing.

title: Tenant property after the writ: 7 days' storage, the writ notice, and your duties
bodyText: After judgment the court issues a writ of possession only once the time to appeal or move to vacate has passed; the constable or sheriff gives at least 24 hours' notice and executes between sunrise and sunset, removing all persons and putting you in full possession; you must notify the constable to take the steps needed. If the tenant has not removed belongings when the writ is executed, you may immediately remove and store them at the tenant's expense for 7 days; if the tenant does not claim them and reimburse your reasonable removal and storage costs by then, they are deemed abandoned and you may dispose of them without further notice or obligation. If an appeal has been filed, storage runs until 7 days after the appeal is decided. Every writ must carry the statutory notice telling the tenant these rules (one version where no appeal is filed and one where it is). Delaware sets no inventory requirement, no warehouse-storage option, no care standard and no rule for pets or other animals left behind (handle animals humanely through animal control). At actual repossession you must change the locks if you will re-lease, or be liable to a new tenant hurt by entry with an old key. A former tenant who returns without license commits criminal trespass (first degree, a class A misdemeanor, in a dwelling). Delaware gives the landlord no special statutory immunity for writ execution; follow the writ terms exactly. If you execute while an appeal is pending and the tenant wins, you owe reasonable cover damages.

title: The right of redemption after a nonpayment judgment (§ 5716A, effective September 1, 2026)
bodyText: In a nonpayment summary possession case (or a manufactured-home lot case) where you requested or obtained a judgment of possession, the tenant may redeem the unit by tendering all past-due amounts as determined by the court, including all rent due under the lease plus all court-awarded costs and fees, at any time before the eviction order is actually executed (there is no 48-hour cutoff). Once you or your agent receive the payment, you must immediately notify the court and the constable or sheriff and make all reasonable efforts to stop execution; the court then issues an immediate stay, allows at least 5 days for filings, and on notice or adequate evidence of redemption vacates the possession judgment and terminates the writ. If payment comes after the writ is posted, a request to stay must be filed, and you may ask the court to wait until checks clear. A charity's or government agency's electronic or written check counts as the tenant's payment. You may restrict payment methods to those in the lease before judgment and require certified check or money order after judgment, except for charity or government payments. Redemption is not available to a tenant against whom 2 nonpayment possession judgments were entered in the 18 months before the case (a vacated judgment still counts). Delaware does not require any reservation-of-rights wording when you accept partial rent, and you may not refuse rent paid by or for the tenant.

title: Eviction counterclaims: mandatory under JP Court rules, no rent paid into court first
bodyText: In a Delaware summary possession (eviction) case, the tenant may answer orally or in writing at the hearing and may raise any legal or equitable defense or counterclaim within the Justice of the Peace Court's jurisdiction. Delaware's statutes and the JP Court Civil Rules do not make the tenant pay rent into court before raising a defense or counterclaim, and nothing ties a jury demand or an adjournment to a rent deposit; the court may adjourn a trial for no more than 10 days unless all parties consent. Under the JP Court Civil Rules, a claim the tenant has against you that arises out of the same transaction is a mandatory counterclaim (exceptions include a counterclaim over $25,000), and in a residential summary possession case a counterclaim not raised because it was over $25,000 is barred unless filed in a competent court within 60 days of the judgment. The judgment also does not bar an action for equitable relief, filed within 60 days, that could not be sought in the JP Court. Rent comes into the case in four places: (1) to stay a judgment while appealing, the tenant must file an undertaking (with any bond the court requires) to pay costs and all damages, including rent, accruing while the appeal is pending, unless the court grants in forma pauperis status; (2) after a nonpayment judgment that arose from a good-faith dispute, the tenant may stay proceedings by paying all rent due and costs, or by an undertaking to pay them within 10 days; (3) a tenant may redeem the unit until the eviction order is actually executed by paying everything the court finds due plus costs and fees (not available after 2 nonpayment possession judgments in the prior 18 months); and (4) if the court finds the tenant wrongfully withheld rent under the essential-services remedy, it orders the amount (double if in bad faith) paid within 10 days, or you get a money judgment plus possession. No published case was searched.

title: Expunged records: applicants need not disclose them and should not be asked
bodyText: Delaware law says a person is not required to disclose, and should not be asked to disclose, to anyone for any purpose, that the person was arrested for, charged with or convicted of an offense whose records were expunged. An offense expunged under the adult expungement law does not have to be disclosed for any reason, and an expunged juvenile arrest does not have to be disclosed as an arrest for any reason. It is a misdemeanor for anyone with access to an expunged record to open it or disclose it without a court order (law-enforcement uses aside). In practice: do not ask applicants about expunged arrests, charges or convictions, phrase any criminal-history question to exclude expunged records, and never treat an applicant's silence about an expunged matter as a false or incomplete application or as a breach of the lease's application-accuracy clause. Expungement is granted by the courts (some cases are eligible automatically, others on petition), so an applicant may honestly answer 'no' about a matter that appears on an old private report.

title: No right to end a lease because a repair would cost too much
bodyText: Delaware's statutes give you no right to end a lease because a needed repair would cost too much compared with the rent or the property's value. Your duties to keep the unit code-compliant, safe and fit, and to make all repairs needed to keep it in as good a condition as at the start of the tenancy, apply at all times during the tenancy, whatever the cost. After a fire or casualty that substantially impairs the unit (not the tenant's fault), the choice belongs to the tenant: quit immediately (notifying you in writing within 1 week after vacating) or, if continued occupancy is lawful, stay in the usable part at a proportionally reduced rent; the statute gives you no matching right to terminate. If you decide not to repair, the lawful routes are the ordinary ones: give at least 60 days' written notice before the end of a fixed term, or 60 days' written notice to end a month-to-month tenancy (the 60 days start on the first day of the month after actual notice). If the tenant recently complained of code violations or exercised a legal remedy, a non-renewal within 90 days is presumed retaliatory; it is a defense that you seek possession in good faith to substantially alter, remodel or demolish the premises, or to stop renting the unit for at least 6 months.

title: Retaliation is prohibited; 90-day presumption; 3 months' rent or treble damages
bodyText: Delaware prohibits retaliation. You may not seek summary possession or otherwise try to make the tenant leave involuntarily, demand a rent increase, or decrease services after (1) the tenant complained in good faith to you or to a code authority of a building, housing, sanitary or other code violation affecting the unit, (2) a state or local authority filed a notice or complaint of such a violation, (3) the tenant organized or is an officer of a tenants' organization, or (4) the tenant has pursued or is pursuing any legal right or remedy arising from the tenancy. The protection is not limited to complaints: any of the four triggers counts. If you take one of those actions within 90 days after the complaint or act, retaliation is presumed. Defenses include: you gave proper notice under a Code section allowing early termination; you seek possession in good faith to live in the unit yourself, to substantially alter, remodel or demolish it, or to stop renting it for at least 6 months (or you contracted to sell to a buyer who represents one of those uses); the condition was caused by the tenant's household or guests' lack of ordinary care; the unit was fully code-compliant when the complaint was made or when you gave proper end-of-term notice; you are relying on a notice to end a periodic (for example month-to-month) tenancy given before the complaint; the condition could not be fixed before the end of the cure period; or a rent increase is justified by tax or operating-cost increases incurred at least 4 months earlier, a substantial capital improvement completed at least 4 months earlier (within straight-line depreciation), or comparable rents in the complex, or is not directed at this tenant. A tenant you try to dispossess in violation of the rule recovers 3 months' rent or treble damages, whichever is greater, plus court costs (no attorney's fees). Separate, parallel rules protect victims of domestic abuse, sexual offenses and stalking (a 90-day presumption after an incident), and Delaware's fair housing law bars coercing, intimidating, threatening or interfering with anyone exercising fair housing rights.

title: Seasonal rentals: Code exclusion for short nonrenewable rentals in five named hundreds
bodyText: Delaware has one seasonal-rental rule in its Landlord-Tenant Code. A nonrenewable rental agreement of 120 days or less for any calendar year, for a dwelling located within Broadkill Hundred, Lewes-Rehoboth Hundred, Indian River Hundred, Baltimore Hundred or Cedar Creek Hundred, is excluded from the Code. Under the version in force now, the exclusion does not apply if the arrangement was created solely to avoid the Code; a new version of the exclusions section taking effect March 8, 2027 (the bill page says March 9, 2027) keeps the same seasonal exclusion but drops that 'solely to avoid' qualifier. Outside those five hundreds, or for a renewable agreement or one longer than 120 days in a calendar year, a seasonal rental is an ordinary tenancy with the Code's usual notice, deposit, habitability and eviction rules (a lease with no stated term is month-to-month). Transient lodging in a hotel, motel or similar lodging is also excluded. Separately, a state short-term rental lodging tax of 4.5% of the rent applies to every occupancy of a short-term rental, meaning a residential dwelling unit where a tourist or transient guest rents sleeping or living accommodations for no more than 31 consecutive nights (with listed exceptions, including a casual owner-arranged rental substantially below market used no more than 10 nights a year). For an excluded seasonal rental, the library's other Delaware clauses, which assume the Code applies, need a separate review.

title: No self-help eviction: court order and writ required; treble-damage remedy
bodyText: In Delaware you may regain possession only through a summary possession case in the Justice of the Peace Court and a writ of possession. If you or your agent remove a tenant from the unit, or exclude the tenant from it, except under a valid court order, the tenant may recover possession or end the lease, and may also recover the greater of treble the damages sustained or 3 times the per-diem rent for the time excluded, plus court costs (not attorney's fees). A wrongfully ousted tenant may also bring a summary possession case to get back in. The writ is directed to the constable or sheriff, issues only after the appeal or motion period, and the officer must give at least 24 hours' notice and execute it between sunrise and sunset; only then may you remove and store property the tenant leaves (for 7 days at the tenant's expense, or until 7 days after an appeal is decided). Other self-help is barred as well: you may not discontinue or terminate utility service for nonpayment of rent, utility charges or any other breach; the landlord's right of distress is abolished and landlord liens on the tenant's personal property are unenforceable; and you may not abuse your right of entry or use it to harass. You are liable for theft, casualty or other harm resulting from an entry made while the tenant is absent and has not specifically consented, or without the tenant's actual consent when present, and repeated unreasonable entry demands or an unreasonable, non-consented entry let the tenant end the lease; any lease term exempting you from that liability (other than consent to a particular entry) is void.

title: Servicemembers: 30-day lease termination on entering active duty, and the Delaware SCRA
bodyText: Delaware gives servicemember tenants two sets of state protections, on top of the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act. (1) Lease termination: a tenant who, after signing the rental agreement, enters the military service of the United States on active duty may end the tenancy on 30 days' written notice, with the 30 days starting on the first day of the month after you actually receive the notice. The Delaware statute is narrower than the federal Act: it covers entering active duty after the lease was signed, and does not itself mention permanent change-of-station or deployment orders for someone already serving, or Delaware National Guard state duty. The federal Act's broader termination rights still apply. (2) Delaware Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, which supplements federal law and covers residents of Delaware and people stationed in Delaware in the armed forces, the NOAA and Public Health Service commissioned corps, and the Delaware National Guard (including Guard members called to state duty for more than 30 consecutive days): before a default judgment (including in an eviction case where the tenant does not appear) you must file an affidavit stating whether the tenant is in military service; if the tenant is, the court must appoint an attorney first and must stay the case at least 90 days if a defense may exist; a servicemember with notice of the case may obtain a stay of at least 90 days; the court may stay execution of a judgment if military service materially affects the tenant's ability to comply; stays may run through service plus 90 days with installment terms; and a court may reduce or waive contract penalties (such as late fees) incurred while service materially affected performance, with no penalty accruing during a stay. A false affidavit is perjury (a class F felony), and the Attorney General may seek a civil penalty of up to $10,000 per violation. Military status is also a protected class under Delaware's fair housing law, so you may not refuse to rent or set different terms because of it.

title: No late-benefit eviction defense; shutdown stay for federal workers; third-party payments
bodyText: Delaware's statutes and JP Court Civil Rules give a tenant no special defense, continuance or reinstatement in a nonpayment eviction because a Social Security check, other government benefit or rental-assistance payment arrived late. Related rules still help such tenants. If the tenant, or another person or entity on the tenant's behalf, pays all rent due before you file, you may not then file for that nonpayment; if all rent due under the lease is paid after you file, you may not maintain the case; and you may not refuse rent paid by or on behalf of a tenant (before judgment you may limit payment to the methods your lease accepts; after judgment you may require a certified check or money order; neither limit applies to a redemption payment by a charitable organization or government entity). Until the eviction order is actually executed, a tenant may redeem by paying everything the court finds due plus costs and fees, and a check from a charitable organization or government entity counts as the tenant's payment (unless the tenant had 2 nonpayment possession judgments in the prior 18 months). Every possession case is scheduled for mediation through the JP Court's eviction diversion program before trial (with limited exceptions). One narrow stay exists: under the Delaware Federal Employees Civil Relief Act, during a federal shutdown (a lapse in appropriations of more than 24 hours) and for 30 days after it ends, you may evict a Delaware-resident federal worker (or federal contractor employee) for nonpayment only with a court order, the court may stay the eviction 30 days (and extend it) if the shutdown materially affected the worker's ability to meet the lease, and the worker may ask a court to suspend rent obligations during the shutdown.

title: Tenant's statutory termination rights for landlord breach (beyond the 30-day § 5314 list)
bodyText: Besides the 30-day early-termination grounds (job relocation, illness, senior or subsidized housing, military duty, domestic abuse, death), Delaware lets a tenant end the lease when you breach your own duties. (1) First month: if you fail to substantially conform to the rental agreement, or there is a material code noncompliance, the tenant may end the lease on written notice and move out any time during the first month of occupancy, as long as the tenant stayed relying on your promise to fix it; if substantially the same problem recurs within 6 months, the tenant may end the lease on at least 15 days' written notice specifying the breach. (2) Loss of the bargain: if a condition deprives the tenant of a substantial part of the benefit of the bargain and you do not fix it within 15 days after written notice, the tenant may terminate; if it makes the unit uninhabitable or poses an imminent threat to health or safety, the tenant may terminate immediately after notice. If you caused the condition willfully or negligently, the tenant recovers the greater of the extra cost of equivalent housing for the rest of the term or 1 month's rent plus the security deposit. (3) Possession not delivered at the start of the term: rent abates and the tenant may end the lease and get back all money paid, including prepaid rent and pet and security deposits. (4) Essential services: if you substantially fail to provide hot water, heat, water or electricity for 48 hours after notice, the tenant may terminate immediately on written notice. (5) Fire or casualty not caused by the tenant's side that substantially impairs the unit. (6) Unlawful ouster. (7) Repeated unreasonable entry demands or an unreasonable non-consented entry. The first-month and loss-of-bargain rights do not apply to a condition caused by lack of due care by the tenant, family or guests, and the casualty right requires that the tenant's side was not at fault; a tenant who terminates wrongfully stays bound by the lease. Delaware has no landlord-tenant statute that specifically lets a tenant end the lease for your misrepresentation, but the Consumer Fraud Act makes any misrepresentation, deception or concealment of a material fact in connection with the lease of real estate an unlawful practice, and the consumer-contract statute treats obscuring a contract's terms or omitting legally required disclosures as a deceptive practice. Separately, if you fail to put the deposit in a qualifying Delaware-office bank escrow account, or fail to disclose the account's location within 20 days of a written request, you forfeit the deposit to the tenant.

title: No separate tenancy at will: an agreement with no term is month-to-month
bodyText: Delaware's Landlord-Tenant Code does not recognize a separate residential tenancy at will, and sets no separate week-to-week rule. Where no term is expressly provided, a rental agreement is treated as month-to-month, whether it is written or oral, and whatever the rent interval. An unwritten rental agreement cannot be effective for a term longer than 1 year. Either you or the tenant ends a month-to-month tenancy with at least 60 days' written notice, and the 60 days begin on the first day of the month after the day of actual notice (so notice given on March 10 starts the 60 days on April 1). A lease of 1 year or more that neither side ends with the required notice becomes month-to-month on the same terms. Title 25's agricultural-lease chapter has its own rules for leases of agricultural land (a 1-year term ending December 31 and year-to-year renewal absent 4 months' notice), and one rule for a tenant house on a poultry farm: under a verbal lease, or a written lease with no term, either side may end the lease of the tenant house with 14 days' notice, but only where the tenant is involved with the management or supervision of poultry; check that chapter if you rent such a house.

title: No Delaware rule on a tenant's bankruptcy; federal law governs
bodyText: Delaware's statutes have no rule of their own on what happens to a residential tenancy, a security deposit or an eviction when a tenant files for bankruptcy. Federal bankruptcy law, including the automatic stay, governs that situation and was outside the searched material, so get advice before you serve a notice, start or continue a summary possession case, or try to collect pre-filing rent from a tenant who has filed. A lease term that ends the tenancy or treats the tenant as in default just because the tenant files for bankruptcy should not be relied on. Delaware does address the reverse situation: the tenant's claim to the security deposit comes before any creditor of yours, including a trustee in your own bankruptcy, even if the money was commingled.

title: Death of a sole tenant: register-of-wills documentation, 30-day access, 20-day deposit accounting
bodyText: Delaware has a specific procedure when the only leaseholder dies (a deceased sole tenant). Any right of other, non-leaseholder occupants to live there at the tenant's discretion ends immediately at the death. Possession returns to you without an eviction case if an affiant or personal representative of the estate gives you valid documentation from the register of wills (you must then let that person in to remove the tenant's belongings) and either tells you further access is not needed or 30 days pass after the death without written notice that access is still needed. Separately, the named executor (first) or next of kin may enter, with a register-of-wills form, to take possession (not ownership) of the decedent's belongings, during business hours at mutually agreeable times, within 30 days of the death. You may instead file for summary possession and money due at any time (the death of a sole tenant is itself a ground): sue the estate and serve the affiant or personal representative at the address given, or, if no one presents documentation or no good address is given, serve the register of wills in the county, after publishing a notice of the action in a county newspaper naming you, the deceased tenant, the unit address, the type of action, the court and the claim amount. Property left at execution of the writ may be removed and stored for 7 days at the estate's expense, then treated as abandoned if not claimed by a documented estate representative who pays the reasonable storage costs. Within 20 days after you get possession (or after storage ends) you must return any deposit not owed, with an itemized list of damages, to a documented estate representative. If the representative presents no documentation or no good address, you are relieved of the notice and double-damages exposure but remain liable for the unused deposit on a written claim within 1 year. Delaware's statutes give no role to a contact person named in the lease: do not let a lease-named contact remove belongings or receive the deposit in place of a documented estate representative or the executor or next of kin. A surviving spouse or personal representative may also end the tenancy on 30 days' written notice, starting the first day of the month after actual notice.

title: Ending a tenancy: 60 days' written notice for fixed terms and month-to-month
bodyText: Delaware sets one notice period for both sides and both tenancy types, and a lease cannot shorten it. Fixed term: you or the tenant may end the lease at its expiration by giving at least 60 days' written notice before the end of the term; your notice must say the agreement will terminate on its expiration date. Month-to-month (including any agreement with no stated term, whatever the rent interval; Delaware has no separate week-to-week period): either side gives at least 60 days' written notice, and the 60 days begin on the first day of the month after the day of actual notice. If neither side gives notice under a lease of 1 year or more (you at least 60 days before the end, the tenant at least 45 days before), the lease continues month-to-month on the same terms. If you want to renew with changed terms (rent, deposit, length or anything else), give at least 60 days' written notice before expiration specifying the changes, amounts and effective date; the changes are accepted unless the tenant gives notice of termination at least 45 days before the last day of the term, and a rejected renewal notice works as a termination notice (these renewal rules do not apply where HUD rules set rent and deposit by income). Shorter periods apply only to specific grounds: 7 days after a written nonpayment demand, a 7-day cure notice for a material rule or covenant breach, immediate termination on notice for irreparable harm, the tenant's 30-day statutory early-termination grounds, and a landlord-occupied building renting no more than 3 single rooms to no more than 3 tenants (immediate termination for a material rule violation under a written lease; 15 or 30 days without one). Serve notices personally, by leaving a copy with an adult at the unit, or by registered, certified or first-class mail with a certificate of mailing (posting works only together with a return receipt or certificate of mailing). In counting days, skip the day of the notice and, if the last day falls on a weekend or legal holiday, run to the next business day. With a nonpayment demand, a 7-day breach notice or a termination notice in a tenancy that may end only for good cause, you must also give the tenant the Right to Representation informational materials. Federally subsidized tenancies follow federal rules where they conflict.

title: No squatter-removal procedure outside eviction; criminal trespass and summary possession
bodyText: Delaware's statutes have no special procedure for removing a squatter or other unauthorized occupant outside the courts: no sheriff or police removal on an owner's affidavit, no fast-track squatter hearing and no squatting crime of its own. What exists is the general criminal trespass law: a person who knowingly enters or remains unlawfully in a dwelling (that is, without license or privilege) commits criminal trespass in the first degree, a class A misdemeanor; remaining unlawfully on other real property is a lesser offense. Whether police will treat a particular occupant as a trespasser is their call, and a person who moved in with a tenant's permission, or who has an oral rental agreement (Delaware's Code covers oral agreements), may be a tenant or have a claim to possession. In those cases use the summary possession process: the owner or landlord may file it, and you may not remove anyone yourself without a court order and writ. When a sole tenant dies, any right of the tenant's non-leaseholder occupants to stay ends immediately at the death, but possession is still regained through the deceased-tenant procedure or summary possession.

title: Accepting rent: full payment ends a nonpayment case; you may not refuse rent
bodyText: Delaware has a statutory acceptance rule for nonpayment, and since September 1, 2026 no written reservation of rights avoids it. If the tenant, or anyone on the tenant's behalf, pays all rent due before you file, you may not then file a summary possession case based on that nonpayment; if all rent due under the lease is paid after you file, you may not maintain the case. You may not refuse rent paid by or on behalf of a tenant, though before judgment you may limit payment to the methods your lease accepts and after judgment you may require a certified check or money order; after judgment the tenant may also redeem until the writ is executed (not if 2 nonpayment possession judgments were entered against the tenant in the 18 months before the case), and a redemption payment by a charitable organization or government entity is not subject to those method limits. (The Attorney General's October 2024 summary still describes a written reservation of rights that let a landlord accept rent and keep suing; that rule was removed by the September 1, 2026 amendments.) The statutes do not say whether accepting a partial payment waives anything, or whether accepting rent waives a non-rent breach; for a rule or covenant breach the 7-day written cure notice controls, and a substantially similar breach within 1 year lets you rely on the earlier notice. Accepting rent without reservation also makes a lease the tenant signed and tendered effective as if you had signed it. A lease clause saying acceptance never waives any remedy cannot override these rules.

title: No rule letting the parties add their own method of 'actual notice'
bodyText: Delaware's Landlord-Tenant Code uses 'actual notice' in a few places (for example, the 60-day month-to-month termination period and the 30-day early-termination period both start on the first day of the month after the day of actual notice; a tenant need not report a defect you already have actual notice of), but it has no provision letting you and the tenant agree on an extra method, such as text messages, that counts as notice for a Code requirement. The Code's own rule is that a person has notice of a fact if the person actually knows it, has received a notice under the Code, or has reason to know it from the facts and circumstances. Notices the Code requires must be served by its listed methods (personal delivery, leaving a copy with an adult at the unit, registered, certified or first-class mail with a certificate of mailing, or posting combined with mail). Electronic records can satisfy a writing requirement when both sides have agreed to deal electronically, but Delaware's electronic transactions law keeps any method a statute specifies, so an agreed text or e-mail does not replace the Code's service methods. The one Code notice that may expressly be sent electronically is the bed bug determination notice, which may go by e-mail or through a portal or management communication system available to both of you. Use text or e-mail as an extra courtesy copy, not as the notice of record.

title: Tenant must tell you at once of an ejectment or other action against the premises
bodyText: Delaware puts the duty in the statute, so it applies whether or not the lease says so: a tenant who is served with a complaint in ejectment or an action against the premises must immediately notify you in writing. (The duty does not apply where you already have actual notice.) A lease may repeat it and ask the tenant to forward the papers. In a mortgage foreclosure, tenants holding an estate for years or at will are not necessary parties and need not be joined, but they must be given written notice in the manner the Superior Court's civil rules prescribe. The posted and mailed notice to tenants in an owner-occupied foreclosure is accompanied by the foreclosure-mediation notice. The purchaser at a foreclosure sale may obtain a writ of possession against anyone in possession whose rights arose after the mortgage, and after a foreclosure sale and perfected title, a tenant who holds over for more than 5 days may be removed through summary possession. Delaware's statutes do not require you to tell tenants or applicants that a foreclosure or other claim against the property is pending; federal law on tenants in foreclosed properties was not searched.

title: Automatic renewal: the Code converts long leases to month-to-month; consumer auto-renewal law mostly excluded
bodyText: Delaware renews leases by statute, not by lease clause. If a lease is for 1 year or more and neither you (at least 60 days before the end) nor the tenant (at least 45 days before the end) gives written notice of termination, the term becomes month-to-month and every other term continues. If you want to renew with changes, you must give at least 60 days' written notice before expiration specifying the changed terms, the rent and deposit amounts and the effective date; the tenant is deemed to accept unless the tenant gives notice of termination at least 45 days before the last day of the term, and a rejected renewal notice works as a termination notice (not for HUD income-based rent and deposits). A lease term that instead renews the lease automatically for another fixed term conflicts with the statutory month-to-month rule, and terms that conflict with the Code and are not expressly authorized by it are unenforceable; do not rely on one. Delaware's general consumer automatic-renewal statute (clear and conspicuous disclosure, a reminder 30 to 60 days before the cancellation deadline) expressly does not apply to leases under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Code. The same consumer-contract subchapter separately makes it a deceptive practice, for any contract that automatically renews, to fail to provide a cost-effective, timely and easy-to-use way to cancel (and a consumer who signed online must be able to cancel online); that rule is not among the exclusions, its remedies include treble actual damages plus attorneys' fees, and the subchapter does not apply to contracts whose total price exceeds $50,000. Whether it reaches a lease that continues month-to-month by statute is unresolved, so let tenants give their termination notice by at least the same means they used to sign.

title: Rules some states have that Delaware does not (and one it reverses)
bodyText: Several rules found in other states are not in Delaware's statutes. (1) No statute bans renting the same unit to two tenants for the same period; the Code's possession rules apply instead (rent abates, the tenant may end the lease and get all money back, and limited substitute-housing costs may be recovered). (2) No statute gives you a special right to end a lease because the rental application was false; a material misstatement is handled as a breach of the lease through the 7-day written breach-and-cure notice and summary possession, and applicants need not disclose, and should not be asked about, expunged records. (3) No statute bans or caps a convenience or processing fee for a particular way of paying rent. Be careful anyway: you may not charge any nonrefundable fee as a condition of occupancy except an optional fee for actual services rendered, and you may not refuse rent paid by or on behalf of the tenant, though you may limit payment to the methods your lease accepts. (4) Smoke detectors: rather than making compliance inadmissible, Delaware says a failure to comply with the smoke detector law is not evidence of comparative or contributory negligence and is not admissible in a civil suit or insurance claim arising from a fire; the detector duties and fines still apply.

title: Whole-code checks: squatters, cash receipts, landlord registration
bodyText: Delaware's whole Code, Constitution, 2025-2026 session laws in the corpus and the JP Court Civil Rules were searched, not only the Landlord-Tenant Code, for three things landlords ask about. (1) Squatters: there is no squatter-specific removal procedure; criminal trespass law covers anyone who knowingly enters or remains unlawfully in a dwelling, and anyone with a claim to possession is removed through summary possession and a writ, never by self-help. (2) Cash receipts: Delaware does require them. If you accept a cash payment for rent, you must give the tenant a receipt within 15 days, and keep a record of all cash rent receipts for 3 years. (3) Landlord registration: no state statute requires you to register or license a residential rental, or to prove registration, before you can win a possession case. Entity and trade-name laws can still reach you. An out-of-state limited liability company or corporation doing business in Delaware may not maintain any action, a possession case included, until it registers (an LLC) or qualifies (a corporation) with the Secretary of State and pays the fees and penalties owed; whether renting out property is doing business is a case-law question (6 Del. C. §§ 18-902 and 18-907; 8 Del. C. §§ 371 and 383). An individual or partnership renting under a trade name that does not disclose the legal name must first file a trade name certificate with the Division of Revenue; not doing so is punishable by a fine of up to $100 or up to 3 months in prison, though the trade-name law sets no bar on suing (6 Del. C. §§ 3101 and 3106). The state business-license law lists a commercial lessor, not a residential one. Cities and counties (for example Wilmington, Newark, Dover and New Castle County) may run their own rental permit or licensing programs, which were not searched.

title: Delaware's DV protection-order law has not moved; Code definitions use general references
bodyText: Delaware has not moved or repealed the laws its landlord-tenant protections for survivors rely on, and the Landlord-Tenant Code's definitions are written so that renumbering elsewhere does not break them. 'Domestic abuse' means any act or threat against a victim that is a crime under Delaware law or that is domestic violence or domestic abuse as defined anywhere in the Delaware Code, and 'sexual offenses' and 'stalking' have their Title 11 meanings. Each can be verified by an official document such as a court order, or by a reliable third-party professional (law enforcement, a domestic violence or sexual assault service provider, or a health care provider), and it is the victim's responsibility to provide that statement. Protection-from-abuse orders still issue under the Family Court domestic violence chapter (10 Del. C. §§ 1041 and following). One change to note: from January 1, 2027, that chapter's definitions section adds 'military protective order' (an order issued by a commanding officer under federal law) and renumbers the later definitions, so if your lease or forms cite a paragraph number there (for example the definition of 'protective order'), cite the section or quote the words instead.

title: Electronic leases and records: Delaware's UETA, consent, and the right to stop
bodyText: Delaware's Uniform Electronic Transactions Act lets you sign leases and addenda electronically: a record or signature may not be denied legal effect solely because it is electronic, and where a law requires a writing or a signature, an electronic record or electronic signature satisfies it. Three limits matter for landlords. (1) Consent: the Act applies only between parties who have each agreed to conduct the transaction electronically (judged from the context and conduct), and it never requires anyone to use electronic records. (2) Right to stop: a party who agreed to deal electronically may refuse to conduct other transactions electronically, and that right cannot be waived by agreement, so a lease clause cannot lock a tenant into e-signatures or e-delivery for everything that follows. (3) Delivery and methods: where a law requires information to be provided in writing, an electronic record works only if it is capable of retention by the recipient (you may not block printing or saving, or the record is not enforceable against the tenant); and where a law requires a record to be sent by a specified method, it must still be sent that way. Delaware's Act has no exclusion for eviction, default or cure notices (unlike some states), but because the Landlord-Tenant Code specifies how every Code notice is served (personal delivery, leaving a copy with an adult at the unit, mail with proof, or posting with mail), an e-mail does not replace those methods. The Act's only alternative for a mail requirement is a USPS-style electronic postmark with an electronic postmark certificate, delivered to a system the recipient designated and used only with both parties' consent. Keep each signed lease in a form the tenant can print and store, and give the tenant a free copy of the written lease, as the Code requires.

title: No duty to give tenants an emergency or 24-hour phone number
bodyText: Delaware's statutes do not require you to give tenants an emergency or 24-hour telephone number, to post one, or to keep an emergency contact list of residents. What the Code does require is that every written lease prominently disclose the names and usual business addresses of the owners (or their appointed resident agents) and of anyone who would be treated as a landlord. Practical reasons to give a working emergency number anyway: the essential-services remedy runs from 48 hours after the tenant gives you actual or written notice of a loss of heat, hot water, water or electricity, a condition making the unit uninhabitable lets the tenant end the lease immediately after notice, and you must acknowledge a bed bug complaint within 120 hours. If you collect a tenant's own emergency contact, it gives that person no rights in the unit; after a sole tenant's death only a documented estate representative, or the executor or next of kin under the probate statute, may remove belongings.

title: No building energy-benchmarking or tenant usage-data release statute
bodyText: Delaware's statutes have no building energy-benchmarking program and no provision letting a lease clause authorize a utility to release a tenant's energy usage data to you. The energy-usage reporting provisions in the Code run from energy providers to the State for planning reports, not to building owners. If you want usage data for a unit whose utility account is in the tenant's name, get the tenant's separate written authorization in the form the utility accepts. If you submeter and bill utilities yourself, the Landlord-Tenant Code instead requires you to keep the bills and records your charges are based on for 1 year and let the tenant inspect them at your regular business office during business hours.

title: Mandatory eviction mediation after filing; no statute on pre-suit resolution clauses
bodyText: Delaware has a statutory dispute-resolution step for possession cases, but it comes after filing, not before. Once you file a summary possession action, the case is scheduled for mediation through the JP Court's residential eviction diversion program between filing and trial; the trial may not start until you have engaged in mediation (unless the tenant fails to engage within 15 calendar days after service), and mediation must be scheduled and completed at least 48 hours before trial. The program includes an initial mediation conference and a HUD-certified housing counselor or other approved representative who meets with the tenant beforehand. You are not required to participate in forthwith-summons cases, cases for irreparable harm or a qualifying conviction, or where you show by substantial evidence that the tenant caused or threatens substantial or irreparable harm. Delaware's statutes neither authorize nor regulate a lease clause requiring an informal meeting before going to court. Such a clause may not delay or condition any Code notice period or remedy, because a lease may not make the tenant waive or forgo Code rights; if used, it should exclude possession actions and all statutory notices and deadlines. A written agreement to arbitrate is generally valid and enforceable, subject to ordinary contract defenses, and the Court of Chancery enforces it: under Delaware's Uniform Arbitration Act only if the agreement specifically references that Act and the parties' wish to have it apply, otherwise under the Federal Arbitration Act standard; summary possession itself belongs in the JP Court.

title: No statewide landlord registration or rental license; check local programs
bodyText: Delaware's statutes do not require residential landlords to register with the State or a county, hold a state rental license, use an in-state broker if they live out of state, or prove a rental registration before an eviction. Two general filing rules can still apply. An out-of-state limited liability company or corporation doing business in Delaware must register or qualify with the Secretary of State, naming a Delaware registered agent, and cannot maintain an eviction until it does; whether renting out property is doing business is a case-law question (6 Del. C. §§ 18-902, 18-904(b) and 18-907; 8 Del. C. §§ 371 and 383; see `edu-no-nonresident-owner-agent-de`). And an individual or partnership renting under a trade name that does not disclose the legal name must first file a trade name certificate with the Division of Revenue (6 Del. C. §§ 3101 and 3106). The state business-license law lists a commercial lessor as a licensed occupation and has no residential-lessor category, but it also levies a $75 general service license on any business not specifically listed; whether a residential rental business needs that license is a question for the Division of Revenue. What state law does require: every written lease must prominently disclose the names and usual business addresses of all owners (or their appointed resident agents) and of anyone who would be treated as a landlord, and an owner or resident agent who does not deal with the tenant directly is still responsible for that disclosure and cannot benefit from a failure of service caused by not complying with it. Any person who owns, manages or possesses Delaware real estate, resident or not, submits to Delaware courts for Code obligations. Cities and counties may run rental permit, licensing or inspection programs of their own; those local codes were not searched.

title: No blank-space rule for residential leases; required disclosures still must appear
bodyText: Delaware has no statute requiring every blank in a residential lease to be filled in before signing or making an incomplete lease a breach. Delaware's blank-space rules apply to other contracts (retail installment sales and rent-to-own lease-purchase agreements for goods), not to Landlord-Tenant Code leases. Complete every blank anyway, for three reasons. First, every written lease must prominently disclose the names and usual business addresses of the owners or their resident agents, and of anyone who would be treated as a landlord. Second, under Delaware's consumer-contract law (which covers leases of real estate up to a $50,000 total contract price), it is a deceptive practice to knowingly or recklessly obscure a contract's terms or omit information the law requires to be disclosed, with remedies including treble damages and attorney's fees. Third, a lease with no stated term is treated as month-to-month, and if the rental agreement sets no rent, the tenant owes only a reasonable sum for use and occupation.

title: Give the tenant a free copy of the written lease
bodyText: Where there is a written rental agreement, you must give the tenant a copy of it free of charge. Under an oral agreement, you must, on the tenant's demand, give the tenant a written statement of the owner disclosures (the names and usual business addresses of the owners or their appointed resident agents, and of anyone treated as a landlord). If the tenant buys a surety bond instead of paying a deposit, you or the surety must deliver to the tenant a copy of the rental agreement and the bond form the tenant signed at the time of purchase. Delaware's statutes do not make failure to deliver the lease copy a defense to enforcing the lease and set no separate penalty for it; the general remedy is a court action for any Code violation. Two related deliveries do carry consequences or deadlines: if you fail to give a new tenant the Attorney General's Landlord-Tenant Code summary at the beginning of the term, the tenant may plead ignorance of the law as a defense; and you must give the Right to Representation informational materials on signing a lease (written or oral) and at the first renewal or modification after November 22, 2023. Keep a dated record of each delivery.

title: No rule requiring tenant initials on a lease term; some terms need a separate signed writing
bodyText: Delaware's statutes never require a tenant to initial a particular lease term for it to bind, including a notice period. The Code's termination notices are stated as minimums ('a minimum of 60 days' written notice') for both you and the tenant, and the statutes do not say whether a lease may lengthen the tenant's notice; do not rely on a longer tenant notice period to withhold the deposit or charge rent beyond what the Code allows. Two Delaware rules go further than initials and require a separate signed document: a tenant's waiver of the 48-hour entry notice for showings to prospective tenants or purchasers must be in a signed addendum or other separate signed document, and any agreement for the tenant to do repairs, maintenance, alterations or remodeling must be in a conspicuous writing separate from the rental agreement, for adequate consideration apart from the lease or a rent reduction, and only for work that is for the unit's primary benefit and not needed to bring it up to code; it may not be made a condition of the lease. Initials on key terms remain good evidence that the tenant saw them.

title: Lease length: oral or unsigned agreements are capped at 1 year
bodyText: Delaware sets no maximum length for a written residential lease, but how the lease is made limits its term. An unwritten rental agreement cannot be effective for a term longer than 1 year, and an agreement with no stated term is month-to-month. If a written lease takes effect only through conduct (you accept rent without reservation on a lease the tenant signed and tendered, or the tenant takes possession and pays rent without reservation on a lease you signed and tendered), it creates only a 1-year term even if its text says longer. Delaware's general statute of frauds also requires a signed writing to enforce a contract for an interest in land or an agreement not to be performed within 1 year. So for any term over 1 year, have both sides sign. Term length matters elsewhere in the Code: for an unfurnished unit on a lease of 1 year or more the security deposit may not exceed 1 month's rent (the cap does not apply to furnished units), and if neither side gives notice the lease becomes month-to-month at the end of the term.

title: No minimum type size for a residential lease
bodyText: Delaware sets no minimum type size for a residential lease and has no rule barring you from relying on a lease, or part of one, because the print is small. Delaware's type-size and boldface rules apply to other contracts, such as rent-to-own lease-purchase agreements for goods, retail installment contracts, time-share and campground disclosures, foreclosure-rescue deed-transfer notices, recorded instruments, and self-storage rental agreements. Two softer rules still reach a residential lease. Every written lease must disclose the owner information prominently, and under Delaware's consumer-contract law (leases of real estate up to a $50,000 total contract price) it is a deceptive practice to knowingly or recklessly distort or obscure a contract's terms or create a likelihood of confusion through unintelligible wording; a court may consider whether conditions, exceptions and restrictions on the consumer's rights are given equal prominence with the main provisions. Use a readable type size and give key restrictions the same prominence as the rest of the lease.

title: Out-of-State Owners: Agents, Foreign Companies and Tenant Withholding
bodyText: Delaware's statutes do not require a nonresident individual owner to name an in-state agent before renting or suing, do not require an in-state broker or manager, and do not require tenants to withhold income tax from rent paid to a nonresident owner. An out-of-state company is different. A foreign limited liability company must register with the Secretary of State before doing business in Delaware, and a foreign corporation must qualify, each naming a Delaware registered agent. One doing business here unregistered may not maintain any action, an eviction included, until it registers and pays the fees and penalties owed (for an LLC, $200 for each year; for a corporation, a fine of $200 to $500), and is deemed to have appointed the Secretary of State as its agent for service of process in suits arising from that business; its leases remain valid. Whether renting out property is doing business for these rules is a case-law question; the statutes' lists of activities that are not doing business do not mention it (6 Del. C. §§ 18-902, 18-904(b), 18-907, 18-911 and 18-912; 8 Del. C. §§ 371, 373, 378, 382 and 383). What applies to every landlord, resident or not: each written lease must prominently disclose the names and usual business addresses of all owners, or the names and business addresses of their appointed resident agents, and of anyone treated as a landlord; an owner or resident agent who does not deal with the tenant directly is responsible for that disclosure and cannot take advantage of a failure of service caused by not complying with it; and anyone who owns, manages or possesses Delaware real estate submits to the Delaware courts for Code obligations, whether or not a Delaware resident. Separately, Delaware withholds income tax when a nonresident individual sells or exchanges Delaware real estate, which matters when you sell a rental, not when you collect rent.

title: How Code notices must be served, and where e-mail fits
bodyText: Every notice the Landlord-Tenant Code requires (nonpayment demands, breach notices, termination and renewal notices and the like) must be served in one of the Code's ways: (1) personally on the tenant; (2) by leaving a copy at the rental unit or usual place of abode with an adult residing there; (3) instead of personal service, by registered or certified mail or by first-class mail evidenced by a certificate of mailing, postage prepaid, addressed to the tenant at the leased premises (the signed, refused or unclaimed return receipt, or the certificate of mailing, is prima facie evidence of service); or (4) by posting the notice on the unit combined with a return receipt or certificate of mailing, or by personal service by a special process server appointed by the court. Anyone may serve personally; no sheriff or constable is required for a notice. Tenants serve you the same ways at the address in the lease or one you provided, or on an agent or employee responsible for accepting notices; an entity landlord may be served at its office or place of business listed in the lease. A lease cannot make some other method (such as text or e-mail) count for a Code notice, and Delaware's electronic transactions law keeps the method a statute specifies (its only substitute for mail is a USPS-style electronic postmark with an electronic postmark certificate, used only with both sides' consent). The bed bug determination notice is the one Code notice that may go by e-mail or a portal available to both of you. Deposit communications and the deposit refund go to the address in the lease or a forwarding address the tenant gives in writing at or before the end of the tenancy. With a nonpayment demand, a breach notice, or a termination notice under a lease that may be ended only for good cause or a material violation, you must also give the Right to Representation materials.

title: No rule on move-out notice forms that add terms; keep them to the facts
bodyText: Delaware has no statute governing a move-out (intent-to-vacate) form you ask a tenant to sign, and no required warning if the form adds terms the lease does not contain. Keep such a form to the move-out date and the tenant's forwarding address (which matters: deposit communications and the refund go to the address in the lease or a forwarding address the tenant gives in writing at or before the end of the tenancy). A new term slipped into the form cannot waive any Code right, because a rental agreement may not make the tenant waive or forgo Code rights, and conflicting terms are unenforceable. The Code does set required content for your own notices: a notice ending a fixed term must say the agreement will terminate on its expiration date; a renewal-with-changes notice must specify the changed provisions, the rent and deposit amounts and the date the changes take effect; a breach notice must identify the rule breached, warn that you may terminate and sue for possession if the violation continues after 7 days, and state that it is given under the breach section and may be relied on for a substantially similar breach within 1 year.

title: Delaware rules that depend on what the lease says
bodyText: Many Delaware rules apply only if, or unless, the rental agreement says so; a silent lease takes the default. (1) Late charge: only where the lease provides for one, capped at 5% of monthly rent and not imposed within 5 days of the due date. (2) Rent timing and place: as agreed; otherwise the whole rent is due at the start of a term of 1 month or less, and monthly for longer terms. (3) Payment methods: you may limit payments to the methods the lease accepts. (4) Utilities: you may bill separately metered utilities only if the lease so provides; non-consumption utility charges may be passed through at actual cost only if the lease provides; you must supply garbage receptacles and removal and water, hot water, heat and electricity if the lease so specifies. (5) Tenant repairs or maintenance: only by a conspicuous writing separate from the lease, for adequate consideration apart from the lease or a rent reduction, for work that benefits the unit and is not needed to bring it up to code, and never as a condition of the lease. (6) Extended absence: you may require in the lease that the tenant tell you in writing of an absence of more than 7 days no later than its first day; a tenant who fails then indemnifies you for resulting harm. (7) Use: unless the lease says otherwise, the tenant must use the unit only as the tenant's home. (8) Subletting and assignment: allowed unless restricted in writing; the lease may restrict or prohibit assignment in any manner, and may condition subletting on your consent, which you may not unreasonably withhold. (9) Showing notice: the 48-hour notice for showings to prospective tenants or buyers may be waived only in a signed addendum or separate signed document. (10) Rules: binding if brought to the tenant's attention at entry and reasonable; later rules that substantially modify the lease need the tenant's written consent. (11) Deposit increase: only if the lease so specifies, commensurate with a rent increase, prorated if over 10% of monthly rent. (12) Pet deposit: you may require one, capped at 1 month's rent. (13) Key return: if the lease makes key surrender a condition of the deposit refund, it must set a clear procedure and cannot require surrender before the end of the term.
