(14) Eviction grounds: the statutory grounds for summary possession apply unless otherwise agreed in a written rental agreement. (15) Marijuana: a lease may ban smoking and growing marijuana, but may ban possession or non-smoked use only in a landlord-occupied building renting 3 or fewer rooms to 3 or fewer tenants, in institutional housing, or where federal law requires it. (16) Tenant employees: their rights on termination of employment may be disclosed in the lease or an addendum instead of a separate form. (17) Seasonal rentals in the five hundreds the Code names: a nonrenewable agreement of 120 days or less is outside the Code. (18) E-mail: electronic dealings depend on each party's agreement, and a party who agreed for one transaction may refuse to deal electronically in other transactions; a lease cannot waive that right. (19) A surety bond instead of a deposit, and optional service fees (such as pool fees), are permitted only as the tenant's choice.

title: Consumer-contract law reaches leases: no unintelligible terms, no omitted disclosures
bodyText: Delaware's consumer-contract statute applies to residential leases: it covers any lease of 'merchandise', which includes real estate, to an individual for personal, family or household purposes, except contracts whose total price exceeds $50,000 (for example, a 12-month lease at more than about $4,166 a month). In such a lease you engage in a deceptive practice if you knowingly or recklessly (1) distort or obscure the terms, conditions or meaning of the lease or create a likelihood of confusion by using unintelligible words, phrases or sentences, (2) omit information the law requires to be disclosed (such as the owner disclosures), or (4) fail to provide a cost-effective, timely and easy way to cancel a contract that automatically renews (online for leases signed online). In judging a contract, a court may consider confusing cross-references, unreasonably long or complex sentences, double negatives and exceptions to exceptions, confusing or illogical order, obsolete words or words whose legal meaning differs from ordinary meaning, and whether conditions, exceptions and restrictions of the consumer's rights get equal prominence with the main provisions. A consumer may recover treble actual damages plus reasonable attorney's fees, and may get an injunction; a violation is also an unlawful practice under the Consumer Fraud Act. Unlike some states, Delaware has no numeric readability test, no required statement listing every restriction of the consumer's rights, and no Attorney General preapproval process. The subchapter's automatic-renewal disclosure rules do not apply to Landlord-Tenant Code leases. Note also that a lease term giving the landlord attorney's fees is unenforceable under the Code, while this statute's fee award runs to the consumer.

title: Delaware rules that turn on how many units or rooms you have
bodyText: Most of Delaware's Landlord-Tenant Code applies the same way however many units you own; there is no general small-landlord exemption. The size thresholds that do exist: (1) Right to counsel: a tenant is not eligible for free representation from a designated organization if the landlord owns an interest in 3 or fewer rental units and is not represented by an attorney or an authorized agent. (2) Rooms in your own home: if the building is your primary residence and you rent no more than 3 rooms to no more than 3 tenants, a written rental agreement for a single room may be ended immediately on notice for a material violation of a regulation given at the start (an unwritten one on 15 days' written notice for breach of quiet enjoyment or similar conduct, or 30 days' for any other reason; from Mar. 8, 2027 (Mar. 9 on the bill page) this shortcut is not available where state reentry funds pay part of the rent under § 5512A, which governs rental agreements entered into on or after that date); the same building profile is one of the cases in which a lease may ban marijuana possession and non-smoked use. (3) Fair housing: the State Fair Housing Act's rental provisions (other than the ban on discriminatory notices and advertising) do not apply to rooms or units in a building of up to 4 families where the owner lives in one of them; but the Landlord-Tenant Code's own fair housing section, which bars refusing to rent, cancelling, or charging more because of race, creed, religion, sex, disability, source of income, military status, familial status and the other listed classes, has no such exemption, so do not treat owner-occupancy as a license to discriminate. The design-accessibility rules for covered multifamily dwellings reach buildings of 4 or more units that have an elevator, and ground-floor units in other buildings of 4 or more units. (4) Lead-safe certification (once implemented): owners of 20 or more rental units are 'large property owners' and owners of 19 or fewer are 'small property owners' for that chapter's deadlines and assistance. (5) State Housing Code (where it applies): an owner of a dwelling with 2 or more units must keep shared areas clean and sanitary and exterminate pests in shared areas, while the occupant of a single-unit structure is responsible for extermination in it (subject to the bed bug rules). A statute with two size limbs (for example, primary residence and no more than 3 rooms and no more than 3 tenants) requires all of them.

title: No statute on requiring renter's insurance; the coming state guide will mention it
bodyText: Delaware's statutes do not regulate a lease requirement that the tenant carry renter's insurance: no rule on who chooses the carrier, no force-placed insurance procedure or capped administrative fee, and no required statement that your insurance does not cover the tenant's belongings. Limits from other Code rules still apply. A lease may not make the tenant exculpate you, limit your liability arising under law, or indemnify you for that liability, so an insurance clause cannot be used to shift your own repair or negligence liability onto the tenant or the tenant's policy. You may not charge any nonrefundable fee as a condition of occupancy except an optional fee for actual services rendered, so be cautious about adding an insurance-placement or administrative fee. A surety bond a tenant buys instead of a deposit is not insurance for the tenant, and the surety must say so in writing. Once the state Rights and Responsibilities Guide is published (it must be given before signing and acknowledged), it must include information about the availability of renter's and flood insurance for tenants.

title: Selling or changing management: few statutory rules; protect the deposit and the tenancy
bodyText: Delaware's Landlord-Tenant Code has few rules specific to selling a rented property or changing managers. It has no statute releasing a selling landlord from deposit liability on notice, no rule on assigning deposits to the buyer, and no required notice to tenants of a new owner or manager. What does apply: (1) The deposit is held for the tenant's benefit in a Delaware-office escrow account, and the tenant's claim comes before any of your creditors; so transfer the deposits, and the account information, to the buyer at closing and make sure the tenants know where they are held (failing to disclose the account location within 20 days of a tenant's written request forfeits the deposit). (2) If the tenant bought a surety bond instead of a deposit, the new landlord must accept it and may not demand an additional deposit during the current term, or, at renewal, a bond or deposit that brings the total above 1 month's rent. (3) The lease and the Code's rules continue; anyone who manages the premises, collects rent or is held out as the party to deal with is a 'landlord' with the landlord's duties, and each written lease must disclose the owners (or their resident agents) and anyone treated as a landlord, so new leases and renewals must show the new owner. (4) Showings: you may enter to show the unit to prospective purchasers or mortgagees on at least 48 hours' notice between 8 a.m. and 9 p.m., unless the tenant has waived notice for showings to prospective purchasers in a signed addendum or other separate signed document (the waiver cannot cover entry for mortgagees). (5) Possession for the buyer comes only through proper notice at the end of the term or month, and a good-faith sale to a buyer who represents an intended owner-occupancy, renovation or withdrawal from the rental market is a defense to a retaliation claim. (6) Foreclosure: tenants get written notice under the Superior Court rules, and the foreclosure purchaser may obtain possession against occupants whose rights arose after the mortgage. Condominium and common-interest conversions have their own tenant notice rules.

title: What the Landlord-Tenant Code covers, and what it excludes
bodyText: Delaware's Residential Landlord-Tenant Code governs every rental agreement for a rental unit in Delaware, wherever the agreement was signed, and applies statewide (counties and cities may add their own codes, which were not searched). It covers written and oral agreements, and a 'rental unit' is any house, building, structure or part of one occupied, rented or leased as the home of one or more people. Excluded: commercial rental units (general contract law applies, plus the summary possession chapter); residence incidental to institutional services (until March 8, 2027: residence at any public or private institution merely incidental to detention or to medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious or similar services, such as prisons, college or school student housing, old-age and nursing homes, monasteries and hospitals; from March 8, 2027: only facilities of health care providers licensed by the Division of Health Care Quality, school-operated student housing, Department of Correction institutions, and monasteries and convents); fraternal-organization housing; hotel, motel and similar lodging (from March 8, 2027: transient lodging in a hotel, motel or tourist home as Title 30 defines them); nonrenewable agreements of 120 days or less a year in five named coastal hundreds; ground leases where the tenant owns the improvements; and certified recovery houses. Until March 8, 2027 an arrangement created solely to avoid the Code is not excluded; the new version drops that qualifier (the bill page gives March 9, 2027). Manufactured home community lot rentals are governed first by their own chapter (outside this library's scope), but the Landlord-Tenant Code governs the rental of a manufactured home itself and fills gaps in the lot-rental chapter. Leases of agricultural land have their own chapter, and a conditional sale of a home converted into a tenancy by statute is covered. Within the Code, a few rules depend on the tenancy: furnished units are outside the deposit cap, federally subsidized and HUD income-based tenancies follow federal rules where they conflict, and rooms rented in a landlord-occupied building of no more than 3 rooms and 3 tenants have special termination rules.

title: Writing and recording rules: leases over 1 year must be in writing; over 5 years may need recording
bodyText: Delaware has two layers of formality rules for lease length. (1) Writing: an unwritten rental agreement cannot be effective for more than 1 year, a lease that takes effect only by conduct (acceptance of rent or possession without a signature) creates only a 1-year term, and the general statute of frauds bars suing on a contract for an interest in land, or one not to be performed within 1 year, unless it or a memorandum of it is signed by the party to be charged. (2) Recording and transfer tax for long leases: Delaware's realty transfer tax treats as a taxable 'document' a writing that transfers a possessory interest for more than 5 years in a condominium or unit-property unit, and a writing that assigns or transfers a leasehold or possessory interest in residential property under a lease for a term of more than 5 years, counting all renewal or extension options as if they will be exercised. Unless the document is exempt from the tax, it is not enforceable in any Delaware court unless the document, or a memorandum identifying the parties, the premises and the duration including renewals and purchase options, is recorded with the county recorder of deeds within 15 days after the term begins; late recording with payment of the tax and penalties revives it. Whether the residential-property limb reaches the original lease itself or only later assignments is not settled by the text, so for any residential lease that could run more than 5 years with options, get advice on recording and transfer tax before signing. Ordinary leases of 5 years or less are unaffected.

title: Delaware prescribes no lease form; a few side documents come from the State
bodyText: Delaware does not prescribe a form or verbatim text for the lease itself. The State supplies or fixes the text of a few side documents instead. (1) The Attorney General's Consumer Protection Unit prepares the Landlord-Tenant Code summary you must give a new tenant at the start of the term (the current October 2024 edition predates the September 1, 2026 nonpayment-notice change, so do not rely on it for the notice period). (2) The Right to Representation Coordinator approves the informational materials on legal representation (in English, Spanish and Haitian Creole) that you must give at signing, at the first renewal or modification after November 22, 2023, with nonpayment, breach and certain termination notices, and on termination of a housing subsidy. (3) Once published, the Real Estate Commission's Rights and Responsibilities Guide must be given before signing with the tenant's acknowledgment, and at renewals of 1 year or more; it is deemed a statutorily required form. (4) Writs of possession must carry statutory notice language about removal and storage of the tenant's property (one version where no appeal is filed, another where an appeal is pending); the court issues these. (5) After a sole tenant's death, the executor or next of kin uses a Register of Wills form to enter and remove belongings. Delaware prescribes content but not verbatim text for your own notices (termination, renewal with changes, nonpayment demand, breach notice) and for the tenant-employee disclosure form. Giving the guide does not satisfy any other disclosure or document requirement unless the law allows it.

title: No portal statute; payment-office, payment-acceptance and UETA limits apply
bodyText: Delaware has no statute that directly allows or forbids requiring rent payments, applications or signatures through an online tenant portal. Other rules limit a portal-only setup. (1) In-county payment place: you must maintain, in the county where the unit is, an office or other permanent place for receipt of payments where rent may be timely paid; if you do not, the due date is extended by 3 days. A portal alone may not satisfy that, so keep a physical payment place or expect the 3-day extension (which also pushes back the 5-day late-fee window). (2) Payment methods: you may limit payments to the methods your lease accepts, but you may not refuse rent paid by or on behalf of the tenant, and after a judgment you may require a certified check or money order. In a nonpayment possession case (from the time you request possession until the eviction is carried out), an electronic or written check from a charitable organization or government entity counts as the tenant's redemption payment, and you may not restrict the payment method for those payers. (3) Electronic dealings: Delaware's electronic transactions law applies only between parties who each agreed to deal electronically, a party who agreed may refuse to conduct further transactions electronically (a right a lease cannot waive), and an electronic record you deliver must be capable of being printed and stored by the tenant. So a lease cannot require that every signature or notice go through the portal. (4) Code notices must still be served by the Code's methods; the only Code notice that may go through a portal is the bed bug determination notice, if the portal is available to both of you. (5) If you take a cash payment in person, you must give a receipt within 15 days.

title: Records you must keep, and protecting applicants' personal data
bodyText: Delaware has no general rent-ledger statute (no duty to give a ledger on request or with a nonpayment notice), but several specific record duties apply. (1) Cash rent: give a receipt within 15 days and keep a record of all cash rent receipts for 3 years. (2) Application fees: give a receipt for the full amount and keep complete records of all application fees charged and received for at least 2 years. (3) Submetered or billed utilities: keep the bills and records your charges are based on for 1 year and let the tenant inspect them at your regular business office during business hours. (4) Bed bugs: keep a written record of all complaints and control measures, including pest-professional reports, for 2 years. (5) Deposits: keep the escrow account information you must disclose. Applicant and tenant data: anyone conducting business in Delaware who owns, licenses or maintains personal information (a Delaware resident's name with, for example, a Social Security number, driver's license number or financial account number) must implement and maintain reasonable procedures and practices to prevent its unauthorized acquisition, use, disclosure or destruction. After a breach of computerized personal information you must notify affected Delaware residents without unreasonable delay and within 60 days (unless an investigation shows harm is unlikely), notify the Attorney General if more than 500 residents are affected, and offer 1 year of free credit monitoring if Social Security numbers were involved. A business entity disposing of records containing consumers' personal identifying information must shred, erase or otherwise make that information unreadable; a consumer harmed by a reckless or intentional violation may sue.

title: Changing lease terms (not only rent): the 60/45-day renewal notice and the rules on rules
bodyText: Delaware uses one procedure for changing any lease term, not only the rent: the renewal-with-modifications notice. Give the tenant at least 60 days' written notice before the rental agreement expires that it will renew with amended or modified provisions (the statute expressly includes the length of the term, the deposit and the rent, 'including, but not limited to'), specifying each changed provision, the rent and deposit amounts and the date the changes take effect. Unless the tenant gives notice of termination at least 45 days before the last day of the term, the changes are deemed accepted; a tenant who rejects them is treated as having given a termination notice. Raising a fee the lease already provides for follows the same rule; Delaware sets no longer notice for fee changes than for rent changes. Changing the terms does not require ending the tenancy and offering a new one. For month-to-month tenancies the statute's 'expiration' language fits awkwardly; give the 60 days before the end of a monthly period and make the change effective at the start of a later month. Two other routes exist: a deposit increase commensurate with a rent increase is allowed only if the lease so specifies (prorated if over 10% of monthly rent); and new or changed house rules bind the tenant once brought to the tenant's attention, but a rule that substantially modifies the lease needs the tenant's written consent. Rent increases during a fixed term need a lease provision allowing them (see the rent-increase row). HUD income-based rents and deposits follow HUD rules.

title: No core landlord-tenant statute on a repeal clock; dated changes to watch
bodyText: As of October 16, 2026, none of Delaware's core Residential Landlord-Tenant Code provisions is scheduled to expire. Dated changes to track instead: (1) The State's language and communication assistance program for housing matters (interpretation and translation help for tenants with limited English proficiency or disabilities in leases and evictions) carried an expiration of September 30, 2026, so it has lapsed unless extended by a later act. (2) On December 31, 2028, new versions of the Code's fair housing section and the Fair Housing Act's exemptions take effect: they drop the rule letting you deny an application when a housing authority fails to follow the standardized voucher-processing sequence, and instead say a landlord is not required to participate in a voucher or rental assistance program. (3) Other dated starts, not repeals: the Right to Representation program is phased in through June 30, 2028 (subject to funding); lead-safe certification starts the earlier of 12 months after a published notice or March 1, 2028; the Rights and Responsibilities Guide starts the earlier of one year after enactment or a published notice; and new definitions, exclusions, rooming-house and reentry-fund sections take effect March 8, 2027 (the bill page says March 9).

title: No duty to translate the lease; state materials come in other languages
bodyText: Delaware's statutes do not require you to translate a lease, even if you advertise or negotiate in another language, and set no lease type-size or verbatim-text rule tied to translation. The State instead supplies some materials in other languages: the Right to Representation informational materials you must give tenants are prepared by the Coordinator in English, Spanish and Haitian Creole (give the version the tenant can read), and the foreclosure-mediation notice carries English and Spanish headings. A state program to provide interpretation and translation help to tenants with limited English proficiency or disabilities in leases and evictions was headed to expire on September 30, 2026. If you negotiate in another language, consider giving a translation as a courtesy while keeping the English lease as the signed agreement, and remember that obscuring a consumer contract's terms through unintelligible wording can be a deceptive practice under Delaware's consumer-contract law.

title: Which Delaware notices must be in writing (and which need not be)
bodyText: Delaware specifies notice by statute, and where the Code says written, a lease cannot substitute a verbal notice (a lease may not waive Code rights). Your notices that must be in writing: ending a fixed term (60 days before expiration) or a month-to-month tenancy (60 days); renewal with changed terms (60 days); the nonpayment demand (at least 7 days); the 7-day breach-and-cure notice; and the 15-day or 30-day notices for rooms in your own home without a written lease. The tenant's notices that must be in writing: termination at the end of a term or month (60 days); the 30-day statutory early-termination notice; the first-month termination notice; the 15-day notice for a recurring problem; notice of a condition depriving the tenant of the bargain (15 days to fix); notice for repair-and-deduct (30 days to fix, 10 days to start); notice of continuing loss of essential services before terminating or withholding; written notice of election to quit after a casualty within 1 week after vacating; reporting defective conditions as soon as practicable; immediate written notice of an ejectment or action against the premises; written notice of an extended absence where the lease requires it; written notice and a key for a tenant-installed lock; any objection to your itemized deposit deductions within 10 days; and a forwarding address. Not required to be written: your 48-hour entry notice (the Code says notice, not written notice; a written notice is still the safer record), the tenant's initial report of a loss of essential services (actual or written notice starts the 48 hours), notice terminating for an uninhabitable condition or failure to deliver possession (notice, not written notice), and the tenant's 45-day notice to avoid month-to-month conversion of a lease of 1 year or more or to reject a renewal-with-changes notice (the statutes say notice or notifies, not written; ask for it in writing). Serve written Code notices by the Code's service methods.

title: No special right to enter for or take custody of a tenant's animal
bodyText: Delaware's statutes give you no special right to enter a unit to check on or remove a tenant's animal, and no procedure for a landlord to take custody of an animal a tenant leaves behind. The general rules apply: you may enter in an emergency at any time (an animal in distress may be one), otherwise on 48 hours' notice between 8 a.m. and 9 p.m. for the Code's purposes, and during an extended absence (more than 7 days) as reasonably necessary for inspection, maintenance and safekeeping. Abandoning a domesticated animal without reasonable arrangements for someone else to take custody is cruel neglect, and cruelty to animals is a crime; that duty is the owner's or custodian's. Certified animal welfare officers and law-enforcement officers may impound an animal subjected to cruel mistreatment or neglect, leave written notice for the owner, and return it within 48 hours unless a complaint is filed. So if you find an animal left behind, contact animal welfare or the police rather than removing or rehoming it yourself; the writ-of-possession storage rules for leftover property do not address animals. A lease may ask the tenant to name someone who can care for or collect the animal in an emergency; that person gets no right to enter except with the tenant's consent or as the Code otherwise allows.

title: Assistance animals in Delaware: fair housing accommodation, guide-dog statute, no pet deposit
bodyText: Three Delaware sources apply. (1) Fair housing: refusing a reasonable accommodation in rules, policies, practices or services that may be necessary for a person with a disability to use and enjoy a dwelling is discrimination, which covers waiving a no-pets rule for an assistance animal (including an untrained emotional-support animal, if the accommodation is reasonable and necessary). You may not ask whether an applicant has a disability or about its nature or severity, except for the limited inquiries the statute allows of all applicants. The law does not require renting to someone whose tenancy would be a direct threat to others' health or safety or would cause substantial physical damage to others' property. The State Fair Housing Act's discrimination and disability sections (other than the advertising ban) do not apply to rooms or units in an owner-occupied building of up to 4 families, though federal law may, and the Landlord-Tenant Code's own ban on refusing to rent because of disability has no such exemption. (2) Guide dogs: a person who is totally or partially blind and has a guide dog is entitled to full and equal access to all housing accommodations offered for rent (other than a single-family home renting no more than 1 room), may not be charged extra for the dog, and is liable for damage the dog does. The housing provision has no direct-threat exception (the public-places provision does), and violations are fined $100 each in the JP Court. (3) Deposits: you may not require any pet deposit for a duly certified and trained support animal (an animal individually trained to do work or perform tasks for a disabled resident). Delaware has no statute of its own on emotional-support-animal documentation, online certificates, or misrepresentation of an assistance animal in housing.

title: No pet-and-eviction fact sheet to deliver
bodyText: Delaware does not require you to give tenants a state fact sheet about caring for pets in an eviction, and no state agency publishes one under any statute. The documents you must deliver at the start of a tenancy are the Attorney General's Landlord-Tenant Code summary, the Right to Representation informational materials and, once published, the Rights and Responsibilities Guide. If an eviction is likely and you know the tenant has an animal, it is good practice to remind the tenant that animals are the tenant's responsibility to remove; abandoning a domesticated animal without arranging for someone else to take custody is cruel neglect under Delaware's cruelty law, and animal welfare officers, not landlords, impound animals.

title: Pet deposits are separate, capped at 1 month's rent and handled like security deposits
bodyText: Delaware treats a pet deposit as its own category. A pet deposit is any deposit a tenant makes to be held for the term (or part of it) for the presence of an animal, and the Code's definition of 'security deposit' expressly excludes it, so the pet deposit does not count toward the security-deposit cap. Its own cap is 1 month's rent, regardless of the length of the rental agreement. It is subject to the same escrow, return, itemization, penalty and address rules as a security deposit: hold it in a Delaware-office federally insured escrow account and disclose the location, return it (less proper deductions) with an itemized list within 20 days after the tenancy ends, and face double damages for wrongful withholding. Damage caused by an animal is deducted from the pet deposit first, and only the excess from the security deposit. No pet deposit may be required for a duly certified and trained support animal of a disabled resident, and no extra charge for a blind tenant's guide dog. Nonrefundable pet fees are risky: you may not charge any nonrefundable fee as a condition of occupancy except an optional fee for actual services rendered, and whether a one-time 'pet fee' fits that exception is unsettled, so use a refundable pet deposit instead. Monthly 'pet rent' is not addressed by statute; if you charge it, write it into the rent so it is treated as rent (subject to the late-charge cap and nonpayment rules), and do not charge it for assistance animals.

title: Denying a blind tenant's guide dog: $100 fine per violation, plus fair housing remedies
bodyText: Delaware has a landlord-facing penalty for refusing a guide dog. A person who is totally or partially blind and has a guide dog is entitled to full and equal access to all housing accommodations offered for rent (other than a single-family home renting no more than 1 room), and may not be charged extra for the dog; anyone who violates this guide-dog chapter is fined $100 for each violation on conviction in the Justice of the Peace Court. The housing provision has no exception for disturbance or danger (that exception applies only to the public places listed elsewhere in the chapter) and does not require you to modify the property. Refusing a reasonable accommodation for any assistance animal a person with a disability needs is also discrimination under the State Fair Housing Act, enforced through its complaint and court process (outside owner-occupied buildings of up to 4 families), and refusing to rent because of disability is barred by the Landlord-Tenant Code's fair housing section, under which the tenant may recover damages including substitute-housing costs. The guide-dog chapter speaks of persons who are blind or visually impaired (with physical disabilities included in the general access right), not other disabilities or emotional-support animals.

title: No Delaware crime for misrepresenting a service or assistance animal
bodyText: Delaware's statutes do not make it a crime or civil violation to misrepresent an animal as a service, assistance, support or guide animal, in housing or anywhere else, and set no rule about online registrations or certificates. If you doubt a request, use the fair housing process: where the disability or the need for the animal is not apparent, you may ask for reliable information about the disability-related need (without asking about the nature or severity of the disability beyond what the law allows), and you need not grant an accommodation for an animal whose presence would be a direct threat to others' health or safety or would cause substantial physical damage to others' property. A blind tenant's guide dog is different: the housing statute gives full and equal access without a direct-threat exception. A false statement made to obtain an accommodation may still be addressed as a lease breach (through the 7-day breach notice) or under general fraud law, but there is no Delaware penalty specific to it.

title: No tenant right to install EV charging; new-construction and municipal-permit rules only
bodyText: Delaware's statutes give tenants no right to install an electric vehicle charger at a rental, and do not require landlords to approve one. A tenant's installation is an alteration governed by your lease and consent. Delaware's EV statutes reach landlords only indirectly. (1) New construction: a developer of a single-family dwelling permitted on or after January 1, 2024 must provide at least 1 'electric vehicle capable' parking space (conduit and panel capacity ready for a charger), in the garage if there is one; a developer of a multi-family dwelling (more than 2 units) whose final site plan application was submitted on or after January 1, 2025 must make at least 5% of parking spaces charger-equipped (served by at least a 30-amp unit) and another 10% EV-capable, and provide at least 1 accessible charging space available to all residents; residents may request the construction documents showing where those spaces are; and a covered dwelling may not be used or occupied until the developer complies. (2) Municipal permits: a municipality of 30,000 or more must have a permit process for a residential charging station abutting a residential street, which requires the written permission of the owner of the real property; the municipality may not make an owner install a charger for a tenant unless a general zoning or building code requires it. If you allow a tenant charger, settle in writing who pays for installation, electricity, maintenance and removal, and require a licensed electrician.

title: No rule on a tenant's EV charger at move-out
bodyText: Because Delaware gives tenants no statutory right to install an EV charger, it also has no rule on who owns, removes or pays for a tenant-installed charger at the end of the tenancy. Settle it in the written consent you give for the installation: whether the tenant must remove the charger and restore the property, whether it stays as a fixture and on what terms, and who pays. Restoration and removal costs beyond normal wear and tear can come from the security deposit only for actual damage the tenant caused, itemized within 20 days after the tenancy ends.

title: EV-ready parking required in new residential construction (not tenant installation rules)
bodyText: Delaware has no rules on the safety, registration or insurance requirements a landlord may impose on a tenant-installed charger, because tenants have no statutory installation right. The requirements Delaware does impose fall on developers of new residential buildings, and they matter if you build or buy new rental housing: single-family dwellings with building permits issued on or after January 1, 2024 need at least 1 EV-capable space (in the garage if there is one, otherwise in the driveway, assigned space or an unassigned off-street project space); multi-family dwellings whose final site plan application was submitted on or after January 1, 2025 need at least 5% of spaces with charging infrastructure (at least a 30-amp unit) and another 10% EV-capable, rounded up, plus at least 1 charging space available to all residents and accessible to a person with a disability; the locations must be shown in construction documents and available to residents on request; space dimensions follow the county or municipal code; and the dwelling may not be used or occupied until the developer complies. If you permit a tenant charger, set your own conditions in writing (licensed electrician, permits, insurance, metering and electricity cost, removal); for separately charged electricity, the Code's submetering rules apply.

title: Shared EV charging: one resident-wide space in new multi-family buildings; no tenant installation rules
bodyText: Delaware has no rule on a tenant installing a charger in a shared parking area, reserving a space for it, or sharing its costs; those are matters for your written consent. The one shared-area rule is for new construction: a developer of a multi-family dwelling covered by the EV statute (final site plan application on or after January 1, 2025) must provide, in addition to the 5% charger-equipped and 10% EV-capable spaces, at least 1 charging space in an area available for use by all residents, accessible to a person with a disability. A municipality of 30,000 or more may provide a process for dedicated or reserved parking for a charging station it permits along a residential street. If you charge tenants for using a shared charger, keep it optional, and because electricity is a 'utility service' under the Code, bill any electricity component only as the submetering rules allow (lease provision, separate metering, no more than actual cost); Delaware does not say whether a common-area charger fee is a utility charge, so do not mark up the electricity.

title: Parking and towing rules: tell the tenant at signing; post towing signs
bodyText: Delaware has no parking-rules statute of its own, but two rules control how parking and towing rules take effect. (1) Lease rules generally: a parking rule binds the tenant and the tenant's guests only if it promotes the listed purposes (health, safety, quiet enjoyment, protection of your property, fair distribution of facilities), is brought to the tenant's attention when the tenant enters into the agreement, is reasonably related to its purpose, applies fairly to all tenants, and is explicit enough to tell the tenant what to do; a rule adopted later must be brought to the tenant's attention, and if it substantially modifies the lease (for example, taking away a parking space the lease provided) it needs the tenant's written consent. In an eviction for a rule breach, your complaint must state when and how the rule was made known and attach a copy. (2) Towing: if you authorize nonconsensual towing from a private parking area, you must have a towing contract and post a sign at every vehicle entrance (lettering at least 1 inch high) stating when and for what purpose parking is allowed, that unauthorized vehicles will be towed at the owner's expense, the tow company's name, address and phone number, the towing and storage charges, the storage address and redemption hours, and your contact information. Delaware does not limit the vehicle information you may request or tie permits to the lease term; give parking rules in writing at signing and keep any later change within the Code's rules.

title: Vehicle rules and removing tenants' vehicles: what Delaware towing law allows
bodyText: Vehicle rules (operable and registered vehicles only, no commercial vehicles or trailers, no repairs) are lease rules: they bind if they meet the Code's rules test and were given at signing. Enforcing them by removing a vehicle depends on which Delaware statute applies. (1) Unauthorized parking: Delaware's private towing law covers nonconsensual towing of vehicles of 5,000 pounds or less parked for an unauthorized purpose or at an unauthorized time in a 'private parking area', defined as a privately owned facility held open to the general public for parking and intended primarily for the owner's customers, residents, lessees or guests. It is not limited to strangers' cars, so a tenant's own car parked in violation of posted rules can be towed if the conditions are met: a towing contract, conforming signs at every entrance, photographs of the violation, and (when the area is open to the public at the time) your prior written authorization with your name, phone, e-mail, date, time and signature. Whether a gated or residents-only lot that is not held open to the general public falls inside that law is unsettled. (2) Abandoned or inoperable vehicles: an inoperable or wrecked vehicle, or one with plates expired at least 30 days or no plates, that appears abandoned on private property is removed under the abandoned-vehicle law only at the direction of the police or other listed authorities; where the vehicle belongs to the property's occupant (such as your tenant), the authority must first give 7 days' certified-mail notice and then a 24-hour sticker. You may not have such a vehicle removed on your own authority as an 'abandoned' vehicle. (3) Accessible spaces: you may have a vehicle without a valid disability plate or placard removed from a designated accessible space at the owner's or operator's expense. Never tow in retaliation, and do not charge nonrefundable fees for parking tags beyond optional service fees.

title: Towing from your rental property: contract, signs, photos, written authorization, fee caps
bodyText: Delaware's private towing law (21 Del. C. ch. 69A) governs nonconsensual towing of vehicles of 5,000 pounds or less from a private parking area, meaning a privately owned facility held open to the general public for parking and intended primarily for the owner's customers, residents, lessees or guests. As the owner or operator, you may not permit a nonconsensual tow unless you have contracted with a private tow company for such tows and a conforming sign is posted at every vehicle entrance (lettering at least 1 inch high) stating: the purposes and times parking is allowed; that unauthorized parking is prohibited and vehicles will be towed and stored at the owner's expense; the tow company's name, address and phone number; the towing and storage charges; the storage facility's street address and redemption hours; and your contact information. Before each tow the tow operator must confirm the signs, photograph the violation, and, if the lot is open to the public at the time, obtain your prior written authorization (it may be electronic) with the authorizer's name, a business-hours phone number and e-mail, the date and time, and a signature. A tow must stop if the driver returns before the car leaves the lot (drop fee capped at 50% of the tow fee; no fee before hook-up). For a noncommercial vehicle the tow fee may not exceed $250 and storage $50 a day, with no other towing-related charges, and the storage facility must release personal items free during business hours and offer reasonable after-hours release. Tow companies may not pay you or anyone for tips about parked vehicles, and may patrol your lot only under a contract and with your specific prior written authorization for each tow. Violations are unlawful practices under the Consumer Fraud Act; the vehicle owner recovers all fees paid plus actual damages, every company involved is jointly liable, and the court awards attorney's fees if the owner's pre-suit settlement offer was rejected. You may not direct or knowingly allow anyone working for you to violate the chapter. Separate rules: abandoned or inoperable vehicles are removed only through the police or listed agencies under the abandoned-vehicle law; vehicles in accessible spaces without a valid plate or placard may be removed at the owner's expense.

title: No rule requiring or regulating parking separate from rent
bodyText: Delaware's statutes neither require you to unbundle parking from rent nor regulate a separate parking agreement. If you charge for parking separately, Code rules still shape it: a nonrefundable fee charged as a condition of occupancy is barred except an optional fee for actual services rendered, so make parking an optional, separately priced service (or include it in the rent); a parking charge written into the lease as rent is treated as rent for the late-charge cap and nonpayment remedies; and taking away a parking space the lease provides, by a new rule, is a substantial modification that needs the tenant's written consent. Local zoning codes (not searched) may set parking requirements for buildings.

title: Marijuana in rentals: you may ban smoking and growing; possession and edibles only in narrow cases
bodyText: Delaware's adult-use marijuana law lets property owners prohibit or regulate marijuana on their property, with one landlord limit. In a residential rental you may prohibit smoking marijuana (which includes vaping with an electronic smoking device) and growing it, but you may prohibit possession of marijuana, or consumption by non-smoked means (such as edibles), only if (1) the building is your primary residence, no more than 3 rooms are rented and no more than 3 tenants live there, (2) residence is merely incidental to detention or to medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious or similar services (for example student housing or long-term care), or (3) failing to prohibit it would violate federal law or regulations or cost you a monetary or licensing-related benefit under federal law (for example in federally assisted housing). Medical marijuana: you may not refuse to lease to, or otherwise penalize, a person solely because the person is a registered qualifying patient or designated caregiver, unless that would cost you a monetary or licensing-related benefit under federal law; the medical program does not require any person in lawful possession of property to let guests or visitors smoke marijuana there, and the program will confirm a cardholder's status to a landlord with the cardholder's permission. A general 'criminal activity' or 'illegal drug' lease clause should not be applied to lawful adult possession or non-smoked use that the lease may not ban. Put any marijuana rule in the lease or rules given at signing.

title: No rule on housing disaster-displaced guests
bodyText: Delaware's statutes have no special rule letting tenants house people displaced by a declared disaster despite a guest limit, and no rule on when a displaced person staying in a hotel or other lodging becomes a tenant. Your lease's guest and occupancy terms apply, subject to the Code's rules test (reasonable, fairly applied, made known at signing) and to occupancy limits in housing codes. Delaware does have a state disaster recovery fund, administered under the emergency management laws, that may assist disaster-affected housing and residents; it creates no landlord duties. Hotels and other transient lodging are outside the Landlord-Tenant Code. If you allow displaced relatives or friends to stay longer than your guest limit, put the consent and its end date in writing.

title: No statute on firearm rules in private leases; constitutional right binds government landlords
bodyText: Delaware's statutes neither prohibit nor expressly authorize a private landlord's lease rule restricting firearms, and there is no statute protecting firearms locked in vehicles in a rental's parking area. Delaware's Constitution provides that a person has the right to keep and bear arms for the defense of self, family, home and State, and for hunting and recreational use. Constitutional rights of this kind limit government action, so they matter most for public housing authorities and other government landlords, which should get legal advice before adopting any firearm restriction; no published case was searched. A private landlord's firearm rule is a lease rule like any other: it must meet the Code's rules test (reasonably related to safety or protection of property, fairly applied, explicit, and made known at signing) and may not be adopted mid-tenancy as a substantial modification without the tenant's written consent. Criminal laws (for example, on discharging a firearm toward a dwelling) apply regardless of the lease.

title: No statutory right for tenants' guests or suppliers
bodyText: Delaware's statutes give tenants no statutory right to have guests, caregivers or service providers visit regardless of the lease, and set no rule barring fees for guests in larger buildings. The Code instead treats guests as people for whom the tenant answers: the tenant and everyone in the premises with the tenant's consent must obey valid rules, and tenants and their guests must not unreasonably interfere with other tenants' peaceful enjoyment; the tenant must not permit anyone on the premises with the tenant's permission to wilfully or wantonly destroy, deface, damage or remove any part of the unit or its facilities. Your guest rules must meet the Code's rules test (reasonable, fairly applied to all tenants, explicit, made known at signing). Two outside limits apply: fair housing law bars different terms or privileges because of a protected class (for example, a stricter guest rule for families with children), and a tenant with a disability may need a reasonable accommodation such as a live-in aide. Charging a guest fee as a condition of occupancy is risky under the Code's ban on nonrefundable fees.

title: Criminal nuisance law: act on notice of a tenant's illegal activity; protect victims who call for help
bodyText: Delaware has no crime-free lease addendum statute and no general rule on landlord cooperation with police, but its criminal nuisance abatement law (10 Del. C. ch. 71) pushes landlords to act. If you are notified by certified or registered mail of facts about a tenant's illegal activity on the leased premises that would make a reasonable person believe the allegations are likely true, and you do not start an eviction or summary possession action, that failure is prima facie evidence that you knowingly permitted the nuisance, which exposes you to a civil penalty of $25,000 (or up to $1,000 a day, whichever is greater) and to damages suits by people harmed by the nuisance, who also recover their attorney's fees. It is an affirmative defense that you tried to abate the nuisance before getting the State's written notice of intent to sue, for example by sending a breach notice or termination notice under the Code, filing for summary possession, or seeking police intervention and helping the police prosecute. If a tenant who appeared at a hearing is found to have used the unit for a criminal-nuisance purpose, the lease becomes void at your option and possession reverts to you; the court may also suspend leases, rental licenses or tenant-assistance payments, and in multi-unit premises may order an owner who knew of the nuisance to pay relocation help to uninvolved tenants. The Code itself lets you end a lease on notice for a breach causing or threatening irreparable harm, or for a tenant's conviction of a class A misdemeanor or felony during the term that caused or threatened irreparable harm. The other side: you may not evict, raise rent, cut services or otherwise force out a tenant who is a victim of domestic abuse, sexual offenses or stalking and has sought help from a court, the police, medical emergency services or a victim program (an action within 90 days of an incident is presumed unlawful, subject to the rebuttals the statute lists; the protection does not cover a tenant otherwise delinquent in rent), so do not treat calls for police or emergency help by a victim as a lease violation. Delaware's reporting laws also bind you and your staff as they bind anyone. Any person who knows or in good faith suspects child abuse, neglect or human trafficking must report it to the Department of Services for Children, Youth and Their Families (calling the police alone is not enough), on pain of a civil penalty of up to $10,000 for a first violation and $50,000 after that (16 Del. C. §§ 903 and 914). A person with reasonable cause to believe that an impaired or incapacitated adult is in need of protective services must report it to the Department of Health and Social Services (31 Del. C. § 3910(a)). And a person who knows of a death from violence, suicide, accident, poison or overdose, or one that is sudden, unattended by a physician or suspicious, as when a tenant is found dead in a unit, must immediately notify the Medical Examiner, and must not touch or move the clothing or articles on or near the body without the Division of Forensic Science's order; a wilful violation can bring up to 1 year in prison or a $1,000 fine, or both (29 Del. C. § 4706(a)).

title: No right of access for candidates or canvassers; tenant organizing is protected
bodyText: Delaware's statutes do not require you to let political candidates, campaign workers, petition circulators or voter-registration volunteers into an apartment building or other multi-unit property, and do not require a place for voter information. Delaware's Constitution protects free speech, but like other constitutional rights it limits government action rather than private landlords (no published case was searched). What the Landlord-Tenant Code does protect is tenant organizing: if a tenant has organized or is an officer of a tenants' organization, seeking possession, raising the rent or cutting services within 90 days is presumed retaliatory, with recovery of 3 months' rent or treble damages. Signs: Delaware gives tenants no statutory right to post political signs against a clear, evenly applied lease rule (the U.S. flag is protected); in a condominium or other common-interest community, unless the declaration provides otherwise, association rules may not prohibit unit owners' signs about candidates or ballot questions, though they may regulate time, place, size, number and manner.

title: No tenant right to a window or portable air conditioner, and no cooling standard
bodyText: Delaware's statutes give tenants no right to install a portable or window air conditioner or other cooling device despite a lease restriction, and require no lease statement about window units. Delaware's housing-code and Landlord-Tenant Code duties address heat, hot water, water and electricity, not cooling, unless your lease or a local code makes you supply cooling. A rule on window units is a lease rule: it must be reasonable (for example, safety and installation standards), fairly applied, explicit, and given at signing. If you do supply air conditioning as a facility, you must maintain it in good working order like any other facility you supply. Requests to use a cooling device because of a disability may call for a reasonable accommodation.

title: No tenant right to plug-in or balcony solar; Delaware's solar-access law protects owners' roofs
bodyText: Delaware's statutes give tenants no right to install a plug-in, balcony or other portable solar device, or a solar system of any kind, at a rental, and no utility statute lets a tenant connect one without approval. Delaware's solar-access law protects property owners, not tenants: a covenant, restriction or condition in a deed, contract or other instrument affecting real property that effectively prohibits or unreasonably restricts the owner of a single-family home or owner-maintained townhouse from installing or using a roof-mounted solar system on that owner's property is void, though reasonable restrictions that do not significantly raise cost or reduce efficiency are allowed, and the owner must give certified-mail notice to the homeowners' association (if any) and neighbors within 150 feet at least 60 days before installing. As a landlord-owner, that law can help you install roof solar despite HOA rules; it does not give your tenant a right to install anything. A tenant's solar device is an alteration under your lease and rules; if you allow one, set safety, electrician, utility-interconnection and removal terms in writing.

title: Multi-family complexes: give residents recycling instructions every year
bodyText: Delaware law does not require a recycling notice in the lease, but if you own or operate a multi-family complex (3 or more attached units, such as apartments or condominiums, with central trash collection), you must give residents instructions on how to take part in the complex's recycling program, with information about what is recyclable, at least once every calendar year. Your hauler must provide single-stream recycling and a central recycling container; your local government may require you to supply your own containers. The Landlord-Tenant Code makes trash receptacles your duty only if the lease says so. Check local recycling ordinances.

title: Religious and cultural displays: no statutory right, but rules must be neutral
bodyText: Delaware's statutes do not give tenants a right to put up religious or cultural items (such as a mezuzah on the door frame) despite a lease rule, and do not stop you from having a reasonable, neutral rule on door and exterior decorations. Any rule must be applied the same way to everyone: Delaware fair housing law bars different terms, conditions or privileges, or higher rent, because of religion or creed. A rule that singles out religious items, or is enforced only against one faith, risks a discrimination claim; a neutral rule with a reasonable-accommodation approach for small door-frame items is the cautious course.

title: Smoking banned in apartment common areas; no smoke-drift waiver
bodyText: Smoking and vaping are banned by state law in the lobbies, hallways and other indoor common areas of apartment buildings, condominiums and other multi-unit residential buildings, whether or not staff work there; violations carry an administrative penalty of $100 for a first violation and at least $250 for each later one. The ban does not reach inside a private unit, so whether tenants may smoke in their own units is up to your lease and rules. Delaware has no statute on smoke drifting between units, and you may not use a lease clause in which the tenant gives up claims or remedies against you for drifting smoke: such a clause is unenforceable, and knowingly enforcing it exposes you to a claim for 3 months' rent. If smoke drift is a concern, a building-wide no-smoking rule (applied to all tenants and disclosed at signing) is the lawful tool.

title: Tenant display rights: U.S. flag protected; signs follow your rules
bodyText: Whatever your lease or rules say, a tenant may display the United States flag (up to 3 by 5 feet) on a pole attached to the exterior of the building within the leased property, or on a flagpole within the property's boundaries; you may require conformity with setback rules and a flagpole height of no more than 25 feet. Delaware has no statute giving tenants a right to display other flags, banners or political signs against your lease rules, so a clear, evenly applied sign and display rule is enforceable. If the unit is in a condominium or other common interest community, the association generally may not ban the U.S. flag, the Delaware flag, or signs about candidates or ballot questions on or next to a unit (unless the declaration provides otherwise), but it may regulate their time, place, size, number and manner; follow the association's rules in your lease.

title: Security cameras and video doorbells: lease rules govern; privacy crime limits
bodyText: Delaware has no statute on tenant-installed security cameras or video doorbells, so your lease may set reasonable rules, such as requiring your written consent before anything is drilled or mounted, no recording of common areas or neighbors' units, and removal and repair at move-out. Delaware's criminal privacy law applies to everyone: it is a misdemeanor to install a device to watch, photograph or record in a private place without the consent of the people entitled to privacy there, or to use a device outside a private place to pick up sounds from inside that would not normally be heard. Never place a camera inside an occupied unit, and keep any building cameras in common areas pointed away from unit interiors.

title: Waterbeds: no Delaware statute; deposit and fee limits apply
bodyText: Delaware has no statute on waterbeds or other water-filled furniture in rentals, so your lease may forbid them or allow them on conditions such as your written consent, professional installation and proof of renter's insurance covering water damage. Any extra money you require counts toward Delaware's limits: no nonrefundable waterbed fee, and any additional deposit must fit within the security deposit cap (one month's rent for leases of a year or more, and for month-to-month tenancies after their first year; no cap for furnished units).

title: Common interest community: give the tenant the association rules at signing
bodyText: If your rental unit is in a condominium, cooperative or planned community governed by Delaware's Uniform Common Interest Ownership Act (generally communities created on or after September 30, 2009 with more than 20 units, or older ones that opted in), you must get a current copy of the community's rules from the association's executive board and give it to your tenant when the lease is signed (or when an oral tenancy begins), and pass along any new or revised rules as the board adopts and notices them. Your tenant is bound by the rules once noticed, and you must take lawful action against a tenant who materially violates them; if you don't act within a reasonable time after the board's written demand, the board may enforce the rules against your tenant directly, including by an action for possession. Attach the rules to the lease and have the tenant acknowledge receipt.

title: Bed bugs: inspect before renting and disclose infested adjacent units
bodyText: Before you rent a unit, visually inspect it for signs of bed bugs (live bugs, shells, eggs, or brownish or blood spotting on linens, mattresses or furniture). You may not show, rent or lease a vacant unit you know or reasonably suspect is currently infested, and before renting you must tell the prospective tenant if any adjacent unit is currently infested or being treated. Once anyone reports a suspected infestation, you must acknowledge it and have it inspected within 120 hours, start professional treatment within 14 days if an infestation is found, check adjacent, above and below units within 5 days (not counting intermediate Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays), tell affected tenants the pest professional's findings within 120 hours of receiving them (email or a shared tenant portal is allowed), and keep records of complaints and treatment for 2 years. You pay for treatment if the tenant reports within 60 days after move-in or within 30 days after an infestation is found in an adjoining unit; after that the tenant shares the reasonable cost of treating their own unit (not in housing-authority properties). These rules apply to single-family homes as well as apartments.

title: Certificate of occupancy: no state disclosure duty; check local licensing
bodyText: Delaware state law does not require you to tell a tenant whether the unit has a certificate of occupancy or to hand over a copy. Many Delaware cities and counties do require occupancy permits or rental licenses before a unit is rented, and some require inspections, so check your local code. Separately, if a code official has served you with a notice of violation or compliance order under the State Housing Code, you may not lease the unit until it is fixed. The Housing Code's alternative (giving the new lessee a copy of the order and filing the lessee's notarized acceptance of responsibility for the repairs) does not fit a residential tenancy: under the Landlord-Tenant Code you must keep the unit code-compliant, and a tenant cannot agree to do work needed to bring a noncomplying unit up to code, so make the repairs before renting. Never let anyone occupy a unit placarded as condemned.

title: Defective drywall: no tenant disclosure statute
bodyText: Delaware has no statute requiring you to tell a tenant about defective or corrosive drywall. If drywall causes a condition that endangers the tenant's health or safety, your general duty to keep the unit safe and fit applies, and the tenant has the usual repair remedies. If you rent a one-to-four-family home with an option to purchase, Delaware's seller disclosure law applies to that transfer, and you must disclose all known material defects in writing.

title: Submetered electricity and other utilities: Delaware billing rules
bodyText: If you meter electricity (or water, sewer or fuel) to each unit yourself and bill tenants for it, Delaware lets you do so only if the lease says so and only if each unit is separately metered with a system approved by the Division of Weights and Measures (systems already in use before July 17, 1996 are excepted). You may charge no more than your actual cost from the provider; you must bill at least monthly, take actual readings at move-in and move-out, send no more than two estimated bills in a row, let tenants inspect the underlying bills at your office, keep those records for one year, and test a meter when a tenant asks (the tenant pays for the test only if the meter proves accurate). You may never shut off utility service for nonpayment. Utility charges you bill count as rent. The Attorney General's Consumer Protection Unit enforces these rules.

title: Flood disclosure: no Delaware lease requirement
bodyText: Delaware does not require you to tell tenants whether the property is in a flood zone or has flooded before, and has no flood disclosure form or flood-based right to end the lease. Once Delaware's landlord-tenant rights and responsibilities guide takes effect (by June 10, 2027 at the latest), the guide you must give every prospective tenant before signing will include information about renters insurance and flood insurance. Telling tenants about known flooding is still the cautious course, because concealing a known material fact in a lease transaction can be a consumer fraud problem. If you lease a one-to-four-family home with an option to buy, Delaware's seller disclosure law applies and you must disclose known material defects in writing.

title: Foreclosure: no Delaware disclosure statute
bodyText: Delaware has no statute requiring you to tell a prospective tenant (or a current one) that the property is in foreclosure. A tenant whose rights began after the mortgage can be removed after a foreclosure sale: the buyer can get a writ of possession, and a tenant who stays more than 5 days after the sale is completed can face a summary possession action. Federal law gives many tenants extra time after a foreclosure. Renting out a property you know is about to be sold at foreclosure without saying so risks a consumer fraud claim for concealing a material fact, so disclose a pending foreclosure before signing.

title: Good-cause eviction notice: none in Delaware
bodyText: Delaware has no statewide good-cause eviction law and no required notice telling tenants whether one applies. You may end a fixed-term lease at the end of its term, or a month-to-month tenancy, by giving at least 60 days' written notice without stating a reason (for month-to-month, the 60 days start on the first day of the month after the tenant actually receives the notice), as long as the decision is not retaliatory or discriminatory. Federally subsidized and some other assisted tenancies have their own good-cause rules that override Delaware's where they conflict, and a tenant served with a termination notice under such a lease may have a right to free legal representation. For rental agreements entered into on or after March 8, 2027 (March 9 on the bill page), if part of a tenant's rent is paid from a state reentry fund, you must help the tenant complete a discharge plan and give notices before terminating for nonpayment or breach.

title: Environmental covenants: give occupants a copy when DNREC requires
bodyText: Delaware has no statute requiring you to disclose known environmental contamination in a lease. If your property is subject to a recorded environmental covenant (activity and use limitations from a DNREC-supervised cleanup, such as limits on groundwater wells, gardening or digging), the covenant runs with the land and may restrict how the property is used, and the owner must give a copy to people in possession of the property when DNREC requires it. Give tenants a copy of any environmental covenant, and make the lease's use rules consistent with it. Hiding known contamination from a prospective tenant risks a consumer fraud claim.

title: Associations and your tenant: fines, rent diversion and leasing limits
bodyText: If your rental is in a condominium, cooperative or planned community under Delaware's Uniform Common Interest Ownership Act, the association can act against your tenant directly when the tenant breaks the community's rules: it can suspend privileges, fine the tenant after notice and a chance to be heard, and, if the violation isn't cured within 10 days of notice to you and the tenant, require the tenant to pay rent to the association up to the amount of the tenant's own unpaid fines or fees (not your unpaid assessments). Leasing restrictions must be in the declaration (or be reasonable board rules tied to lender requirements), and a later amendment restricting use or occupancy needs an 80 percent vote and must reasonably protect uses already allowed. Delaware has no statutory cap on association lease-approval or move-in fees. Older (pre-September 30, 2009) and small communities may be governed mainly by their own documents, so read your declaration and rules and build their leasing terms into your lease.

title: Open housing-code violation orders: fix them or disclose before leasing
bodyText: If a code official has served you with a notice of violation or a compliance order under the Delaware State Housing Code, it is unlawful to lease the unit until the order is complied with, unless you first give the new tenant a true copy of the order and file with the code official the tenant's signed, notarized statement acknowledging it and accepting responsibility for the repairs. Because Delaware's Landlord-Tenant Code makes you responsible for keeping the unit code-compliant and a lease cannot shift that duty, the safe course is to finish the repairs before renting. Never let anyone occupy a unit placarded as condemned: that is a misdemeanor (fine of $25 to $1,000, up to 30 days in jail, each day a separate offense). Many Delaware cities and counties enforce their own housing codes instead of the State Housing Code; check yours for any further disclosure rule.

title: Landlord liability insurance: no Delaware mandate
bodyText: Delaware state law does not require you to carry liability insurance on a rental property, to register a policy, or to tell tenants about your coverage. Insurance is still prudent, and lenders and associations commonly require it. Some Delaware cities may require proof of insurance as part of a rental license, so check local rules.

title: Meter conservation charge: none in Delaware
bodyText: Delaware has no meter conservation charge or similar energy-efficiency loan tied to a utility meter that you must disclose to new tenants. Delaware utilities may include a small state energy-efficiency charge on every customer's bill, but that is the utility's charge, not yours, and it requires nothing in your lease. If you bill tenants for submetered utilities, you may charge only your actual cost.

title: Former drug labs: no Delaware disclosure statute
bodyText: Delaware has no statute requiring you to tell tenants that a unit was used to make methamphetamine or other drugs, no reporting duty, and no state cleanup standard you must meet before re-renting. Operating a clandestine drug lab is a felony, and a convicted operator must pay the cleanup costs. If a unit was used as a lab, have it professionally assessed and remediated before anyone moves in: renting a contaminated unit would breach your duty to provide a safe, fit unit, and hiding known contamination from a prospective tenant risks a consumer fraud claim.

title: Military air zones: no Delaware lease disclosure
bodyText: Delaware state law does not require you to tell tenants that a rental is in a military aircraft noise or accident-potential zone or near a base such as Dover Air Force Base. Kent County or City of Dover zoning around the base may have its own rules, so check locally; telling tenants about known aircraft noise before they sign is the cautious course.

title: Mold: no Delaware disclosure statute; moisture rules apply
bodyText: Delaware has no statute requiring you to disclose mold, hand out a mold pamphlet, or test for mold. You must still keep the unit free of the moisture problems that cause mold: under the State Housing Code (or your local equivalent), walls and roofs must keep out rain and dampness and basements and crawl spaces must be kept free of standing water, and the Landlord-Tenant Code requires a unit that does not endanger tenants' health or safety. Tell prospective tenants about known mold or water problems before they sign; hiding a known material problem risks a consumer fraud claim.

title: Ordnance, demolition and shared-meter disclosures: none in Delaware
bodyText: Delaware does not require you to tell prospective tenants about a former military ordnance site nearby, about plans to demolish the building, or about shared gas or electric meters. Two related rules apply. You may not make a tenant open a utility account, or bill a tenant separately for a utility, unless the unit is separately metered, so a tenant cannot be billed separately for consumption measured on a meter serving other units or common areas (non-consumption charges such as fixed service fees may be passed on at actual cost and prorated among units if the lease so provides, and metering systems in use before July 17, 1996 are excepted). And if you plan to demolish or substantially remodel, a good-faith plan is a defense to a retaliation claim, but you must still give the normal 60 days' written notice before the end of the term (or of a month-to-month tenancy). Telling applicants about a planned demolition before they sign is the cautious course.

title: Pest control: no notice statute; extermination duties apply
bodyText: Delaware does not require you to give tenants notice of pest-control treatments or a copy of a pest-control company's notice. Under the State Housing Code (or your local equivalent), you must exterminate before renting, and you remain responsible for pests in shared and public areas of multi-unit buildings; in a single-family rental, the tenant is responsible for later extermination (other than bed bugs, which have their own rules). Treatments must use methods not injurious to health. Give the normal 48 hours' notice before entering a unit for treatment, and telling tenants what will be applied is good practice.

title: Private wells: no testing or disclosure statute; multi-unit systems may be public
bodyText: Delaware does not require you to test a private well that serves a rental home or to give tenants well test results. If you supply well water to tenants in a multi-unit property, though, your water system may be a regulated public water system under Department of Health rules, which can require a licensed operator, regular testing, and notices to residents when contaminants exceed drinking water standards; check with the Division of Public Health. For a single-family rental on a well, testing periodically and sharing results with your tenant is good practice.

title: Chemical exposure warnings: no Delaware Prop 65 analog
bodyText: Delaware has no Proposition 65-style law requiring you to post or give warnings about chemicals that cause cancer or reproductive harm. Specific hazards have their own rules (for example federal lead-based paint disclosure for pre-1978 housing and Delaware's bed bug rules), and California-style warning language does not belong in a Delaware lease.

title: Property-tax share of rent: no Delaware statement required
bodyText: Delaware does not require you to tell tenants how much of their rent goes to property taxes, annually or when rent changes. If a tenant ends up paying a property tax on the rental that the law levies on the owner, the tenant can deduct it from rent or recover it from you, unless your lease makes the tenant responsible for the tax. A substantial property-tax increase that you became liable for at least 4 months earlier can justify a matching pro-rata rent increase without it being treated as retaliation.

title: Radon: no lease disclosure, except lease-with-option-to-buy
bodyText: Delaware does not require you to tell tenants about radon or to test for it before renting. Delaware's radon disclosure applies to sales: a buyer must be told the property may present a potential for radon exposure, and the seller must share any radon test results and known radon hazards on a state form. That sale rule also covers a lease with an option to purchase a one-to-four-family home, so if you offer a rent-to-own lease, give the radon notice and disclosure. Sharing any radon test results you have with tenants is the cautious course.

title: Delaware lead rules beyond the federal disclosure
bodyText: On top of the federal lead disclosure for pre-1978 housing, Delaware has its own rules. If a child living in your rental is found to have an elevated blood lead level, the state may assess the home, and if it finds a lead hazard it may abate it at state expense; you must give the state's contractors access, and missing the program's deadlines is a criminal nuisance and costs you the free abatement. If the state abates a rented or multi-unit property, you may not raise any tenant's rent there for 3 years unless you pay the state's estimated cost within 30 days. Never apply paint with more than 0.5 percent lead. By March 1, 2028 at the latest, Delaware's lead-safe certification law takes effect for pre-1978 units: certification before each new tenancy, a lease disclosure, educational materials before move-in with a signed acknowledgment, no retaliation against tenants who complain about lead, and proof of compliance when you file for eviction.

title: Delaware lead notices for pre-1978 units (from implementation)
bodyText: Delaware's own lead notices are coming but are not yet in force: they start when Delaware's lead-safe certification law is implemented (no later than March 1, 2028). From then, for any unit built before 1978: every lease (including renewals) must state whether the unit is certified lead safe or lead free, the certification date and the inspector's name; you must give the tenant a copy of the certificate within 7 days of a request; you must give the state and federal lead educational materials before the tenant moves in, and the lease must include the tenant's acknowledgment of receipt; if your multi-unit building was certified by sampling, you must tell tenants in uninspected units that their unit was not inspected; and you must give at least 10 days' notice of any move into or out of alternative housing during lead work. Until then, follow the federal lead disclosure rules.

title: Delaware required disclosures checklist
