bodyText: Delaware requires these documents and disclosures for a residential tenancy: the names and business addresses of the owners (or their resident agents) and anyone acting as landlord, printed prominently on the written lease, plus a free copy of the signed lease; the Attorney General's Landlord-Tenant Code summary at the start of the tenancy; the state right-to-representation notice (English, Spanish or Haitian Creole versions) at signing, at the first renewal or modification, with any past-due or breach notice and any termination notice under a lease that may be ended only for good cause or a material violation, and when a housing subsidy ends; the location of the security deposit bank account; before renting, whether any adjacent unit has bed bugs or is being treated; a signed disclosure for an employee who lives in the unit as part of pay; and, if deposit return depends on returning keys, a clear key-surrender procedure in the lease. Coming soon: the state rights and responsibilities guide, before signing and at renewals of a year or more (by June 10, 2027 at the latest), and lead-safe certification disclosures for pre-1978 units (by March 1, 2028 at the latest). In some situations you must also give association rules (condominiums and HOAs), copies of open housing-code violation orders, and yearly recycling instructions (multi-family complexes). Delaware has no required first-page form or type-size rule for leases.

title: Housing code variances: no tenant notice or lease attachment required
bodyText: Delaware does not require you to give tenants a copy of a housing-code variance or attach it to the lease. A code official may grant you a variance from the State Housing Code on written application when strict compliance would cause undue hardship or displace low-income occupants, as long as safety is assured. If you have a variance affecting a unit, giving the tenant a copy is good practice, and your local housing code may have its own rules.

title: Sex offender registry: no landlord disclosure duty
bodyText: Delaware does not require you to tell tenants about registered sex offenders in the area or to put a registry notice in the lease. If a real estate licensee handles the rental, the licensee may not volunteer that someone in the community is a registered sex offender without consent, but if asked must refer the person to the Delaware State Police. You may point any tenant or applicant to the State Police's public sex offender registry.

title: Shoreline access: no Delaware lease disclosure
bodyText: Delaware does not require you to tell tenants of beachfront or shoreline property about public access rights along the shore. Where the State has funded beach restoration on a private beach, the public keeps rights on the beach seaward of the dune vegetation line or structure line for activities like fishing and swimming, so if your rental is in such an area, telling tenants is helpful. Note that short, nonrenewable seasonal rentals (120 days or less a year) in the coastal Sussex County hundreds fall outside the Landlord-Tenant Code.

title: First-page and font-size lease rules: none in Delaware
bodyText: Delaware has no required first-page notice about squatters or unlawful occupancy for single-family rentals, and no rule on font size or first-page placement for lease disclosures. The one prominence rule is that the owners' (or agents') names and business addresses must appear prominently on every written lease. Writing the lease in clear, readable type with key terms easy to find is still wise, because Delaware's consumer-contract law penalizes leases that obscure their terms.

title: Source of income (including vouchers) is protected
bodyText: You may not refuse to rent, renew, sublet or assign, end a tenancy, or charge more rent because of a person's source of income, which includes housing vouchers and other government or private rental assistance. You may apply income-sufficiency and credit standards if you apply them in a commercially reasonable way regardless of where the income comes from. If a public housing authority does not follow the state's standardized process for approving a voucher tenancy, you may deny that application. The state Fair Housing Act exempts owner-occupied buildings of up to four units from most of its rules (but never from its advertising ban), while the Landlord-Tenant Code's source-of-income ban has no such exemption, so treat it as applying to every rental. A version of the law taking effect December 31, 2028 says landlords are not required to participate in voucher programs.

title: Sprinkler systems: no lease disclosure; maintain any system
bodyText: Delaware does not require you to tell tenants in the lease whether the building has sprinklers or when they were last inspected. If your rental has a sprinkler or other fire suppression system, you must keep it in good condition, with sprinkler heads clean, unpainted and undamaged. Sprinkler information duties in Delaware apply to builders and sellers of new homes, not landlords.

title: Stigmatized property: no duty to volunteer; answer written questions truthfully
bodyText: Delaware does not require you to tell a prospective tenant that a property is psychologically impacted, meaning it was (or was suspected to be) the site of a homicide, suicide or other felony other than arson, or an occupant had HIV, AIDS or a similar disease not spread by living in a home, and you cannot be sued for not raising it. But if a prospective tenant asks you in writing about psychological impacts on a specific property, you must answer truthfully to the best of your knowledge. You must never disclose that a prior occupant had HIV, AIDS or any other disease that medical evidence shows is highly unlikely to be spread by living in a home, even if asked. Arson and physical problems with the property are not covered by this rule.

title: Rent cap or tenant protection notice: none in Delaware
bodyText: Delaware has no statewide rent cap, rent control, just-cause eviction law or tenant right to buy for ordinary residential rentals, so there is no notice to give about one. To raise rent or change other terms at renewal, give written notice at least 60 days before the lease ends stating the new terms and when they take effect; the tenant is treated as accepting unless the tenant gives notice of termination at least 45 days before the term ends, and a rejection ends the lease at the end of the term. Rent increases must not be retaliatory. Manufactured home communities have their own rent rules, not covered here.

title: Delaware truth-in-renting equivalent: the AG Landlord-Tenant summary
bodyText: Delaware's version of a truth-in-renting statement is the Attorney General's summary of the Landlord-Tenant Code: give every new tenant a copy at the start of the tenancy (the summary itself says at lease signing), or the tenant may defend any case by pleading ignorance of the law. Use the current edition from the Department of Justice, and note that the October 2024 edition still describes the old 5-day notice for unpaid rent; the notice is now at least 7 days. By June 10, 2027 at the latest, you will also have to give the state's rights and responsibilities guide before the lease is signed and get the tenant's acknowledgment. No special notice paragraph is required in the lease itself.

title: Utility disclosure attachment: not required; lease must authorize charges
bodyText: Delaware does not require a separate utility disclosure form attached to the lease. What it requires is authorization in the lease itself: you may bill tenants for metered utilities only if the lease provides for it and each unit is separately metered, and you may pass through flat (non-usage) utility charges, such as a flat sewer or trash fee, and split them among units only if the lease provides for it and the total does not exceed your actual cost. Tenants may inspect the bills behind any utility charge. State the utility arrangements clearly in the lease.

title: Accessory dwelling units: local zoning governs; state plans must authorize them
bodyText: Delaware does not require towns or counties to allow accessory dwelling units (ADUs) by right or forbid owner-occupancy rules, so whether you may build and rent an ADU depends on local zoning. State planning law does push in that direction: larger local governments must adopt affordable housing plans that authorize ADUs (among other housing types) without a conditional use permit or special exception, phased in as each updates its comprehensive plan. Once you rent an ADU as someone's home, the full Landlord-Tenant Code applies to it.

title: Smoke and CO alarm tampering: no lease fee; actual costs and state fines
bodyText: Delaware does not authorize a set fee for a tenant who removes or disables a smoke or carbon monoxide detector. The law itself forbids tenants from removing or tampering with working detectors (including pulling working batteries), and the state can fine anyone who tampers $100 to $500 per offense, but that fine goes to the state, not to you. On a lease of a month or more, the tenant must keep working batteries in the detectors in the unit. If a tenant damages a detector, you may replace it and bill the tenant the actual, reasonable cost as additional rent (or deduct it from the security deposit) and treat repeated tampering as a lease breach, rather than writing a flat penalty fee into the lease.

title: Asbestos: certified abatement only; no lease disclosure
bodyText: Delaware does not require you to disclose asbestos to tenants or to inspect for it. If you remove, encapsulate, repair or renovate materials containing asbestos (beyond routine day-to-day maintenance), only state-certified asbestos contractors and workers may do the work, and you may not hire or let uncertified workers do it. If damaged or crumbling asbestos endangers your tenants, your duty to provide a safe unit applies; tell prospective tenants about known asbestos hazards rather than concealing them.

title: Balconies and decks: no inspection mandate; keep them safe
bodyText: Delaware does not require scheduled engineering inspections of balconies, decks or other elevated exterior structures. You must keep every stair, porch and balcony safe, sound and able to carry the loads it will bear, with railings adequate for safety, and make the repairs needed to keep them in good condition. Periodic professional inspection of older wood balconies and decks is a prudent way to meet that duty. Check your local property-maintenance code for any inspection program.

title: Casualty and mitigation rules cannot be waived
bodyText: Your lease cannot waive Delaware's fire and casualty rule or your duty to mitigate. If fire or another casualty that is not the tenant's fault substantially impairs the unit, the tenant may move out immediately and end the lease (by notifying you in writing within a week after vacating), or, if staying is lawful, stop using the damaged part and pay reduced rent in proportion to the lost value; you must return deposits and prepaid rent as the Code allows. If a tenant abandons the unit, you must make reasonable efforts to re-rent, and the tenant owes the lesser of the remaining rent or your actual re-renting losses. A lease clause waiving these rights is unenforceable, and knowingly trying to enforce it can cost you 3 months' rent.

title: Children in the household: familial status protected; neutral occupancy limits only
bodyText: Delaware does not require your lease to address children, but you may not refuse to rent to, charge more, or set different terms for households with children under 18 (including pregnant applicants and people getting custody), and ads may not express a preference against children. You may set an occupancy limit only if it is reasonable, follows the applicable government occupancy standard, and is applied to all occupants without singling out children. The State Housing Code's floor-area minimum (where it applies) is 150 square feet for the first occupant and 100 for each additional one, with at least 64 square feet in a one-person bedroom. Qualifying senior housing is exempt from the familial-status rules.

title: Confession of judgment clauses are void
bodyText: Do not put a confession-of-judgment clause (a clause letting the landlord, or anyone else, enter a judgment against the tenant without a court hearing) in a Delaware lease. Delaware law makes such a clause void, and if you knowingly try to enforce it the tenant can sue you for 3 months' rent plus court costs. To collect rent or recover possession you must file in the Justice of the Peace Court like any other landlord.

title: Consumer Fraud Act applies to residential leases
bodyText: Delaware's Consumer Fraud Act applies to renting homes: any deception, false promise, misrepresentation, unfair practice, or concealment of a material fact (intending that the tenant rely on it) in advertising, offering or carrying out a lease is unlawful, whether or not anyone was actually misled. Tenants may sue you directly, and the Attorney General can seek injunctions, restitution and civil penalties of up to $10,000 per wilful violation. Delaware's consumer-contract law also treats a lease written in unintelligible language, or one that leaves out legally required disclosures, as deceptive (for leases totaling $50,000 or less). Delaware does not list blank spaces at signing as a named violation, but you must give the tenant a free copy of the signed lease. Fill in every blank, use plain language, and describe the unit, fees and policies truthfully.

title: Domestic violence information: no confidentiality statute; protect it anyway
bodyText: Delaware has no statute that specifically requires you to keep a tenant's domestic-violence status, supporting documents, or forwarding address confidential. Treat that information as confidential anyway: a victim's safety may depend on it, federally assisted housing has its own confidentiality rules, and if the tenant is enrolled in the state's Address Confidentiality Program you may not post their actual address or phone number online after a written demand or to incite or threaten harm. Remember that a victim of domestic abuse, sexual offenses or stalking may end the lease on 30 days' written notice (the 30 days begin on the first day of the month after you receive the notice), and you may not evict, raise rent or cut services where such a victim has sought help from a court, the police, medical emergency services or a domestic violence or sexual offenses program (unless the tenant is otherwise behind on rent).

title: Calling for help: protection for abuse victims, no general statute
bodyText: Delaware has no statute giving all tenants a general right to call police or emergency services without penalty, but you must not use a lease or nuisance clause to punish victims. You may not evict, raise rent, cut services or pressure a tenant to leave where the tenant is a victim of domestic abuse, sexual offenses or stalking and has sought help from a court, police, emergency medical services or a victim program; an adverse action within 90 days of an incident is presumed unlawful unless you can show a listed reason (a tenant who is behind on rent does not get this protection). Such a victim may also end the lease on 30 days' written notice, counted from the first day of the month after you receive it. Do not write crime-free clauses that treat calls for help as lease violations; calling police about criminal activity is in fact one of the steps that helps you defend a nuisance action.

title: Eviction notice or filing penalties: not authorized
bodyText: Do not put fees or penalties tied to eviction notices or court filings in a Delaware lease. Delaware makes lease clauses awarding attorney's fees unenforceable, the Justice of the Peace Court never awards attorney's fees in residential landlord-tenant cases, and the Code authorizes only a capped late fee (5 percent, not charged within 5 days) and actual, reasonable repair or cleaning costs when you fix a tenant's breach. Court costs are whatever the court awards in the case, and a tenant can usually stop a nonpayment eviction by paying all past-due amounts the court determines plus court-awarded costs and fees before the eviction is carried out (not if 2 nonpayment possession judgments were entered against the tenant in the prior 18 months).

title: Exculpatory and landlord-indemnity clauses are prohibited
bodyText: Your Delaware lease may not excuse or limit your legal liability to the tenant, or make the tenant indemnify you (or pay your costs) for your own legal liability. Common clauses such as 'landlord is not liable for any injury or damage on the premises' or 'tenant will hold landlord harmless from all claims' are unenforceable in Delaware, and if you knowingly try to enforce one the tenant can sue you for 3 months' rent plus court costs. The rest of the lease still stands. You may make the tenant responsible for damage the tenant, household members or guests cause, and require the tenant to carry renters insurance.

title: Delaware fair housing: protected classes and exemptions
bodyText: Delaware bans housing discrimination based on race (including hair texture and protective hairstyles), color, national origin, religion, creed, sex, marital status, familial status, source of income (including vouchers), age (18 and over), sexual orientation, gender identity, disability, military status, and housing status (including homelessness); the Landlord-Tenant Code adds occupation. That covers refusing to rent, renew, sublet or assign, ending a tenancy, charging more, different terms or services, discriminatory advertising, saying a unit is unavailable when it is not, and retaliating against anyone who asserts these rights. Narrow exemptions exist (religious organizations, private clubs, qualifying senior housing, reasonable occupancy limits, and owner-occupied buildings of up to four units), but even exempt owners may not publish discriminatory ads, and the Landlord-Tenant Code's ban has no owner-occupied exemption. Disabled tenants are entitled to reasonable accommodations and modifications. Claims can go to the Division of Human and Civil Rights or to court within two years, with actual and punitive damages and attorney's fees.

title: Fire code: the State Fire Prevention Regulations
bodyText: Delaware's fire code is the State Fire Prevention Regulations, adopted by the State Fire Prevention Commission based on nationally recognized fire safety standards; they have the force of law statewide, and stricter local rules apply where they exist (Wilmington, Newark, Dover and New Castle have their own assistant fire marshals). New requirements generally do not apply to existing installations unless the Commission finds them hazardous. For rentals, the code governs things like smoke detector installation and, in buildings for more than two families, testing of fire and smoke dampers in mechanical rooms and common areas; the State Housing Code also requires clear exits, working exit signs and maintained fire escapes and suppression systems. Check the current Regulations for the code editions in force.

title: Fire sprinklers: no retrofit duty for rentals; maintain existing systems
bodyText: Delaware does not require you to add sprinklers to an existing rental building; the only statewide retrofit mandate covered school and college dormitories. Sprinkler requirements for new or substantially renovated multi-family buildings come from the State Fire Prevention Regulations and local building codes. If your property has a sprinkler or other fire suppression system, you must keep it in good working order, with sprinkler heads clean, unpainted and undamaged.

title: Foreign ownership or leasing: no Delaware restriction
bodyText: Delaware does not restrict foreign nationals, foreign companies or foreign governments from owning or leasing real property, and has no foreign-adversary land law. State law expressly lets aliens acquire, hold and dispose of property in Delaware just like citizens, so you may rent to or from foreign nationals on the same terms as anyone else (and national origin is a protected class under fair housing law). Federal sanctions and national-security review rules can still apply in unusual cases.

title: Outside safety standards: mostly current editions, not frozen
bodyText: Most Delaware safety rules that affect rentals either state their requirements directly (the State Housing Code's space, heat and maintenance standards) or follow current nationally recognized standards as the State Fire Prevention Commission and building codes update them, rather than locking in an old edition of an outside code. When a statute points to the fire regulations or building code, check the edition currently adopted by the State Fire Prevention Regulations and your county or city, because that is what inspectors apply.

title: Government fines: no pass-through of your own violations
bodyText: Delaware has no statute aimed at passing government fines to tenants, but the general rules settle it: your lease may not make the tenant indemnify you for liability the law puts on you, so you cannot shift fines for your own code violations (for example, failing to maintain the building) to the tenant, and trying to enforce such a clause knowingly can cost you 3 months' rent. If the tenant caused the violation (for example, trash or damage the tenant created), the tenant breached its own duty to obey codes, and you may fix the problem and bill the tenant the actual, reasonable cost. Some code fines are issued directly to occupants. Write any fine clause narrowly: only fines resulting from the tenant's, household's or guests' conduct.

title: Habitability cannot be waived; what a separate writing may shift
bodyText: Your lease cannot waive Delaware's habitability requirements: at all times you must keep the unit code-compliant, safe and fit, keep common areas clean, make repairs and keep supplied facilities working, and the heating system must be able to keep living rooms and bathrooms at 65 degrees. You may make the tenant responsible for paying for heat, water or electricity if the lease says so, and you may have the tenant do specific repair or maintenance work only through a separate, conspicuous written agreement, for real consideration or a rent reduction, for work that mainly benefits the unit and is not needed to fix a code violation, and never as a condition of renting. Delaware has no procedure for a tenant to accept substandard conditions in exchange for lower rent.

title: Immigration status: no Delaware rule; avoid national-origin discrimination
bodyText: Delaware has no law that stops you from asking about immigration status, and none that forbids renting to undocumented immigrants. But national origin is a protected class: asking only some applicants about citizenship, or treating applicants differently because of where they or their families come from, can be unlawful discrimination. If you screen for identity or lawful income, apply the same documentation rules to everyone and accept a range of documents. Large rental operators covered by Delaware's privacy law (those that handled personal data of at least 35,000 consumers in the prior year, dropping to 10,000 on January 1, 2027) must treat citizenship and immigration status as sensitive data.

title: Jury trial waivers: unenforceable in Delaware residential leases
bodyText: Do not put a jury-trial waiver in a Delaware residential lease. Either side in an eviction (summary possession) case may demand a 6-person jury: the landlord when filing, the tenant within 10 days after being served. That right is part of the Landlord-Tenant Code, and a lease term making the tenant give up rights under the Code is unenforceable; knowingly trying to enforce it can cost you 3 months' rent. Delaware's Constitution also preserves jury trial as it historically existed.

title: Knowingly enforcing a prohibited term: 3 months' rent
bodyText: If you knowingly try to enforce a lease clause that Delaware prohibits (a waiver of the tenant's rights under the Landlord-Tenant Code, a confession of judgment, a clause excusing your legal liability or making the tenant indemnify you for it, or a cat-declawing requirement), the tenant can sue you for 3 months' rent plus court costs. Merely having such a clause in an old form makes it unenforceable but does not by itself trigger the penalty; trying to use it does. Other unenforceable terms, such as attorney's-fee clauses, carry no automatic penalty, but they are still void. Strip prohibited terms from your forms rather than relying on a severability clause.

title: What a Delaware lease must contain, and what it must say to be used
bodyText: Delaware has no checklist of required lease terms, but a written lease must prominently state the names and business addresses of the owners (or their resident agents) and anyone acting as landlord, and, if you condition deposit return on returning keys, a clear key-return procedure. For pre-1978 units, lead certification disclosures and an acknowledgment of lead materials will be required once Delaware's lead law takes effect (by March 1, 2028). Several rights exist only if the lease spells them out: late fees (up to 5 percent of monthly rent, not charged within 5 days of the due date, counted without intermediate weekends and legal holidays), separate utility charges, required notice of extended absences, deposit increases with rent, the services you provide, limits on assignment and subletting, and any agreed changes to eviction grounds. A tenant repair agreement and a waiver of showing notice must be in separate signed documents, not the lease. Oral leases cannot run more than a year, and you must give the tenant a free copy of the signed lease.

title: The Landlord-Tenant Code cannot be waived except where it says so
bodyText: Delaware treats the entire Landlord-Tenant Code as protection the tenant cannot sign away. A lease term that conflicts with the Code is unenforceable unless the Code itself allows the parties to agree otherwise, and a clause making the tenant waive Code rights or remedies is prohibited (knowingly enforcing it costs 3 months' rent). The Code allows agreement only on specific points, such as rent timing, late fees, utilities and services, deposit increases, subletting and assignment, notice of extended absences, use of the unit, and some eviction grounds; tenant repair duties and showing-notice waivers need separate signed documents. Everything else in the Code applies regardless of what the lease says.

title: Plain language: Delaware consumer-contract rules apply to leases
bodyText: Delaware's consumer-contract law applies to residential leases whose total rent over the term is $50,000 or less (for example, a one-year lease up to about $4,166 a month). Knowingly or recklessly using unintelligible words or sentences that obscure the lease's terms, or leaving out disclosures the law requires, is a deceptive practice treated as consumer fraud, which tenants can sue over. Courts look at confusing cross-references, overly long or complex sentences, double negatives and exceptions to exceptions, illogical order, legalese, and whether tenant protections and restrictions on the tenant are as prominent as the main terms. Write the lease in plain, well-organized language even for higher-rent leases.

title: Pools: no lease notice or barrier statute; health rules may apply
bodyText: Delaware has no statute requiring you to fence a rental pool or give tenants a pool safety notice. If your apartment or residential community has a pool, the Division of Public Health's swimming pool sanitation rules may apply, but the state may not require a lifeguard if the pool is not open to the general public. Pool fences and barriers are set by building codes and local ordinances, so check yours. If you provide a pool, keep it in good working order; any pool fee must be an optional fee for the service actually provided.

title: Prohibited and capped lease terms in Delaware
bodyText: Delaware bars these lease terms: any waiver of the tenant's rights under the Landlord-Tenant Code; confession of judgment; any clause excusing or limiting your legal liability or making the tenant indemnify you for it; requiring a cat to be declawed; attorney's-fee clauses; nonrefundable fees as a condition of renting (other than optional service fees such as a pool fee); 'assurance money' (any application-stage payment other than an application fee, security deposit, surety bond fee or premium, pet deposit, or a deposit reserving the unit for a time certain) and screening charges above their actual cost; application fees above the greater of 10 percent of monthly rent or $50; deposits above the legal caps; requiring a surety bond instead of a deposit; late fees above 5 percent or charged within 5 days of the due date; making tenants open utility accounts or pay separate utility charges without separate meters; requiring keys back before the lease ends; entry on less than 48 hours' notice (except emergencies, tenant-requested repairs, or a separately signed showing waiver); making tenant repair work a condition of the lease; landlord liens or distress on the tenant's belongings; lockouts; and discriminatory terms. Knowingly enforcing the first four costs 3 months' rent. Any other term that conflicts with the Code is unenforceable, while the rest of the lease survives.

title: Applicant questions: disability inquiries barred; avoid protected-class questions
bodyText: Delaware specifically forbids asking applicants (or anyone who will live with them) whether they have a disability or about the nature or severity of a disability. You may ask every applicant questions about their ability to meet the tenancy's requirements, whether they qualify for housing or a priority reserved for people with disabilities, and whether they currently use illegal drugs. Delaware has no separate rule against asking about other protected traits, but any application question or statement that suggests a preference based on race, religion, national origin, familial status, source of income, sexual orientation, gender identity, military status or another protected class is itself unlawful, and the answers can be evidence of discrimination. Keep applications limited to rental qualifications.

title: Sex offender residence: 500-foot school rule binds the offender
bodyText: In Delaware it is the offender's crime, not yours, if a registered sex offender lives within 500 feet of a school, and towns may not impose stricter residency limits. No state law makes it unlawful for you to rent to a sex offender, fines you for doing so, or limits how many offenders may live together. If a prospective tenant is a registered sex offender and the unit is within 500 feet of a school, the tenant cannot lawfully live there, which you may take into account. Apply any criminal-history screening policy consistently to all applicants.

title: Single-family zones: no state rental limit; check local zoning
bodyText: Delaware state law does not limit renting out a home in a single-family zone or require the owner to live on the property. Any such limits come from your county or city zoning and rental-licensing rules, or from a homeowners' association's declaration, so check those before renting.

title: Steam radiator covers: no Delaware requirement
bodyText: Delaware does not require radiator covers, a radiator-cover lease rider, or an annual radiator notice. You must keep heating equipment in safe working order, free from fire, health and accident hazards, and provide a unit that does not endanger tenants. Where very hot exposed steam radiators pose a burn risk (for example to young children), offering covers is a sensible way to meet that duty.

title: Voucher inspections: no refusal right, except PHA processing failures
bodyText: Delaware does not let you refuse a housing voucher tenant just because the program requires an inspection; turning away voucher holders is source-of-income discrimination. There is one narrow exception: Delaware's public housing authorities must follow a standardized process for approving voucher tenancies, and if a housing authority does not follow it, you may deny that application to keep your units from sitting vacant, and that denial cannot be the basis of a discrimination case. A version of the law effective December 31, 2028 makes voucher participation voluntary for landlords. Allow program inspections on reasonable notice as with any other entry.

title: Tenant information: no disclosure statute; data security and breach rules apply
bodyText: Delaware has no statute specifically limiting what you may disclose about tenants or applicants, but if you keep their Social Security, driver's license, passport, taxpayer ID or financial account numbers, you must use reasonable security practices, notify affected residents of a data breach within 60 days (and the Attorney General if more than 500 Delawareans are affected), and offer a year of free credit monitoring if Social Security numbers were exposed. Business entities must shred or securely erase records containing such information when disposing of them. Share tenant information only with the tenant's consent or when legally required, and treat screening reports as confidential.

title: Tenant organizing: protected from retaliation
bodyText: Delaware protects tenants who organize: if you try to evict, raise rent or cut services after a tenant has organized or become an officer of a tenants' organization, it is presumed retaliatory if done within 90 days, and the tenant can recover the greater of 3 months' rent or three times their damages. Delaware has no general statute requiring you to give tenant organizers access to common areas, let them distribute flyers door to door, or provide meeting space (federally assisted housing has its own rules). Reasonable, even-handed rules on common-area use are allowed, but enforcing them selectively against organizers invites a retaliation claim.

title: Tenant screening rules in Delaware
bodyText: Delaware limits screening in these ways: an application fee may not exceed the greater of 10 percent of the monthly rent or $50 (give a receipt and keep fee records for 2 years; overcharging costs double the fee), and you may charge no more than the actual cost of any credit or background check; keep application records for 6 months. Income and credit standards must be commercially reasonable and applied without regard to source of income, so count voucher payments. You may not ask about disabilities. Delaware has no ban on criminal-history screening or required look-back limits, but you should not ask about expunged arrests or convictions, and an applicant need not disclose them; opening or sharing an expunged record without a court order is a crime. An eviction case that a court has shielded is treated as never filed, and the applicant may answer questions about it accordingly. Apply your criteria consistently to everyone.

title: Rent-cap exemption notice: not applicable in Delaware
bodyText: Because Delaware has no statewide rent cap, just-cause eviction law or tenant right to buy for ordinary rentals, there is no exemption notice to put in a Delaware lease. Do not copy California-style exemption language into a Delaware lease.

title: Unconscionability: no Landlord-Tenant Code provision
bodyText: Delaware's Landlord-Tenant Code has no unconscionability provision, and the statutory unconscionability rules for leases apply to leases of goods, not homes. Courts can still decline to enforce an unconscionable lease term under general contract law, and the Code itself does most of the work: any term that conflicts with the Code is unenforceable, specific terms are banned outright, every Code duty and remedy must be exercised in good faith, and lease language that obscures its meaning can be consumer fraud. Keep terms fair, clear and consistent with the Code.

title: Renting to veterans: no state incentive; military status protected
bodyText: Delaware law offers no tax credit or other state incentive for renting to veterans. Veterans are protected by Delaware fair housing law (military status covers active service members, reservists, veterans and their dependents), so you may not refuse to rent to them or charge them more; a veterans' preference allowed by law or a government contract is permitted. HUD-VASH and other veteran rental assistance counts as protected source of income. Service members who enter active duty after signing may end the lease on 30 days' written notice, counted from the first day of the month after the landlord receives it.

title: Water heater temperature: 110 degree minimum, no maximum rule
bodyText: Delaware does not require you to turn down a water heater's temperature before a new tenant moves in. The State Housing Code sets a minimum instead: water heaters must deliver an adequate amount of hot water of at least 110 degrees Fahrenheit at every kitchen sink, bathroom sink, tub, shower and laundry, and must be properly installed and maintained without fire or safety hazards. Setting heaters around 120 degrees at turnover is a common scald-prevention practice that also meets the minimum.

title: Window guards: no Delaware requirement
bodyText: Delaware has no requirement to install window guards or window stops where children live and no window-guard notice for the lease. Windows must open, stay in position with working hardware and be weathertight under the State Housing Code, and your general duty to keep the unit safe applies. Offering window stops or guards to families with young children in upper-floor units is a sensible precaution, as long as they do not block required emergency exits.

title: Why the Library Has No Arbitration Clause for Delaware
bodyText: Delaware's arbitration act makes a written agreement to arbitrate an existing or future dispute valid, enforceable and irrevocable except on grounds that would undo any contract, and a party's right to a lawyer cannot be waived in advance (10 Del. C. §§ 5701, 5707). Unless the agreement names that act, the Court of Chancery applies the Federal Arbitration Act instead (§ 5702(c)). The obstacle is the Landlord-Tenant Code. A lease may not have the tenant waive or forgo rights or remedies under the Code, and a lease term that conflicts with the Code is unenforceable unless the Code allows it (25 Del. C. §§ 5101(a), 5301(a)(1)). No Delaware statute says whether sending a tenant's money claims to an arbitrator is such a waiver, and Delaware case law was not reviewed. Guessing wrong is costly: if you try to enforce a lease term you know is prohibited, the tenant can sue you for 3 months' rent plus court costs (§ 5301(b)), and asking a court to send a tenant's claim to arbitration is an attempt to enforce. For that reason this library does not offer an arbitration clause for Delaware. If you want one anyway, have a Delaware lawyer draft it, and keep summary possession in the Justice of the Peace Court.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Delaware follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (6 Del. C. § 3-311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (6 Del. C. § 1-308(b)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Delaware's landlord-tenant law imposes a duty of good faith: every duty under the Code, and every act that must be done before using a right or remedy under it, carries an obligation of good faith in its performance or enforcement (25 Del. C. § 5104). That binds you and the tenant alike. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.

title: Carpet Cleaning at Move-Out
bodyText: No Delaware statute lets you require professional carpet cleaning at move-out, and none sets an age or condition test for carpet or paint charges. You may use the security deposit to reimburse actual damage the tenant caused that exceeds normal wear and tear or that cannot be corrected by painting and ordinary cleaning, plus rent owed and certain re-renting costs (25 Del. C. § 5514(c)). So the cost of routine cleaning, including ordinary carpet cleaning after a normal tenancy, cannot come out of the deposit; a carpet stain, burn or pet damage that ordinary cleaning cannot fix can. Within 20 days after the lease ends you must send an itemized list of damages with the estimated repair cost of each, or you are treated as acknowledging that nothing is due (25 Del. C. § 5514(f)). A lease term that conflicts with the Code and is not expressly authorized by it is unenforceable (25 Del. C. § 5101(a)), so the library does not offer a mandatory professional-cleaning clause for Delaware. Record carpet condition at move-in and move-out with dated photos.

title: No Government Approval Needed for a Delaware Lease
bodyText: Delaware has no communal or native land system and no statute that makes a residential lease wait on a government officer's approval before it is valid. The Residential Landlord-Tenant Code governs every rental agreement for a rental unit in the state, written or oral, from when the parties make it (25 Del. C. § 5101(a)). Nothing in Delaware's property title conditions a dwelling lease on approval by a commission or officer or suspends rent or possession pending one. One formality does attach to long leases: a lease of residential property for more than 5 years (counting renewal options) may be unenforceable in court unless it or a memorandum is recorded within 15 days (see the lease recording row). Land held in trust by the federal government for a tribe is governed by federal law, which this library has not reviewed.

title: Hunting on Rented Farmland in Delaware
bodyText: No Delaware statute says whether the landlord or the tenant of rented farmland holds the hunting rights, but Delaware's game laws give the person in possession a real say. It is an offense to enter the lands or waters of another to hunt, trap or fish without first getting permission from the owner or lessee (7 Del. C. § 714). So your farm tenant can lawfully authorize hunting, and so can you. Within 100 yards of an occupied dwelling or farm building, only the owner or occupant, or someone with their permission, may shoot while hunting (7 Del. C. § 723(a)). Residents who own or live on a farm of 20 or more acres, and their immediate family living there, may hunt, fish and trap on the farm without a license (7 Del. C. § 502(b)). A nonresident owner who does not occupy the farm may hunt there license-free only if the farm's occupant gives written permission or a written lease between them allows it (7 Del. C. § 507(a)(2)). The agricultural leases chapter says nothing about hunting. Put hunting, fishing and trapping rights, and who may grant permission, in the lease.

title: Recording a Long Delaware Lease
bodyText: Delaware has no general requirement to record a residential lease, and recording does not change any right under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Code. One rule reaches long leases. A writing that transfers a possessory interest for more than 5 years in a condominium or unit-property unit, or that assigns or transfers a leasehold or possessory interest in residential property under a lease for more than 5 years, is a taxable document under the realty transfer tax, and renewal or extension options are presumed exercised when counting the term (30 Del. C. § 5401(5)(a), (c), (6)). Unless exempt, such a document is not enforceable in any Delaware court unless it, or a memorandum identifying the parties, the premises and the duration including renewals and purchase options, is recorded with the county recorder of deeds within 15 days after the term begins; recording later with the taxes and penalties revives it (25 Del. C. § 158). Ordinary leases of 5 years or less are unaffected. For any residential lease that could run past 5 years with options, get advice on recording and transfer tax before signing.

title: Time Limit to Sue for Rent or Damages: Three Years
bodyText: In Delaware a suit based on a promise, including a suit for unpaid rent or other money owed under a lease, must be brought within 3 years after the claim accrues (10 Del. C. § 8106(a)). The same 3 years applies to an action for trespass or for injury to property caused indirectly, and a suit for waste must be brought within 3 years after the waste is committed (10 Del. C. §§ 8106(a), 8112). If the tenant signs a written acknowledgment of the debt, a suit on that acknowledgment may be brought within 6 years (10 Del. C. § 8109). While a mutual and running account stays open and current, the 3-year period does not begin (10 Del. C. § 8108). The statute does not say whether a partial payment alone restarts the period, and the 3-year rule's exception for a debt evidenced by an instrument under seal is not applied here; both are case law this library has not reviewed. The Landlord-Tenant Code sets no separate deadline for your claim. Practical guidance: sue for any balance beyond the deposit well within 3 years of move-out.

title: No Special District Statement Required in a Delaware Lease
bodyText: No Delaware statute requires a residential lease to state that the property lies in a special taxing, utility or improvement district, or to have the tenant acknowledge a district's charges, plans or restrictions. The Residential Landlord-Tenant Code's lease disclosures concern the owner and agent, the deposit account, fees and other Code-required items, not districts (the disclosure and fee rows cover them). A lease term the Code does not expressly authorize is unenforceable only if it conflicts with the Code (25 Del. C. § 5101(a)), so a plain informational statement about a district is allowed but not required. If a district or municipality bills for water, sewer or trash, say in the lease who pays it.

title: Renting to Students in Delaware
bodyText: Delaware has no student-housing license, disclosure or lease rule. Its student-housing rule is an exclusion from the Residential Landlord-Tenant Code. Until the change takes effect in March 2027, the Code does not govern residence at a public or private institution merely incidental to educational or similar services, including student housing provided by a college or school, unless the arrangement was created solely to avoid the Code (25 Del. C. § 5102(1) [effective until Mar. 9, 2027]). From March 8, 2027 (the Code page and the bill page now say March 9; this library follows Taylor's decision to comply from March 8), the exclusion reaches residence incidental to student housing provided and operated by a school, including a college (25 Del. C. § 5102(1)(b) [effective Mar. 9, 2027]). Housing for a member of a fraternal organization in a structure operated for the organization is excluded under both versions (25 Del. C. § 5102(2)). So a dormitory a college runs is outside the Code, but a privately owned house or apartment rented to students is an ordinary tenancy covered by every rule in this library. A building a school leases from you but does not operate is likely covered after March 2027; how far the earlier wording reaches is case law this library has not reviewed.

title: Banning a Non-Tenant from the Property
bodyText: Delaware's criminal trespass law lets you keep a non-tenant off the parts of the property you control. A person commits criminal trespass by knowingly entering or remaining unlawfully on real property (third degree, a violation), in a fenced or enclosed building or property (second degree, an unclassified misdemeanor), or in a dwelling (first degree, a class A misdemeanor) (11 Del. C. §§ 821, 822, 823). A person enters or remains unlawfully when not licensed or privileged to be there (11 Del. C. § 829(e)). Premises that appear open to the public, such as a leasing office or an open parking lot, carry a license to be there unless the person defies a lawful order not to enter or remain, personally communicated by the owner or another authorized person (11 Del. C. § 829(e)). So give the person a written no-trespass notice, deliver it in person where you can, keep a copy and tell the police. A person a tenant invites into the tenant's own unit is there with the tenant's license, so enforce a ban there through the lease, not trespass. A tenant or anyone else with a claim to possession is removed only through summary possession.

title: Leasing as a Life Tenant (No Usufruct in Delaware)
bodyText: Usufruct is a civil-law interest that Delaware property law does not use, so the civil-law rules on leases by a usufructuary don't apply. The closest Delaware interest is a life estate. No Delaware statute says what happens to a residential lease signed by a life tenant when the life estate ends; that is case law this library has not reviewed. Delaware's statutes on life tenants deal only with their duties to the remainder: a tenant for life or years who commits waste without special written license is liable in an action for waste (25 Del. C. § 901), and a life tenant's warranty does not bar the life tenant's own title (25 Del. C. § 303). The cautious course if you lease as a life tenant: say so in the lease, keep the term short or month-to-month, and have the remainder owners sign the lease or agree in writing that it will continue if your life estate ends first.
